0.name: Full Stack developer
0.desc: Master both frontend and backend development by building complete, functional web applications from scratch. Learn how to design responsive user interfaces, develop secure server-side logic, manage databases, build APIs, and deploy production-ready applications.

subTopic.name: What full-stack development means
subTopic.notes:
Full-stack development means building BOTH sides of a web application: the part users see (frontend) and the part that works behind the scenes (backend + database).

Think of a restaurant:
- Frontend = the dining area, menu and table (what the customer sees)
- Backend = the kitchen (where the work happens)
- Database = the storeroom (where ingredients/data are kept)

A full-stack developer can work on all three.

Real-world example: On Zomato, the restaurant list you scroll is the frontend. The server that finds restaurants near you is the backend. The saved restaurant data and your order history live in the database.

Remember: Full-stack = Frontend + Backend + Database.

subTopic.name: Frontend, backend, and database responsibilities
subTopic.notes:
Each part has its own job:

1. Frontend (HTML, CSS, JavaScript, React)
- Shows the UI, takes user input, handles clicks and forms.

2. Backend (Node.js, Express, Python, Java)
- Applies business logic, checks login, talks to the database, sends data back.

3. Database (MongoDB, MySQL, PostgreSQL)
- Stores data permanently: users, products, orders.

Real-world example: Login on a website.
- Frontend: you type email and password and press Login.
- Backend: checks if the details are valid.
- Database: holds the saved user record the backend compares with.

Small code idea:
// Frontend
fetch('/api/login', { method: 'POST', body: JSON.stringify({ email, password }) });

// Backend (Express)
app.post('/api/login', (req, res) => { /* check user in DB */ });

Rule: The frontend never talks to the database directly. It always goes through the backend.

subTopic.name: How browsers, servers, and databases work together
subTopic.notes:
Three players work together every time you use a website:

- Browser: asks for things (Chrome, Edge).
- Server: receives the ask, thinks, and replies.
- Database: gives the server the stored data it needs.

Flow:
Browser -> Server -> Database -> Server -> Browser

Real-world example: Opening your Instagram profile.
1. Browser asks the server: 'Give me this user's profile.'
2. Server asks the database for that user's name, photo and posts.
3. Database returns the data.
4. Server packs it as JSON and sends it to the browser.
5. Browser shows it on screen.

Example response from the server:
{ "name": "Anshika", "posts": 12 }

Remember: The browser only displays. The server decides. The database remembers.

subTopic.name: Client-server architecture
Request-response lifecycle
subTopic.notes:
Every action on the web follows this cycle: a REQUEST goes out, a RESPONSE comes back.

A request has:
- URL (where), Method (what to do: GET, POST, PUT, DELETE), Headers, and sometimes a Body (data).

A response has:
- Status code (200 OK, 404 Not Found, 500 Server Error), Headers, and a Body (data/HTML).

Steps:
1. User clicks or types.
2. Browser sends the request.
3. Server processes it (may query the database).
4. Server sends the response.
5. Browser shows the result.

Real-world example: Searching 'shoes' on Amazon.
Request: GET /products?search=shoes
Response: 200 OK + a list of shoes in JSON.

Code:
fetch('/products?search=shoes')
  .then(res => res.json())
  .then(data => console.log(data));

Tip: Open the browser DevTools -> Network tab to see real requests and responses.

subTopic.name: Static websites vs dynamic applications
subTopic.notes:
Static website:
- Same content for every visitor.
- Made of fixed HTML, CSS, JS files.
- Fast and cheap to host.
- Example: a personal portfolio, a college brochure page.

Dynamic application:
- Content changes based on the user, time, or data.
- Needs a backend and usually a database.
- Example: Instagram feed, Swiggy orders, a learning dashboard with your own progress.

Quick comparison:
- Static: no login, no database, same page for all.
- Dynamic: login, database, personalised page.

Real-world example: A restaurant's 'About Us' page is static. Its 'My Orders' page is dynamic because it shows different orders for each customer.

Note: A frontend-only React app can feel dynamic, but it becomes truly dynamic only when it fetches live data from a backend.

subTopic.name: Monolithic vs distributed applications overview
subTopic.notes:
Monolithic application:
- The whole app (UI, logic, database access) is built and deployed as ONE unit.
- Easy to start, easy to test.
- Hard to scale and update when it grows very big.

Distributed application (for example microservices):
- The app is split into small independent services (users, payments, orders) that talk to each other over the network.
- Each part can be scaled and updated separately.
- More complex to manage.

Real-world example:
- Monolith = one big shop where billing, stock and delivery are all in one room. If one part breaks, everything stops.
- Distributed = a mall with many separate shops. If one shop closes, the rest still work.

Simple idea in code:
// Monolith
app.use('/users', userRoutes);
app.use('/orders', orderRoutes);   // all in one project

// Distributed
users-service  -> runs on its own server
orders-service -> runs on its own server

Advice: Beginners and small projects should start with a monolith. Move to distributed only when the app really needs it.

subTopic.name: Common full-stack architectures
subTopic.notes:
A full-stack architecture (stack) is the set of technologies used together.

Popular ones:
1. MERN = MongoDB + Express + React + Node.js
2. MEAN = MongoDB + Express + Angular + Node.js
3. LAMP = Linux + Apache + MySQL + PHP
4. Next.js + Node/API + PostgreSQL (modern popular choice)

MERN flow:
React (UI) -> Express/Node (API) -> MongoDB (data)

Why MERN is loved by students: everything uses JavaScript, so you learn one language for the whole app.

Real-world example: A job portal.
- React shows job listings and the apply form.
- Express API handles /jobs and /apply.
- MongoDB stores users, jobs and applications.

Folder idea:
project/
  client/   (React)
  server/   (Node + Express)

Tip: Don't chase every stack. Master one (like MERN) first, then others become easy.

subTopic.name: Full-stack developer responsibilities
subTopic.notes:
A full-stack developer is expected to:

- Build responsive UI (HTML, CSS, JavaScript, React).
- Create APIs and server logic (Node.js, Express).
- Design and manage databases (MongoDB, SQL).
- Handle authentication and security (login, password hashing, protecting routes).
- Connect frontend with backend (fetch/axios).
- Test, debug and fix bugs.
- Use Git/GitHub for version control.
- Deploy the app (Vercel, Render, etc.).

Real-world example: Your task is 'Add a Wishlist feature'.
- Frontend: add a heart button and wishlist page.
- Backend: create POST /wishlist and GET /wishlist APIs.
- Database: add a wishlist field for each user.
- Finally: test it and deploy.

Small code idea (backend):
app.post('/wishlist', async (req, res) => {
  // save item in the user's wishlist
  res.status(201).json({ message: 'Added to wishlist' });
});

Remember: Being full-stack does not mean knowing everything. It means you can take a feature from idea to live.

subTopic.name: Planning a full-stack learning path
subTopic.notes:
Learn in the right order so you don't feel lost.

Suggested path:
1. Basics: HTML, CSS, JavaScript
2. Frontend: React (components, state, props, routing)
3. Backend: Node.js + Express (APIs, middleware)
4. Database: MongoDB (or SQL)
5. Connect all: build a MERN app with login
6. Tools: Git, GitHub, Postman
7. Deploy: Vercel/Netlify (frontend), Render (backend)

How to study:
- Learn a small concept, then build something with it the same day.
- Do one project per stage.
- Tick off topics and revise weekly.

Real-world example project ladder:
- Stage 1: Portfolio website
- Stage 2: Todo app in React
- Stage 3: Notes API with Express
- Stage 4: Full MERN expense tracker with login

Teacher's tip: Consistency beats speed. Even 1-2 focused hours a day, with a project at each step, will make you job-ready.

subTopic.name: How the internet works
subTopic.notes:
### How the internet works

**Simple idea:** The internet is a giant network of connected computers. Your device (the client) asks for something, and another computer (the server) sends it back.

**Think of it like the postal system:** You write a letter (request), the post office routes it through many sorting centers (routers), it reaches the right house (server), and a reply comes back the same way.

**Steps when you open a website:**
1. You type a URL in the browser.
2. DNS finds the server's IP address.
3. Your request travels through your ISP and many routers.
4. The server processes it and sends back HTML, CSS and JS.
5. Your browser shows the page.

**Real-world example:** When you open Skillora, your laptop sends a request to Skillora's server, and the server sends back the dashboard files.

**Remember:** Client asks, server answers. Data travels in small pieces called packets.

subTopic.name: IP addresses and ports
subTopic.notes:
### IP addresses and ports

**IP address** = the address of a computer on a network, like a building's street address.
**Port** = a specific door in that building. One computer can run many services, and each uses a different port.

```
192.168.1.5      -> IPv4 address
127.0.0.1        -> localhost (your own computer)
http://localhost:5173  -> your React (Vite) app on port 5173
```

**Common ports:**
- 80 = HTTP
- 443 = HTTPS
- 3000 / 5173 = dev servers
- 27017 = MongoDB

**Real-world example:** When you run `npm run dev`, your computer is the building (localhost) and your React app is in room 5173. Your backend might be in room 5000 of the same building.

**Remember:** IP finds the computer, port finds the app inside it.

subTopic.name: DNS and domain names
subTopic.notes:
### DNS and domain names

**Problem:** Humans remember names (skillora.com), but computers need IP addresses.
**DNS (Domain Name System)** is the internet's phonebook. It converts a domain name into an IP address.

**How a lookup works:**
1. The browser checks its own cache.
2. If not found, it asks the DNS resolver (usually your ISP's).
3. The resolver finds the IP and returns it.
4. The browser connects to that IP.

```
nslookup google.com
```
This command shows the IP address of google.com.

**Real-world example:** You save your friend's name in your contacts, not their number. DNS does the same for websites.

**Remember:** A domain has parts: `www` (subdomain) + `skillora` (name) + `.com` (TLD). DNS records have a TTL, which says how long the answer can be cached.

subTopic.name: URLs and URL anatomy
subTopic.notes:
### URLs and URL anatomy

**URL** = the full address of a resource on the web.

```
https://www.skillora.com:443/courses/react?level=beginner#hooks
```

| Part | Example | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| Protocol | https | How to talk to the server |
| Domain | www.skillora.com | Which server |
| Port | 443 | Which door (usually hidden) |
| Path | /courses/react | Which page or resource |
| Query | ?level=beginner | Extra info (key=value) |
| Hash | #hooks | Jump to a section on the page |

**In JavaScript:**
```js
const url = new URL('https://skillora.com/courses?level=beginner');
console.log(url.pathname);                 // /courses
console.log(url.searchParams.get('level')); // beginner
```

**Real-world example:** On Skillora, `/courses/react?level=beginner` shows the React course, filtered for beginners.

subTopic.name: HTTP and HTTPS
subTopic.notes:
### HTTP and HTTPS

**HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol)** is the set of rules a browser and a server use to talk to each other.
**HTTPS** is HTTP plus encryption (the S means Secure).

**Difference:**
- HTTP: data is sent as plain text. Anyone on the network can read it.
- HTTPS: data is encrypted. Only you and the server can read it.

**Real-world example:** Sending a postcard is HTTP, because everyone who handles it can read it. Sending a sealed, locked box is HTTPS. When you enter a password on a login page, it must be HTTPS.

**Good to know:**
- HTTP is stateless. The server does not remember you between requests (that is why cookies exist).
- Always use HTTPS in production. Browsers show a padlock for it.
- HTTP uses port 80 and HTTPS uses port 443.

subTopic.name: HTTP requests and responses
subTopic.notes:
### HTTP requests and responses

Every interaction has two parts: the client sends a **request** and the server sends back a **response**.

**Request has:** method, URL, headers, optional body.
**Response has:** status code, headers, body (the data).

```
GET /api/courses HTTP/1.1
Host: skillora.com
Accept: application/json
```

```
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json

[{"id": 0, "name": "Full Stack"}]
```

**In React:**
```js
const res = await fetch('/api/courses');
const data = await res.json();
```

**Real-world example:** It is like ordering at a restaurant. The request is your order and the response is your food (or a message that the dish is not available).

**Tip:** Open the browser DevTools, go to the Network tab, and reload a page to see real requests and responses.

subTopic.name: HTTP methods and status codes
subTopic.notes:
### HTTP methods and status codes

**Methods tell the server what you want to do:**
- GET = read data
- POST = create new data
- PUT = replace data
- PATCH = update part of the data
- DELETE = remove data

**Status codes tell you what happened:**
- 2xx = success (200 OK, 201 Created)
- 3xx = redirect (301 Moved)
- 4xx = your mistake (400 Bad Request, 401 Unauthorized, 403 Forbidden, 404 Not Found)
- 5xx = server's mistake (500 Internal Server Error)

```js
const res = await fetch('/api/projects/3', { method: 'DELETE' });
if (res.status === 404) console.log('Project not found');
```

**Real-world example:** On Skillora, ticking a subtopic can be a PATCH request. If the subtopic id does not exist, the server replies 404. If you are logged out, it replies 401.

**Memory trick:** 4xx = client messed up, 5xx = server messed up.

subTopic.name: Headers, cookies, and request bodies
subTopic.notes:
### Headers, cookies, and request bodies

**Headers** = extra information about the request or response (like the label on a parcel).
**Body** = the actual data you send (like the content inside the parcel).
**Cookies** = small data the server stores in your browser so it can recognize you next time.

```js
await fetch('/api/login', {
  method: 'POST',
  headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
  body: JSON.stringify({ email: 'a@b.com', password: '1234' }),
  credentials: 'include' // send cookies too
});
```

**Useful headers:**
- Content-Type: format of the body
- Authorization: Bearer <token> (proves who you are)
- Set-Cookie: server asks the browser to save a cookie

**Real-world example:** After you log in, the server sends a cookie. Every next request automatically carries it, so you stay logged in on your dashboard.

**Remember:** GET requests usually have no body. POST, PUT and PATCH do.

subTopic.name: TLS and certificates overview
subTopic.notes:
### TLS and certificates overview

**TLS (Transport Layer Security)** is the technology that makes HTTPS secure. It encrypts data between browser and server.

**Simple handshake:**
1. The browser says hello and asks the server to prove its identity.
2. The server sends its **certificate**.
3. The browser checks that a trusted authority (CA) signed it.
4. Both agree on a secret key.
5. All further data is encrypted with that key.

**Certificate** = a digital ID card for a website. It says 'this server really owns skillora.com'.

**Real-world example:** It is like a shopkeeper showing a government-verified license before you hand over money. If the license is fake or expired, the browser shows a warning like 'Your connection is not private'.

**Good to know:** Free certificates are available from Let's Encrypt. Hosting platforms like Vercel and Netlify set up HTTPS automatically.

subTopic.name: Same-origin policy
subTopic.notes:
### Same-origin policy

**Origin** = protocol + domain + port.

```
https://skillora.com:443   -> origin A
https://skillora.com/page  -> same origin as A
http://skillora.com        -> different (protocol)
https://api.skillora.com   -> different (domain)
https://skillora.com:3000  -> different (port)
```

**Rule:** A web page can freely read data only from its own origin. Scripts from one origin cannot read data from another origin.

**Why it exists:** Imagine you are logged in to your bank in one tab, and a shady site in another tab. Without this rule, the shady site could read your bank data.

**Real-world example:** Your React app at localhost:5173 calling your backend at localhost:5000 is a different origin (different port), so the browser blocks it unless the backend allows it. That leads to CORS, our next topic.

**Remember:** The browser enforces this rule, not the server.

subTopic.name: CORS fundamentals
subTopic.notes:
### CORS fundamentals

**CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing)** is how a server tells the browser: 'It is okay, this other origin is allowed to read my data.'

**The error you will see:**
`Access to fetch at 'http://localhost:5000' from origin 'http://localhost:5173' has been blocked by CORS policy`

**How it works:**
1. For some requests, the browser first sends a **preflight** request (method OPTIONS).
2. The server replies with the header `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`.
3. If the origin is allowed, the browser sends the real request.

**Fix in Express:**
```js
const cors = require('cors');
app.use(cors({ origin: 'http://localhost:5173' }));
```

**Real-world example:** Your Skillora frontend runs on Vercel and your API runs on another domain. You must allow the frontend's origin on the API, or the dashboard will not load data.

**Remember:** CORS is fixed on the server side, not in React. Avoid `origin: '*'` for APIs that use cookies or logins.

subTopic.name: Browser rendering pipeline
subTopic.notes:
### Browser rendering pipeline

**Question:** How does the browser turn code into a visible page?

**Steps:**
1. **Parse HTML** to build the **DOM** (tree of elements).
2. **Parse CSS** to build the **CSSOM** (tree of styles).
3. Combine both into the **Render Tree** (only visible elements).
4. **Layout:** calculate size and position of each element.
5. **Paint:** fill in colors, text, images.
6. **Composite:** layers are combined and shown on screen.

**Why it matters for you:**
- Changing `width`, `height` or `margin` triggers layout again (expensive).
- Changing `transform` or `opacity` is cheaper and smooth for animations.
- A `<script>` without `defer` can block HTML parsing.

```html
<script src='app.js' defer></script>
```

**Real-world example:** It is like building a house. The DOM is the blueprint, the CSSOM is the paint and style plan, layout is placing the walls, and paint is decorating.

subTopic.name: Caching basics
subTopic.notes:
### Caching basics

**Cache** = saving a copy of data so you do not have to fetch it again. It makes websites faster and saves data.

**Where caching happens:** browser cache, CDN, server, and even in your React state.

**Controlled by headers:**
```
Cache-Control: max-age=31536000   -> keep for 1 year
Cache-Control: no-store           -> never save (sensitive data)
ETag: abc123                      -> version tag to check if the file changed
```

**Real-world example:** You keep your favorite snacks at home instead of going to the market every time. A site's logo and CSS file are stored in your browser, so the second visit loads much faster.

**Cache busting:** Build tools rename files like `app.8f3a2c.js`. When the code changes, the name changes, so users get the new version.

**Remember:** Cache static files (images, CSS, JS) for long. Do not cache private data like user profiles.

subTopic.name: CDN fundamentals
subTopic.notes:
### CDN fundamentals

**CDN (Content Delivery Network)** = many servers placed around the world that store copies of your website's files and serve users from the nearest one.

**Problem:** If your server is in the USA and a student in Delhi opens your site, data travels a long way, so it feels slow.
**Solution:** A CDN keeps a copy in a nearby location, for example Mumbai, so it loads faster.

**Benefits:**
- Faster loading (less distance)
- Handles high traffic
- Extra protection against attacks

```html
<script src='https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/axios/dist/axios.min.js'></script>
```

**Real-world example:** Think of a pizza brand with outlets in every city. You do not wait for delivery from the main kitchen; the nearest outlet serves you. Vercel, Netlify, Cloudflare and AWS CloudFront all work this way.

**Remember:** CDNs are best for static files like images, CSS and JS.

subTopic.name: Setting up VS Code
subTopic.notes:
WHAT IT IS:
VS Code is a free code editor where you will write all your code. Think of it as your digital notebook for programming.

SETUP STEPS:
1. Download from code.visualstudio.com and install it.
2. Open the Extensions tab (Ctrl+Shift+X).
3. Install: Prettier, ESLint, ES7 React Snippets, GitLens.
4. Turn on Format On Save in Settings.

USEFUL SHORTCUTS:
Ctrl+P  -> open any file quickly
Ctrl+Shift+P -> command palette
Ctrl+` -> open terminal
Alt+Up/Down -> move a line

REAL-WORLD SCENARIO:
A company gives you a laptop on day one. The first thing your team lead says is: 'Install VS Code with our extensions.' When everyone uses the same setup, the code looks the same and fewer mistakes happen.

TEACHER TIP:
Do not install 50 extensions. Start with 4 or 5 and add more only when you need them.

subTopic.name: Using the terminal and shell
subTopic.notes:
WHAT IT IS:
The terminal is a text window where you give commands to your computer. The shell (bash, zsh, PowerShell) is the program that understands those commands.

MOST USED COMMANDS:
pwd            -> show current folder
ls (or dir)    -> list files
cd folder-name -> go inside a folder
cd ..          -> go back one folder
mkdir my-app   -> create a folder
touch app.js   -> create a file
rm app.js      -> delete a file
clear          -> clean the screen

EXAMPLE:
mkdir skillora
cd skillora
touch index.html

REAL-WORLD SCENARIO:
Your server on the internet has no mouse or screen. You control it only by typing commands. Developers who are comfortable with the terminal can fix problems in minutes.

TEACHER TIP:
Press the Tab key to auto-complete file names and Up Arrow to repeat your last command. It saves a lot of typing.

subTopic.name: Installing Node.js and npm
subTopic.notes:
WHAT IT IS:
Node.js lets you run JavaScript outside the browser. npm (Node Package Manager) comes with Node and lets you download ready-made code (packages) made by other developers.

INSTALL:
Download the LTS version from nodejs.org, then check:
node -v
npm -v

BASIC COMMANDS:
npm init -y            -> create package.json
npm install axios      -> add a package
npm install -D eslint  -> add a dev-only package
npm run dev            -> run a script from package.json

REAL-WORLD SCENARIO:
You need a date picker in your app. Instead of building it for 3 days, you run 'npm install react-datepicker' and use it in 5 minutes.

TEACHER TIP:
Always choose the LTS (Long Term Support) version. It is the stable one. Never edit the node_modules folder by hand.

subTopic.name: Git configuration
subTopic.notes:
WHAT IT IS:
Git tracks every change in your code, like a save history. Before using it, you tell Git who you are so every change has your name on it.

FIRST-TIME SETUP:
git config --global user.name 'Anshika Verma'
git config --global user.email 'you@example.com'
git config --global init.defaultBranch main
git config --list

DAILY COMMANDS:
git init            -> start tracking a folder
git status          -> see what changed
git add .           -> select all changes
git commit -m 'Add login page' -> save a snapshot

REAL-WORLD SCENARIO:
You broke the app at 11 PM. With Git you run 'git log' and go back to yesterday's working version instead of panicking.

TEACHER TIP:
Write clear commit messages. 'Fix navbar bug' is useful, 'changes' is not. Use the same email that you use on GitHub.

subTopic.name: GitHub repositories
subTopic.notes:
WHAT IT IS:
GitHub is a website that stores your Git projects online. A repository (repo) is one project folder on GitHub. It works as a backup, a portfolio, and a way to work in a team.

PUSH YOUR FIRST PROJECT:
git init
git add .
git commit -m 'First commit'
git branch -M main
git remote add origin https://github.com/username/skillora.git
git push -u origin main

TEAM WORKFLOW:
git clone <url>              -> download a repo
git checkout -b feature/login -> make a new branch
git pull                     -> get latest changes
Then open a Pull Request on GitHub for review.

REAL-WORLD SCENARIO:
A recruiter opens your GitHub link. Clean repos with a good README show them you can build real projects.

TEACHER TIP:
Always write a README with what the project does, a screenshot, and how to run it. Never push passwords or API keys.

subTopic.name: Project folder structure
subTopic.notes:
WHAT IT IS:
A folder structure is how you organize files in your project. Good organization means you can find anything in seconds.

TYPICAL REACT PROJECT:
my-app/
  public/          -> images, favicon
  src/
    components/    -> reusable UI (Navbar, Card)
    pages/         -> full screens (Dashboard, Project)
    context/       -> shared state (UserContext)
    data/          -> JSON files
    hooks/         -> custom hooks
    utils/         -> helper functions
    App.jsx
    main.jsx
  .env
  .gitignore
  package.json

NAMING RULES:
- Components: PascalCase (CourseCard.jsx)
- Other files: camelCase (formatDate.js)
- Folders: lowercase

REAL-WORLD SCENARIO:
A new developer joins your team. If the structure is clean, they find the login code in 1 minute. If everything is in one folder, they waste a whole day.

TEACHER TIP:
Group files by purpose. If one folder has more than 10 to 15 files, split it.

subTopic.name: Environment variables and .env files
subTopic.notes:
WHAT IT IS:
Environment variables store secret or changing values (API keys, database URLs) outside your code. They live in a file named .env.

EXAMPLE (.env file):
VITE_API_URL=https://api.example.com
VITE_API_KEY=abc123xyz

USE IT IN VITE + REACT:
const url = import.meta.env.VITE_API_URL;

USE IT IN NODE.JS:
require('dotenv').config();
const port = process.env.PORT;

IMPORTANT:
Add .env to your .gitignore file so it never goes to GitHub:
.env

REAL-WORLD SCENARIO:
A developer once pushed an AWS key to a public repo. Bots found it within minutes and ran up a huge bill. Using .env would have prevented it.

TEACHER TIP:
In Vite, variables must start with VITE_ to be visible in the browser. Remember that anything in frontend code can be seen by users, so keep real secrets on the backend.

subTopic.name: Prettier and ESLint
subTopic.notes:
WHAT IT IS:
Prettier fixes how your code LOOKS (spacing, quotes, line length). ESLint finds MISTAKES and bad practices in your code. Use both together.

INSTALL:
npm install -D prettier eslint

PRETTIER CONFIG (.prettierrc):
{
  "semi": true,
  "singleQuote": true,
  "tabWidth": 2
}

ESLINT CATCHES THINGS LIKE:
const name = 'Anshika';  // 'name' is declared but never used

REAL-WORLD SCENARIO:
In a team of 5, everyone writes in a different style and pull requests become messy. With Prettier on save, all code looks the same, and ESLint stops silly bugs before they reach production.

TEACHER TIP:
Turn on Format On Save in VS Code. Prettier formats, ESLint warns, and you just focus on logic.

subTopic.name: Debugging with browser DevTools
subTopic.notes:
WHAT IT IS:
DevTools is a toolbox built into your browser to inspect and fix your website. Open it with F12 or Ctrl+Shift+I.

IMPORTANT TABS:
- Elements: see and edit HTML/CSS live
- Console: see errors and print values
- Network: check API calls and their status
- Sources: add breakpoints and pause code
- Application: view localStorage and cookies

QUICK DEBUGGING:
console.log('user:', user);
console.table(courses);
debugger; // pauses code here when DevTools is open

REAL-WORLD SCENARIO:
Your button is pushed off the screen on mobile. In Elements you click the button, see a fixed width: 500px in CSS, change it live, and find the fix in 30 seconds. Use the device toolbar to test phone sizes.

TEACHER TIP:
Do not guess. Check the Console for red errors first, then the Network tab for failed requests (status 404 or 500).

subTopic.name: Reading logs and stack traces
subTopic.notes:
WHAT IT IS:
When code crashes, it prints an error message and a stack trace. The stack trace is a list showing the exact path of functions that led to the error.

EXAMPLE:
TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'map')
    at CourseList (CourseList.jsx:12:25)
    at App (App.jsx:8:5)

HOW TO READ IT:
1. Read the first line: it tells the TYPE and the REASON.
2. Look at the first line starting with 'at' that is in YOUR file (CourseList.jsx, line 12).
3. Go to that line and check the variable.

THE FIX HERE:
courses?.map(c => <Card key={c.id} />)
// or set a default: const [courses, setCourses] = useState([]);

REAL-WORLD SCENARIO:
Your app works locally but crashes on the live server. You open the server logs, find the error line, and fix it, instead of guessing.

TEACHER TIP:
Do not be scared of red text. Read it slowly from the top. The error usually tells you exactly what is wrong.

subTopic.name: Documentation and technical research
subTopic.notes:
WHAT IT IS:
Documentation (docs) is the official guide written by the creators of a tool. Technical research is the skill of finding the right answer quickly.

WHERE TO LOOK (in this order):
1. Official docs (react.dev, developer.mozilla.org, tailwindcss.com)
2. GitHub issues and README
3. Stack Overflow
4. Blogs and YouTube

HOW TO SEARCH WELL:
Bad:  'my code is not working'
Good: 'React useState not updating array on push'
Tip: copy the exact error message and search it.

HOW TO READ DOCS:
- Read 'Getting Started' first
- Look at the code example
- Check the API/props table
- Try it in a small test file

REAL-WORLD SCENARIO:
Your manager asks you to add Google login. Nobody on the team has done it. You read the docs, follow the steps, and finish it in a day. Good developers are not people who know everything, they are people who can find things.

TEACHER TIP:
Check the version of the docs. Old tutorials often use outdated methods.

subTopic.name: Managing tasks and issues
subTopic.notes:
WHAT IT IS:
Projects have many small jobs. Task management means writing them down, setting priority, and tracking progress. Tools: GitHub Issues, GitHub Projects, Trello, Jira, Notion.

A GOOD ISSUE HAS:
Title: Navbar menu does not close on mobile
Steps: 1. Open site on phone  2. Tap menu  3. Tap a link
Expected: menu closes
Actual: menu stays open
Labels: bug, frontend, priority-high

BOARD COLUMNS:
To Do -> In Progress -> In Review -> Done

LINK ISSUES TO CODE:
git commit -m 'Fix mobile menu closing, closes #14'
(This automatically closes issue #14 on GitHub.)

REAL-WORLD SCENARIO:
Your team has 20 pending things before launch. With a board, everyone knows who is doing what, and nothing gets forgotten.

TEACHER TIP:
Break big tasks into small ones that take 1 to 2 hours. 'Build the dashboard' is too big. 'Create the course card component' is perfect.

subTopic.name: HTML document structure
subTopic.notes:
Every HTML page follows the same skeleton. Think of it like a house: it needs a foundation and rooms. tells the browser, 'This is modern HTML5.' is the root that wraps everything. holds hidden info (title, meta, CSS links). Users do not see it on the page. holds everything users see: text, images, buttons. Code: My First Page

Hello, World!

Real-world example: When you open Instagram, the logo and posts you see come from the body. The tab title and the icon come from the head. Remember: always add lang='en' and charset='UTF-8'. They help screen readers and make sure text shows correctly.

subTopic.name: Elements, tags, and attributes
subTopic.notes:
An element is a complete building block of a page. It has an opening tag, content, and a closing tag.

Hello

= opening tag, Hello = content,

= closing tag An attribute gives extra information to a tag. It always goes inside the opening tag as name='value'. Open Google Here href and target are attributes. Some tags have no closing tag. They are called void (self-closing) elements:
,
, , . Common attributes: id (unique name), class (group name for CSS), src (file source), href (link), alt (image description). Real-world example: A sign-up form field is . The tag is input, and type, placeholder and required are attributes that tell the browser how it should behave. Tip: id must be unique on a page, but class can be reused many times.

subTopic.name: Headings and paragraphs
subTopic.notes:
Headings give a page its structure. HTML has six levels, from

(most important) to

(least important). Code:

Skillora Learning Path

HTML Basics

Headings and paragraphs

This is a paragraph. Browsers add space before and after it automatically.

Rules to follow: 1. Use only one

per page. It is the main title. 2. Do not skip levels (do not jump from h1 to h4). 3. Do not use headings just to make text big. Use CSS for size. Real-world example: A news article has one main headline (h1), section titles (h2), and sub-section titles (h3). The text under each is in

tags. Google and screen readers use these headings to understand your page. Note: Extra spaces and line breaks in your code are ignored by the browser. Use
for a line break and

for a horizontal line.

subTopic.name: Text semantics
subTopic.notes:
Semantic text tags tell the browser what the text MEANS, not just how it looks. = very important text (bold, and screen readers stress it) = emphasized text (italic, changes the meaning of a sentence) and = only style, with no extra meaning = highlighted text = fine print = deleted text, = inserted text = a piece of code
= a long quote from another source and = subscript and superscript Code:

Please do not share your password.

Water is H2O and 23 = 8.

Old price: Rs 999 New price: Rs 499

Real-world example: On a shopping site, the old price is crossed out with and the sale price is shown with . A blind user's screen reader understands the difference too. Rule of thumb: choose a tag by meaning first, and use CSS for the design.

subTopic.name: Links and URL paths
subTopic.notes: Links are made with the anchor tag . The href attribute tells the browser where to go. Code: Visit Skillora Open in new tab Email us Call us Jump to contact section Types of paths: 1. Absolute URL: full address, like https://example.com/about.html 2. Relative path: address inside your own project about.html (same folder) pages/about.html (inside a folder) ../index.html (go one folder up) 3. Root-relative: /images/logo.png (starts from the site root) Real-world example: The 'Contact us' button in a website menu uses a link to contact.html. The 'Chat on WhatsApp' button uses a link to a wa.me address. Security tip: when using target='_blank', always add rel='noopener noreferrer'.

subTopic.name: Images and alt text
subTopic.notes: Use the tag to show an image. It is a void tag (no closing tag). Code: Important attributes: src = path of the image alt = text description of the image width and height = reserve space so the page does not jump while loading loading='lazy' = load the image only when the user scrolls near it Why alt text matters: 1. Screen readers read it to blind users. 2. It shows if the image fails to load. 3. Search engines use it to understand the image. For decorative images (like a background pattern) use an empty alt: alt=''. Real-world example: On an e-commerce site, a product photo has alt='Red cotton kurta with white embroidery'. If the network is slow, the user still knows what the product is. Common formats: JPG (photos), PNG (transparent background), SVG (logos and icons), WebP (small file size).

subTopic.name: Lists and tables
subTopic.notes:
LISTS
    = unordered list (bullets)
      = ordered list (numbers)
    1. = one list item
      • HTML
      • CSS
      1. Learn HTML
      2. Learn CSS
      TABLES (for data in rows and columns)
      NameMarks
      Anshika92
      Rahul85
      tr = row, th = heading cell, td = data cell. Use colspan and rowspan to merge cells. Real-world example: A navigation menu is usually a
        of links. A result sheet or a pricing comparison is a . Warning: never use tables to design the page layout. Use them only for real data. Use CSS Flexbox or Grid for layout.

subTopic.name: Semantic HTML elements
subTopic.notes:
Semantic elements have names that describe their purpose. They are better than using
everywhere.
= top area (logo, title)
= navigation links
= main content (use only once)
= a themed group of content
= content that makes sense on its own (blog post)
= side content (ads, related links)
= bottom area (copyright, contacts) Code:

My Blog

Home About

My first post

Hello everyone!

Related posts
2026 My Blog
Real-world example: On a news website, the logo bar is the header, the menu is the nav, each story is an article, and the links at the bottom are the footer. Benefits: better SEO, better accessibility, and code that is easier to read. Use
only when no semantic tag fits.

subTopic.name: Audio and video
subTopic.notes:
HTML can play media without any plugin, using <audio> and <video>.

Code:
<video src='intro.mp4' controls width='400' poster='thumbnail.jpg'>
  Your browser does not support video.
</video>

<audio controls>
  <source src='song.mp3' type='audio/mpeg'>
  <source src='song.ogg' type='audio/ogg'>
  Your browser does not support audio.
</audio>

Useful attributes:
controls = show play/pause and volume buttons
autoplay = start automatically (browsers usually need muted too)
loop = repeat again and again
muted = no sound
preload = how much to load in advance
poster = preview image for video

Use multiple <source> tags as a backup, so that if one format fails the browser tries the next.

Real-world example: A course website shows an intro video of a lesson with a play button. A podcast page uses <audio controls> to play episodes.

Tip: Do not autoplay sound. It annoys users. Common formats: MP4 and WebM (video), MP3 (audio).

subTopic.name: Iframes and embedded content
subTopic.notes:
An <iframe> shows another web page inside your page, like a window in a wall.

Code:
<iframe
  src='https://www.youtube.com/embed/VIDEO_ID'
  width='560'
  height='315'
  title='Intro video'
  allowfullscreen
  loading='lazy'>
</iframe>

<iframe src='https://www.google.com/maps/embed?pb=...' width='400' height='300' title='Our location'></iframe>

Important points:
1. Always add a title attribute for accessibility.
2. Some sites do not allow embedding (they block it for security).
3. Use the sandbox attribute to limit what the embedded page can do.
4. Too many iframes make a page slow.

Other embed tags: <embed> and <object> (for PDFs and similar files).

Real-world example: The 'Find us' section of a restaurant website has an embedded Google Map. A blog embeds a YouTube tutorial video.

Security tip: only embed content from sources you trust.

subTopic.name: HTML metadata
subTopic.notes:
Metadata is information ABOUT your page. It goes inside <head> and is not shown on the page, but browsers and search engines use it.

Code:
<head>
  <meta charset='UTF-8'>
  <meta name='viewport' content='width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0'>
  <meta name='description' content='Learn web development step by step on Skillora.'>
  <meta name='author' content='Anshika Verma'>
  <title>Skillora - Learning Path</title>
  <link rel='stylesheet' href='style.css'>
  <script src='app.js' defer></script>
</head>

What each does:
charset = correct letters and symbols
viewport = makes the page work on mobile (a must for responsive design)
description = the small text under your link in Google results
title = shown in the browser tab and in search results

Real-world example: When you search for a website on Google, the blue title and the grey summary come from the title and meta description.

Tip: keep the title under about 60 characters and the description under about 160.

subTopic.name: Favicons and social metadata
subTopic.notes:
FAVICON = the small icon shown in the browser tab.

<link rel='icon' type='image/png' href='/favicon.png'>
<link rel='apple-touch-icon' href='/apple-icon.png'>

SOCIAL METADATA (Open Graph and Twitter Cards) controls how your link looks when someone shares it on WhatsApp, LinkedIn, Facebook or X.

<meta property='og:title' content='Skillora - Learn Web Development'>
<meta property='og:description' content='A simple step by step learning path.'>
<meta property='og:image' content='https://skillora.com/preview.png'>
<meta property='og:url' content='https://skillora.com'>
<meta name='twitter:card' content='summary_large_image'>

Real-world example: When you paste a YouTube link in WhatsApp, you see a big thumbnail, a title and a description. That preview comes from og tags. Without them, your link looks plain and gets fewer clicks.

Tips: use an image of about 1200 x 630 px, and always use a full URL for og:image.

subTopic.name: HTML validation
subTopic.notes:
Validation means checking that your HTML follows the rules. Clean code works the same in all browsers and is easier to fix. Tools: 1. W3C Markup Validator (validator.w3.org): paste your code or URL and see the errors. 2. VS Code extensions and linters like HTMLHint. 3. Browser DevTools (press F12) to inspect problems. Common mistakes: - Forgetting to close a tag:
without
- Wrong nesting: text (should be text) - Missing alt on images - Duplicate id values - Missing or Bad: <p>Hello <b>world</p></b> Good: <p>Hello <b>world</b></p> Real-world example: A form on a shop website breaks because of one missing closing tag, and the Buy button disappears. A validator would have found it in seconds. Also check accessibility with Lighthouse in Chrome DevTools. Validate your code often, not just at the end.

subTopic.name: Form elements and submission
subTopic.notes:
A form collects data from the user and sends it somewhere.

Key points:
- <form> wraps all the inputs.
- action = where the data goes. method = how it goes (GET puts data in the URL, POST hides it in the request body).
- A button with type='submit' sends the form.
- Every input needs a name attribute. Without it, its value is NOT sent.

Code:
```html
<form action='/login' method='post'>
  <input type='text' name='username'>
  <input type='password' name='password'>
  <button type='submit'>Login</button>
</form>
```

Real-world example: On a login page you type your username and password and press Login. The browser packs the values and sends them to the server.

Teacher tip: Use POST for passwords, never GET. GET shows data in the address bar.

subTopic.name: Input types and labels
subTopic.notes:
The type attribute decides what kind of data the input accepts. The browser gives you the right keyboard and checks on mobile for free.

Common types: text, email, password, number, date, tel, url, file.

A label tells the user what to type. Connect it to the input using for and id (they must match). Now clicking the label also focuses the input, and screen readers read the label aloud.

Code:
```html
<label for='email'>Email address</label>
<input type='email' id='email' name='email'>
```

Real-world example: On a signup form, type='email' shows the @ keyboard on a phone, and type='date' shows a calendar picker.

Teacher tip: Never use placeholder as a replacement for a label. The placeholder disappears when you start typing.

subTopic.name: Select, textarea, checkbox, and radio controls
subTopic.notes:
Different controls for different choices:
- <select> = dropdown, choose one option from a long list.
- <textarea> = multi-line text (messages, feedback).
- checkbox = choose zero, one or many options.
- radio = choose only ONE option from a group. All radios in a group must share the same name.

Code:
```html
<label for='city'>City</label>
<select id='city' name='city'>
  <option value='delhi'>Delhi</option>
  <option value='mumbai'>Mumbai</option>
</select>

<label for='msg'>Message</label>
<textarea id='msg' name='msg' rows='4'></textarea>

<label><input type='checkbox' name='newsletter'> Send me updates</label>

<label><input type='radio' name='gender' value='f'> Female</label>
<label><input type='radio' name='gender' value='m'> Male</label>
```

Real-world example: A food delivery app uses radio for payment method (only one allowed), checkboxes for extra toppings (many allowed), and a textarea for 'delivery instructions'.

Teacher tip: Wrap the input inside the label, or use for/id, so the text is clickable.

subTopic.name: Native validation attributes
subTopic.notes:
HTML can check user input for you before the form is submitted, with no JavaScript needed.

Useful attributes:
- required = field cannot be empty
- minlength / maxlength = text length limits
- min / max = number or date limits
- pattern = a regex the value must match
- type='email' / 'url' = built-in format checks

Code:
```html
<form>
  <input type='email' name='email' required>
  <input type='password' name='pass' minlength='8' required>
  <input type='text' name='pin' pattern='[0-9]{6}' title='Enter a 6 digit PIN'>
  <input type='number' name='age' min='18' max='60'>
  <button type='submit'>Register</button>
</form>
```

Real-world example: A job application form blocks you from submitting if you forget your email or enter an age under 18.

Teacher tip: Browser validation is for user comfort only. Always validate again on the server, because users can bypass the browser.

subTopic.name: Accessible error messages
subTopic.notes:
An error message must be clear to everyone, including screen reader users and people who cannot see colors. Rules: 1. Say what went wrong and how to fix it ('Enter a valid email like name@mail.com', not just 'Invalid'). 2. Do not rely on red color alone. Add text or an icon. 3. Connect the error to its input with aria-describedby. 4. Mark the input with aria-invalid='true'. 5. Use role='alert' so screen readers announce the error immediately. Code: ```html

Please enter a valid email, for example name@mail.com

``` Real-world example: On a checkout page, a blind user submits the form with a wrong PIN code. The screen reader reads 'Please enter a 6 digit PIN' and they know exactly what to fix. Teacher tip: Put the error next to the field and move focus to the first error after submit.

subTopic.name: Fieldset and legend
subTopic.notes:
<fieldset> groups related form controls together. <legend> is the title of that group.

It is very important for radio buttons and checkboxes, because a screen reader reads the legend before each option. The user then knows what question the options belong to.

Code:
```html
<fieldset>
  <legend>Choose your delivery speed</legend>
  <label><input type='radio' name='speed' value='normal'> Normal</label>
  <label><input type='radio' name='speed' value='express'> Express</label>
</fieldset>
```

Real-world example: In a long registration form you can make separate groups: 'Personal details', 'Address', and 'Payment'. This makes the form easier for everyone to scan.

Teacher tip: Use fieldset + legend for groups of related inputs. Use a simple label for a single input.

subTopic.name: Keyboard navigation
subTopic.notes: Many people cannot use a mouse (motor disability, broken trackpad, power users). Your site must work with the keyboard alone. Keys to remember: - Tab = move to the next interactive element - Shift + Tab = go back - Enter = activate links and buttons - Space = press buttons, toggle checkboxes - Arrow keys = move between radio buttons or menu items Best practices: - Use real elements ( ``` Real-world example: Try filling a login form using only Tab and Enter. If you get stuck anywhere, that is an accessibility bug. Teacher tip: The tab order should follow the visual order of the page.

subTopic.name: Focus management
Semantic landmarks
subTopic.notes:
Landmarks are HTML tags that tell the browser and screen readers what each part of the page is. Screen reader users can jump directly between them. Main landmarks: -
= top of the page or section (logo, title) -
= navigation links -
= the main content (use only ONE per page) -
= side content (ads, related links) -
= a themed section with a heading -
= bottom of the page or section Code: ```html

Skillora

...

My Courses

Tips
© 2026 Skillora
``` Real-world example: Think of a mall with signboards: Food Court, Exit, Parking. Landmarks are those signboards for your website, so blind users can go straight to
and skip the menu. Teacher tip: Avoid a page full of
s. If you have two
elements, give each an aria-label.

subTopic.name: ARIA roles and attributes
subTopic.notes:
ARIA adds extra information for assistive technology when plain HTML cannot describe something. First rule of ARIA: use the correct native HTML element first. A
    ...
``` ```js menuBtn.addEventListener('click', () => { const open = menuBtn.getAttribute('aria-expanded') === 'true'; menuBtn.setAttribute('aria-expanded', String(!open)); menu.hidden = open; }); ``` Real-world example: A hamburger icon button has no text. Without aria-label, a screen reader just says 'button'. With it, the user hears 'Menu, collapsed button'. Teacher tip: Wrong ARIA is worse than no ARIA. Use it only when needed.

subTopic.name: Screen reader fundamentals
subTopic.notes: A screen reader is software that reads the page aloud (or shows it in braille) for blind and low-vision users. Popular ones: NVDA and JAWS (Windows), VoiceOver (Mac/iPhone), TalkBack (Android). How they work: - They read content in DOM order, not visual order. - Users jump around using headings, links, landmarks and form fields. - They read alt text of images, labels of inputs and the text of buttons. What you should do: 1. Use a proper heading order (one h1, then h2, h3...). 2. Write meaningful alt text. Use alt='' for decorative images. 3. Give every input a label. 4. Make link text meaningful ('Read the course details', not 'Click here'). Code: ```html ``` Real-world example: A blind student opens your dashboard and presses H to jump heading by heading: 'My Courses', 'Pending', 'Completed'. Good headings make the site easy for them to use. Teacher tip: Turn on VoiceOver or NVDA once and try your own site with your eyes closed.

subTopic.name: Color contrast
subTopic.notes:
Contrast is the difference in brightness between text and its background. Low contrast (light grey on white) is hard to read for many people, especially in sunlight or with low vision. WCAG minimum ratios (AA level): - Normal text: 4.5 : 1 - Large text (18px bold / 24px normal and above): 3 : 1 - Buttons, icons, input borders: 3 : 1 Also: never use color alone to give meaning. Add text or an icon too. Code: ```css /* Bad: about 2.3:1, too light */ .hint { color: #aaaaaa; background: #ffffff; } /* Good: about 7:1 */ .hint { color: #595959; background: #ffffff; } ``` ```html

Error: Name is required

``` Real-world example: A student reads your notes on a phone outside in bright sunlight. Dark text on a light background is readable, but light grey text vanishes. Teacher tip: Check your colors with the WebAIM Contrast Checker or the Chrome DevTools color picker.

subTopic.name: WCAG overview
subTopic.notes:
WCAG = Web Content Accessibility Guidelines. It is the international standard that tells us how to make websites usable for everyone. The latest version is WCAG 2.2. Four principles (remember POUR): - Perceivable: users can see or hear the content (alt text, captions, contrast). - Operable: users can use it (keyboard support, enough time, no flashing). - Understandable: content and behavior are clear (simple language, helpful errors). - Robust: works with different browsers and assistive technology (valid HTML, correct ARIA). Three levels: - A = basic - AA = the usual target for most websites (and often required by law) - AAA = highest, not always possible for everything Quick example for each principle: ```html
...
``` Real-world example: Government and banking websites must follow WCAG AA, so every citizen, including people with disabilities, can pay bills or apply for services. Teacher tip: Aim for WCAG 2.2 AA in your projects. It also makes your portfolio stand out in interviews.

subTopic.name: Accessibility testing
subTopic.notes:
Building an accessible site is not enough. You must test it. Use both automated and manual testing, because tools catch only about 30 to 40 percent of the issues.

1. Automated tools (fast):
- Lighthouse (Chrome DevTools > Lighthouse > Accessibility)
- axe DevTools extension
- WAVE

2. Manual checks (must do):
- Keyboard test: unplug the mouse, use only Tab, Shift+Tab, Enter, Space. Can you reach and use everything? Is the focus always visible?
- Screen reader test: try NVDA, VoiceOver or TalkBack.
- Zoom test: zoom the page to 200 percent. Does anything break or get hidden?
- Contrast and color test: is anything shown by color only?

3. Test with real users if you can.

Code (automated test in a project):
```bash
npm install --save-dev jest-axe
```
```js
import { render } from '@testing-library/react';
import { axe } from 'jest-axe';

test('form has no accessibility violations', async () => {
  const { container } = render(<LoginForm />);
  expect(await axe(container)).toHaveNoViolations();
});
```

Real-world example: Before launching the Skillora dashboard, a quick Lighthouse run shows 'Buttons do not have an accessible name'. You add aria-label to the icon buttons and the score goes from 78 to 100.

Teacher tip: Test early and often. Fixing issues during development is much cheaper than fixing them after launch.

subTopic.name: CSS syntax and stylesheets
Selectors and combinators
subTopic.notes:
A selector chooses WHICH HTML element you want to style. A combinator chooses elements based on their relationship to other elements.

Basic selectors:
p { }          /* all paragraphs */
.card { }      /* class */
#header { }    /* id (unique) */
* { }          /* everything */
h1, h2 { }     /* group */

Combinators:
nav a { }      /* descendant: any a inside nav */
nav > a { }    /* child: only direct children */
h1 + p { }     /* adjacent: the p right after h1 */
h1 ~ p { }     /* sibling: all p after h1 */

Real-world example: In a school, '.student' means all students. 'class-5 > .student' means only the students directly in class 5. 'principal + .teacher' means the teacher standing right next to the principal.

Teacher's tip: Prefer classes over ids for styling. Classes can be reused, ids cannot.

subTopic.name: Pseudo-classes and pseudo-elements
Cascade, specificity, and inheritance
subTopic.notes:
When many CSS rules target the same element, the browser must decide which one wins. It checks 3 things: 1. Importance: !important beats normal rules (avoid using it). 2. Specificity: the more specific selector wins. Inline style = 1000 #id = 100 .class / :hover = 10 element (p, div) = 1 3. Order: if specificity is equal, the rule written LAST wins. Example: p { color: black; } /* 1 */ .note { color: blue; } /* 10 */ #intro { color: green; } /* 100 */ If

, the text is green. Inheritance: some properties pass from parent to child automatically (color, font-family, font-size). Others do not (margin, padding, border). Real-world example: A company rule says 'wear white shirts' (general), but your team rule says 'wear blue' (more specific). Your manager's direct order today (inline) beats both. Teacher's tip: If your style is not working, check specificity first in browser DevTools.

subTopic.name: Colors and opacity
subTopic.notes:
CSS gives you many ways to write a colour:

color: red;                    /* name */
color: #ff5733;                /* hex */
color: rgb(255, 87, 51);       /* red, green, blue */
color: rgba(255, 87, 51, 0.5); /* with transparency */
color: hsl(11, 100%, 60%);     /* hue, saturation, lightness */

Useful properties:
color            -> text colour
background-color -> background colour
border-color     -> border colour

Opacity:
.box { opacity: 0.5; }  /* whole element becomes 50% see-through, including text */
.box { background: rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.5); }  /* only the background is see-through */

Real-world example: A dark overlay behind a popup uses rgba(0,0,0,0.6). The page behind is dimmed but the popup text stays fully clear.

Teacher's tip: opacity affects the element AND its children. Use rgba or hsla when you only want a transparent background.

subTopic.name: Units: px, rem, em, %, vw, and vh
subTopic.notes:
Units decide the size of things in CSS.

px   -> fixed pixels (does not scale)
em   -> relative to the PARENT font size
rem  -> relative to the ROOT (html) font size
%    -> relative to the parent's size
vw   -> 1% of the screen width
vh   -> 1% of the screen height

Example:
html { font-size: 16px; }
h1 { font-size: 2rem; }      /* 32px */
.container { width: 80%; }   /* 80% of parent */
.hero { height: 100vh; }     /* full screen height */

Real-world example: A hero banner on a landing page uses 100vh so it fills the whole screen on any device. Using rem for fonts means that if a user increases their browser font size, your whole site scales nicely.

Teacher's tip: Use rem for fonts and spacing, % or vw for layout widths, and px only for small things like borders.

subTopic.name: Typography and web fonts
Box model
Margin, padding, border, and outline
Display types
Positioning and z-index
Overflow and stacking contexts
subTopic.notes:
Overflow controls what happens when content is bigger than its box.

overflow: visible;  /* default, content spills out */
overflow: hidden;   /* extra content is cut */
overflow: scroll;   /* always shows scrollbars */
overflow: auto;     /* scrollbar only when needed */

Cut long text with three dots:
.title {
  white-space: nowrap;
  overflow: hidden;
  text-overflow: ellipsis;
}

Stacking context: a group of elements that are layered together. z-index only compares elements inside the SAME stacking context. A new one is created by:
- position + z-index
- opacity less than 1
- transform
- filter

Real-world example: A chat box uses overflow: auto so old messages scroll inside it. A modal with z-index: 9999 may still appear behind a header if the modal sits inside a parent that created a lower stacking context.

Teacher's tip: If z-index is not working, look at the parents. A trapped child can never go above another stacking context.

subTopic.name: CSS variables and design tokens
CSS reset and normalization
Normal document flow
subTopic.notes:
📘 Normal Document Flow What is it? Normal flow is the default way a browser places elements on a page when you have not applied any layout CSS. Think of it like writing in a notebook: you write left to right, and when the line is full, you go to the next line. Two types of elements: - Block elements (div, p, h1, section) take the full width and start on a new line. - Inline elements (span, a, strong, img) sit side by side inside a line, only as wide as their content. Code: ```html

Title

Hello world and link

``` Real-world example: A blog post. The heading, paragraphs and images stack top to bottom. Words like bold text or links stay inside the paragraph line. You never wrote any layout code, that is normal flow doing its job. Remember: - Width and height work on block elements, not on inline ones. - display: block / inline / inline-block can change this behaviour. - position: absolute and float take elements OUT of normal flow.

subTopic.name: Flexbox
subTopic.notes:
📘 Flexbox

What is it?
Flexbox is a one-dimensional layout system. It arranges items in a single row OR a single column and controls spacing and alignment easily.

How to start:
Add display: flex to the parent (the container). Its direct children become flex items.

Important properties (on the container):
- flex-direction: row | column
- justify-content: alignment along the main axis (flex-start, center, space-between)
- align-items: alignment along the cross axis (stretch, center)
- flex-wrap: wrap items to the next line

On the items: flex: 1 makes an item grow to fill the free space.

Code:
```css
.navbar {
  display: flex;
  justify-content: space-between;
  align-items: center;
}
```

Real-world example:
A website navbar: logo on the left, menu links in the middle, login button on the right, all vertically centered. Flexbox does this in 3 lines.

Remember:
- Main axis = direction of flex-direction. Cross axis = the other one.
- Use Flexbox when you are laying out items in ONE direction.

subTopic.name: CSS Grid
subTopic.notes:
📘 CSS Grid

What is it?
Grid is a two-dimensional layout system. It controls rows AND columns at the same time. Think of it like an Excel sheet where you decide the size of each row and column.

How to start:
Add display: grid to the parent and define columns.

Important properties:
- grid-template-columns: defines the columns
- grid-template-rows: defines the rows
- fr unit: a fraction of the free space
- grid-column / grid-row: make an item span multiple cells
- repeat(), minmax(), auto-fit: for flexible grids

Code:
```css
.cards {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr); /* 3 equal columns */
  gap: 20px;
}
```

Real-world example:
A product listing page like an e-commerce site. 12 product cards arranged in 3 columns and 4 rows, with equal spacing. Grid handles it easily.

Remember:
- Grid = rows + columns. Flexbox = one direction only.
- 1fr 2fr means the second column is twice as wide as the first.

subTopic.name: Alignment and gap
subTopic.notes:
📘 Alignment and Gap

What is it?
Alignment decides WHERE items sit inside a container. Gap decides the SPACE between the items. Both work in Flexbox and Grid.

Key properties:
- justify-content: aligns along the main axis (horizontal in a row)
- align-items: aligns along the cross axis (vertical in a row)
- align-self: aligns ONE single item differently
- place-items: center: shortcut for centering in Grid
- gap, row-gap, column-gap: space between items

Code:
```css
.box {
  display: flex;
  justify-content: center;  /* horizontal center */
  align-items: center;      /* vertical center */
  gap: 16px;                /* space between children */
  height: 100vh;
}
```

Real-world example:
A login form centered exactly in the middle of the screen, with equal space between the email field, password field and button.

Remember:
- Use gap instead of adding margins on every child. It is cleaner.
- gap only adds space BETWEEN items, not on the outer edges.

subTopic.name: Responsive and adaptive design
subTopic.notes:
📘 Responsive vs Adaptive Design

Responsive design:
The layout changes smoothly and continuously as the screen size changes. It uses flexible units (%, rem, fr), flexible grids and media queries.

Adaptive design:
The layout has fixed versions for specific screen sizes (for example 320px, 768px, 1200px). The site jumps to the closest version.

Simple difference:
- Responsive = like water, it fills any container.
- Adaptive = like fixed-size clothes (S, M, L), you pick the closest one.

Code (responsive idea):
```css
.container {
  width: 90%;
  max-width: 1100px;
  margin: 0 auto;
}
img { max-width: 100%; height: auto; }
```

Real-world example:
Open Amazon or any news site on your phone and laptop. The same website rearranges itself to fit your screen. That is responsive design.

Remember:
- Always add this in your HTML head:
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
- Most modern websites use responsive design.

subTopic.name: Mobile-first CSS
Media queries
Container queries
Fluid sizing with clamp()
subTopic.notes:
📘 Fluid Sizing with clamp()

What is it?
clamp() lets a value grow and shrink with the screen, but never go below a minimum or above a maximum.

Syntax:
clamp(MIN, PREFERRED, MAX)

- MIN: the smallest allowed value
- PREFERRED: usually a flexible value like 4vw
- MAX: the largest allowed value

Code:
```css
h1 {
  font-size: clamp(1.5rem, 4vw, 3rem);
}

.container {
  padding: clamp(16px, 5vw, 64px);
}
```

Meaning of the heading: it tries to be 4vw, but it will never be smaller than 1.5rem or bigger than 3rem.

Real-world example:
A hero heading on a landing page. On a phone it is readable (24px), on a laptop it is bold and big (48px), and it scales smoothly in between, without writing many media queries.

Remember:
- vw = 1% of the viewport width.
- clamp() reduces the number of media queries you need.

subTopic.name: Responsive images
subTopic.notes: 📘 Responsive Images What is it? Responsive images adjust to the screen size and load the right file size, so pages look sharp and load fast. Method 1: Simple CSS ```css img { max-width: 100%; height: auto; } ``` Method 2: srcset and sizes (browser picks the best file) ```html ``` Method 3: picture tag (different image for different screens) ```html ``` Real-world example: A travel website. A phone on a slow network loads a small 400px image. A big retina laptop loads the 1600px image. Users save data and the page opens faster. Remember: - Always write the alt text. - Add loading="lazy" for images below the fold.

subTopic.name: Handling overflow
Cross-device testing
subTopic.notes:
📘 Cross-device Testing

What is it?
Checking that your website looks and works properly on different devices, screen sizes and browsers.

What to test:
- Screen sizes: phone, tablet, laptop, large monitor
- Browsers: Chrome, Safari, Firefox, Edge
- Orientation: portrait and landscape
- Touch vs mouse, slow internet

Tools:
1. Chrome DevTools: press F12, then click the device icon (Ctrl + Shift + M) to simulate phones and tablets.
2. Resize the browser window slowly and watch where the layout breaks.
3. Test on a real phone: connect to the same WiFi and open http://YOUR-IP:5173 (for a Vite project).
4. Online tools: BrowserStack, LambdaTest, Responsively App.
5. Lighthouse (in DevTools) checks performance and accessibility.

Real-world example:
Your portfolio looks perfect on your laptop, but when a recruiter opens it on an iPhone, the buttons are cut off. Testing early catches this before they see it.

Remember:
- Emulators are good, but real devices are best.
- Safari on iPhone often behaves differently (for example 100vh issues). Test it.

subTopic.name: Grid vs Flexbox
subTopic.notes:
📘 Grid vs Flexbox

Short answer:
- Flexbox = one dimension (a row OR a column).
- Grid = two dimensions (rows AND columns together).

Comparison:
- Flexbox works from the content outward. Items decide their size.
- Grid works from the layout inward. You define the structure first, then place items.

Use Flexbox for:
- Navbars, button groups, toolbars
- Centering one item
- Small components, aligning icon and text

Use Grid for:
- Full page layouts (header, sidebar, main, footer)
- Card galleries, dashboards
- Anything that needs aligned rows and columns

Code:
```css
/* Flexbox: navbar */
.nav { display: flex; justify-content: space-between; }

/* Grid: page layout */
.page {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: 250px 1fr;
  grid-template-areas:
    "header header"
    "sidebar main";
}
```

Real-world example:
A dashboard page like Skillora: use Grid for the overall page (sidebar + content area), and Flexbox inside each card to align the title, progress bar and button.

Remember:
- They are not enemies. Professionals use both together.
- Quick rule: layout in 2D = Grid, alignment in 1D = Flexbox.
