BEM naming convention
subTopic.notes:
BEM stands for Block, Element, Modifier. It is a naming rule that makes CSS class names clear and prevents style conflicts in big projects. Pattern: - Block: standalone component (card) - Element: part of a block (card__title), joined with two underscores - Modifier: variation or state (card--featured), joined with two hyphens Code:

React Course

.card { padding: 16px; } .card__title { font-size: 20px; } .card--featured { border: 2px solid gold; } Real-world example: In a team project, anyone reading card__title immediately knows it belongs to the card component. No confusion and no accidental overrides. Remember: Keep it flat. Write card__title, not card__body__title.

subTopic.name: Utility classes
subTopic.notes:
Utility classes are small, single-purpose classes that do just one thing. You build a design by combining many of them directly in your HTML. Code: .mt-4 { margin-top: 1rem; } .text-center { text-align: center; } .flex { display: flex; } .hidden { display: none; }
Hello
Benefits: - Fast to write - Very reusable - Less custom CSS to maintain Drawback: HTML can look crowded with many classes. Real-world example: Needing a quick 16px gap above one section? Add mt-4 instead of writing a new CSS rule. Tailwind CSS is built entirely on this idea. Remember: Utilities work best alongside components. Use them for small adjustments, not for everything.

subTopic.name: CSS Modules
Sass/SCSS overview
Tailwind CSS
subTopic.notes:
Tailwind is a utility-first CSS framework. Instead of writing CSS files, you style elements by adding ready-made classes straight in your HTML or JSX.

Code:
<button class='bg-indigo-600 text-white px-4 py-2 rounded-lg hover:bg-indigo-700 transition'>
  Enroll Now
</button>

How to read it:
- bg-indigo-600: background color
- px-4 py-2: horizontal and vertical padding
- rounded-lg: rounded corners
- hover: prefix applies the style on hover

Responsive design uses prefixes:
<div class='grid grid-cols-1 md:grid-cols-3 gap-4'>
(1 column on mobile, 3 columns on medium screens and above)

Real-world example: Building a course dashboard quickly, with cards, grids and buttons, without leaving your component file.

Remember: Tailwind only includes the classes you actually use, so the final CSS file stays small.

subTopic.name: Bootstrap
subTopic.notes:
Bootstrap is a ready-made CSS framework with pre-designed components (buttons, navbars, cards, modals) and a 12-column grid system. You add its classes and get a good-looking, responsive page quickly. Code:
HTML Basics
Start
Grid idea: each row has 12 columns. col-md-4 means 4 of 12 columns, so 3 cards per row on medium screens. Real-world example: Admin panels and quick prototypes or college projects, where speed matters more than a unique design. Remember: Bootstrap sites can look alike. Customize colors and spacing to make your project feel unique.

subTopic.name: Dark mode and themes
Component styling strategies
subTopic.notes:
In component-based apps like React, there are several ways to style a component. A good developer picks the right one for the project.

Options:
1. Plain CSS file: simple, but styles are global.
2. CSS Modules: scoped classes per component.
3. Utility framework (Tailwind): style directly in markup.
4. CSS-in-JS (styled-components): styles written inside JavaScript.
5. Inline styles: quick, but no hover, media queries or reuse.

Code (CSS-in-JS):
const Button = styled.button`
  background: #4f46e5;
  color: white;
  padding: 10px 20px;
`;

Real-world example: A team building a design system for a company picks CSS Modules or Tailwind so every Button, Card and Modal looks the same everywhere.

Remember: There is no single best option. Pick one strategy per project and stay consistent.

subTopic.name: Maintainable CSS architecture
subTopic.notes:
As a project grows, messy CSS becomes hard to change. A maintainable architecture means your CSS is organized, predictable and easy for others to understand.

Good practices:
- Use a clear folder structure
- Use CSS variables for colors, spacing and fonts
- Follow one naming convention (like BEM)
- Keep selectors short and avoid !important
- Build small reusable components
- Remove unused CSS

Example structure:
styles/
  base/       (reset, typography)
  components/ (button, card, navbar)
  layout/     (grid, header, footer)
  themes/     (light, dark)

Code (design tokens):
:root {
  --color-primary: #4f46e5;
  --space-md: 16px;
  --radius: 8px;
}

Real-world example: A new developer joins your team. With good structure, they find and fix a button style in minutes, not hours.

Remember: Write CSS as if someone else will have to read it tomorrow, because that someone is often you.

subTopic.name: Variables with var, let, and const
subTopic.notes:
What is it?
A variable is a named box that stores a value so you can use it later. JavaScript gives you three ways to create one: var, let, and const.

Key Points:
- const: value cannot be re-assigned. Use it by default.
- let: value can change later. Use it when you know it will change.
- var: the old way. It is function-scoped and can cause bugs. Avoid it in new code.
- let and const are block-scoped (they live only inside the { } where they are written).
- const does not freeze objects/arrays; you can still change what is inside them.

Code:
  const name = "Anshika";   // will not change
  let score = 10;           // can change
  score = 15;               // OK
  // name = "Riya";         // Error: cannot re-assign const

  if (true) {
    let x = 5;
    var y = 8;
  }
  console.log(y); // 8  (var leaks out of the block)
  console.log(x); // Error (let stays inside the block)

Real-World Scenario:
On a shopping website, the shop name is a const (never changes), while the cart total is a let (changes every time a user adds an item).

Remember: Start with const. Change to let only when you need to re-assign. Forget var.

subTopic.name: Primitive and reference types
Type conversion and coercion
subTopic.notes:
What is it?
Type conversion means changing a value from one type to another (e.g., string to number). Coercion is when JavaScript does it automatically for you.

Key Points:
- Explicit conversion: you do it yourself with Number(), String(), Boolean(), parseInt().
- Implicit coercion: JavaScript does it silently, which can surprise you.
- The + operator with a string joins text. Other math operators convert to numbers.
- Falsy values: false, 0, "", null, undefined, NaN. Everything else is truthy.
- Prefer === (strict equality) over == to avoid coercion bugs.

Code:
  Number("42");        // 42
  String(100);         // "100"
  Boolean("hello");    // true
  parseInt("25px");    // 25

  "5" + 2;             // "52"  (string joining)
  "5" - 2;             // 3     (number math)
  0 == false;          // true  (coercion)
  0 === false;         // false (strict, no coercion)

Real-World Scenario:
Values from an HTML input box always come as strings. If a user types 10 and 20 in two fields, adding them directly gives "1020". You must convert them with Number() first to get 30.

Remember: Always convert form input to numbers before doing math, and use ===.

subTopic.name: Operators and expressions
subTopic.notes:
What is it?
Operators are symbols that perform actions on values. An expression is any piece of code that produces a value.

Key Points:
- Arithmetic: + - * / % **
- Assignment: = += -= *= /=
- Comparison: === !== > < >= <=
- Logical: && (and), || (or), ! (not)
- Nullish coalescing ??: gives a default only when value is null/undefined.
- Optional chaining ?.: safely reads a property that might not exist.
- Ternary: condition ? valueIfTrue : valueIfFalse

Code:
  let price = 500;
  price += 50;                      // 550
  let isAdult = age >= 18 && hasID; // logical AND

  let name = userName ?? "Guest";   // default value
  let city = user?.address?.city;   // no error if address is missing
  let msg = score >= 40 ? "Pass" : "Fail";

Real-World Scenario:
On an e-commerce site, the discount is applied with an expression like: total > 1000 ? total * 0.9 : total. Customers who spend more than 1000 get 10% off.

Remember: Use ?? instead of || when 0 or "" are valid values.

subTopic.name: Conditionals and switch
Loops and iteration
Functions and arrow functions
Parameters, arguments, and return values
subTopic.notes:
What is it?
Parameters are the placeholders in a function definition. Arguments are the real values you pass when calling it. The return value is what the function gives back.

Key Points:
- Parameters = names (in the definition). Arguments = values (in the call).
- Default parameters give a fallback if no argument is passed.
- A function without return gives back undefined.
- return stops the function immediately.
- You can return only one value, but it can be an array or object holding many.

Code:
  function add(a, b = 0) {   // a, b are parameters
    return a + b;
  }

  add(5, 3);   // 5 and 3 are arguments -> 8
  add(5);      // b uses default 0 -> 5

  function getUser() {
    return { name: "Anshika", role: "Student" };
  }
  const { name } = getUser();

Real-World Scenario:
A login function takes username and password (parameters), and returns true or false. The website then uses that returned value to decide whether to open the dashboard.

Remember: If your function is not giving output, check that you wrote return.

subTopic.name: Scope and hoisting
Closures
Execution context and call stack
The this keyword
call(), apply(), and bind()
subTopic.notes:
What is it?
These three methods let you manually decide what this should be for a function.

Key Points:
- call(thisValue, arg1, arg2): runs the function right now, args one by one.
- apply(thisValue, [args]): runs the function right now, args in an array.
- bind(thisValue): does NOT run it; returns a new function with this fixed.

Code:
  const person = { name: "Anshika" };

  function intro(city, country) {
    console.log(this.name + " from " + city + ", " + country);
  }

  intro.call(person, "Delhi", "India");     // runs now
  intro.apply(person, ["Delhi", "India"]);  // runs now
  const fixed = intro.bind(person, "Delhi", "India");
  fixed();                                   // runs later

Real-World Scenario:
In a React class component, a button click handler loses its this. Using this.handleClick = this.handleClick.bind(this) fixes it so the handler still knows which component it belongs to.

Remember: Call and Apply = Run now. Bind = Run later.

subTopic.name: Arrays and array methods
subTopic.notes:
What is it?
An array is an ordered list of values. JavaScript gives many built-in methods to add, remove, search, and transform the data.

Key Points:
- Index starts from 0.
- Change the array: push, pop, shift, unshift, splice, sort, reverse.
- Create a new array: map, filter, slice, concat.
- find returns the first match. some/every return true or false.
- reduce turns the whole array into a single value.

Code:
  const prices = [100, 250, 400];

  prices.push(500);                          // add at end
  const withTax = prices.map(p => p * 1.18); // transform each
  const cheap = prices.filter(p => p < 300); // keep some
  const first = prices.find(p => p > 200);   // 250
  const total = prices.reduce((sum, p) => sum + p, 0);

  console.log(total); // 1250

Real-World Scenario:
A cart has many products. map shows each item on screen, filter removes out-of-stock items, and reduce calculates the total bill.

Remember: map, filter, and reduce do not change the original array, which keeps your data safe.

subTopic.name: Objects and destructuring
subTopic.notes:
What is it?
An object stores data as key-value pairs. Destructuring is a shortcut to take values out of an object (or array) into separate variables.

Key Points:
- Access values with dot (obj.name) or bracket (obj["name"]).
- Add, change, or delete properties any time.
- Object.keys(), Object.values(), Object.entries() help you loop over an object.
- Destructuring can rename and set default values.
- Works great in function parameters.

Code:
  const user = {
    name: "Anshika",
    age: 21,
    skills: ["React", "JS"]
  };

  user.city = "Delhi"; // add

  const { name, age } = user;           // destructuring
  const { city: location = "NA" } = user; // rename + default
  const [firstSkill] = user.skills;     // array destructuring

  console.log(name, location, firstSkill);

Real-World Scenario:
Your API sends a big user object. Instead of writing data.user.profile.name again and again, you destructure once: const { name, email } = data.user.

Remember: Destructuring = unpacking a box into separate items.

subTopic.name: Spread and rest syntax
Sets and Maps
Strings, numbers, dates, and regular expressions
subTopic.notes:
What is it?
These are the everyday built-in tools for working with text, math, time, and pattern matching.

Key Points:
- Strings: length, slice, split, includes, replace, trim, toUpperCase, template literals.
- Numbers: toFixed, Math.round, Math.floor, Math.random, isNaN.
- Dates: new Date(), getFullYear(), getMonth() (starts at 0!), toLocaleDateString().
- Regex: a pattern to search or validate text. Use .test() or .match().

Code:
  const name = "  Anshika  ";
  name.trim().toUpperCase();          // "ANSHIKA"
  `Hello ${name.trim()}!`;            // template literal

  (10.567).toFixed(2);                // "10.57"
  Math.floor(Math.random() * 6) + 1;  // dice roll

  const d = new Date();
  console.log(d.getFullYear());

  const emailPattern = /^[^\s@]+@[^\s@]+\.[^\s@]+$/;
  emailPattern.test("anshika@gmail.com"); // true

Real-World Scenario:
On a signup form, you trim the name, validate the email with a regex, format the price with toFixed(2), and show the joining date using Date.

Remember: Months in Date start from 0 (January = 0). This surprises everyone once.

subTopic.name: Error handling
Modules and import/export
Promises
async/await
Event loop and task queues
subTopic.notes:
Event loop and task queues

JavaScript has only one thread, so it can do one thing at a time. The event loop is the manager that decides what runs next.

How it works:
1. Synchronous code runs on the Call Stack.
2. Async work (timers, fetch, clicks) is handled by the browser (Web APIs).
3. When that work finishes, its callback waits in a queue.
4. When the call stack is empty, the event loop moves the next callback from the queue to the stack.

Code:
console.log("1");
setTimeout(() => console.log("2"), 0);
console.log("3");
// Output: 1, 3, 2

Even with 0 ms, setTimeout runs last because it must wait in the queue until the stack is empty.

Real-world example: A cashier (call stack) serves one customer at a time. Other customers stand in a line (queue). The next one is called only when the cashier is free.

subTopic.name: Microtasks and macrotasks
Callbacks and callback hell
Higher-order functions
Pure functions and immutability
Prototypes and inheritance
Classes and OOP
Iterators and generators
Symbols and proxies overview
Garbage collection and memory leaks
Shallow vs deep copy
JSON serialization
Debouncing and throttling
Performance fundamentals
DOM tree and node selection
subTopic.notes:
What is it?
The DOM (Document Object Model) is the browser's tree-shaped copy of your HTML page. Every tag becomes a "node" that JavaScript can find and change.

Key points:
- document is the root. Inside it: html > head + body > all your elements.
- querySelector("css") gives the FIRST match. querySelectorAll("css") gives ALL matches (a NodeList).
- getElementById("id") is the quickest way to grab one element.
- If nothing matches, querySelector returns null. Always check before using it.
- You can walk the tree: parentElement, children, nextElementSibling.

Code:
const title = document.querySelector("#title");
const cards = document.querySelectorAll(".course-card");

cards.forEach(card => console.log(card.textContent));
console.log(title.parentElement, title.children, title.nextElementSibling);

Real-world example:
On Skillora, you select all ".course-card" elements to count how many courses are shown on the dashboard.

Remember: JS can only select elements that already exist. Load your script at the end of body or use the defer attribute.

subTopic.name: Creating and updating elements
subTopic.notes:
What is it?
Creating and updating elements means building new HTML from JavaScript, or changing what is already on the page.

Key points:
- document.createElement("li") makes a new element (not on the page yet).
- Add it with append(), prepend(), before(), or after().
- textContent changes the text safely. innerHTML parses HTML (use carefully).
- remove() deletes an element. replaceWith() swaps it. cloneNode(true) copies it.

Code:
const list = document.querySelector("#subtopic-list");

const li = document.createElement("li");
li.textContent = "Event handling";
list.append(li);

li.textContent = "Event handling (done)";   // update
li.remove();                                 // delete

Real-world example:
When a student adds a new subtopic to their study list on Skillora, JS creates a new li and appends it, with no page reload.

Remember: Creating an element does nothing until you put it in the page with append().

subTopic.name: Attributes, classes, and styles
subTopic.notes:
What is it?
Every element has attributes (id, src, href), classes, and inline styles. JavaScript can read and change all of them.

Key points:
- getAttribute / setAttribute / removeAttribute work with any attribute.
- dataset reads custom data-* attributes (data-id becomes el.dataset.id).
- classList.add, remove, toggle, contains manage CSS classes.
- el.style.color = "red" sets inline style (camelCase names like backgroundColor).
- Best practice: change classes, keep the styling inside CSS.

Code:
const card = document.querySelector(".card");

card.setAttribute("title", "Open course");
console.log(card.dataset.id);        // from data-id="st-144"
card.classList.add("completed");
card.classList.toggle("hidden");
card.style.backgroundColor = "lightgreen";

Real-world example:
When a student ticks a subtopic as complete, Skillora adds the class "completed" which turns the text green and strikes it through.

Remember: Prefer classList over style. It keeps your design in CSS and your logic in JS.

subTopic.name: Event handling
Event bubbling and capturing
Event delegation
Form handling and validation
localStorage and sessionStorage
Cookies overview
subTopic.notes:
What is it?
Cookies are tiny pieces of data stored by the browser and sent to the server with every request to that site. They are mainly used for login sessions.

Key points:
- Set with document.cookie = "name=value; attributes".
- Useful attributes: expires or max-age, path, Secure, SameSite.
- HttpOnly cookies cannot be read by JS. The server sets them, and this protects against XSS.
- Size is about 4KB, much smaller than localStorage.
- Difference from localStorage: cookies are automatically sent to the server.

Code:
document.cookie = "theme=dark; max-age=604800; path=/; SameSite=Lax";

console.log(document.cookie);   // "theme=dark"

// delete a cookie
document.cookie = "theme=; max-age=0; path=/";

Real-world example:
When you log in to Skillora, the server sends a session cookie. Every next request carries it, so the server knows who you are.

Remember: Use cookies for things the server needs. Use localStorage for things only the browser needs.

Component-based thinking
subTopic.notes:
WHAT IT IS
Component-based thinking means breaking a screen into small, independent pieces. Each piece does one job. You build the pieces first, then put them together like LEGO blocks.

HOW TO THINK
1. Look at the design.
2. Draw a box around every repeating or separate part.
3. Give each box a name (Header, Card, Button).
4. Ask: 'Can I use this again somewhere else?' If yes, it should be its own component.

REAL-WORLD EXAMPLE
Open Swiggy or Zomato. The restaurant list has 50 cards, but the card is built only once and reused 50 times with different data. The page is just: Header + SearchBar + RestaurantList + Footer.

CODE
function App() {
  return (
    <>
      <Header />
      <SearchBar />
      <RestaurantList />
      <Footer />
    </>
  );
}

TEACHER TIP
If a component is more than about 100 lines, it is probably doing too many jobs. Split it.

subTopic.name: Reusable UI components
Responsive landing page
subTopic.notes:
WHAT IT IS A landing page is the first page a visitor sees. Responsive means it looks good on mobile, tablet and desktop without breaking. STANDARD SECTIONS Navbar -> Hero (headline + button) -> Features -> Testimonials -> Pricing -> Call to Action -> Footer KEY IDEAS - Mobile-first: design for small screens first, then add rules for bigger screens. - Use flexible layouts (flex, grid) instead of fixed widths. - Use relative units (%, rem) and max-width. - Test at 360px, 768px and 1280px. REAL-WORLD EXAMPLE The Notion or Stripe homepage: on a phone the features are stacked in one column; on a laptop they sit in three columns. CODE (Tailwind)

Learn Skills Faster

TEACHER TIP No class prefix means 'mobile'. md: means 'tablet and above'. lg: means 'laptop and above'.

WHAT IT IS Accessible navigation can be used by everyone, including people who use only a keyboard or a screen reader. MUST-DO LIST - Use real tags:

subTopic.notes:
WHAT IT IS A dashboard shows a lot of information in one organized place so users can understand it quickly and act on it. COMMON LAYOUT - Sidebar (left): navigation. - Top bar: search, profile, notifications. - Main area: stat cards on top, then charts or tables below. DESIGN RULES - Put the most important numbers at the top. - Use a grid so cards line up. - Keep spacing consistent. - On mobile, hide the sidebar behind a menu button. REAL-WORLD EXAMPLE The Skillora dashboard: cards for Pending, Completed and Wishlist projects, with a progress bar under each course. CODE function DashboardLayout() { return (
Sidebar
Courses list here

subTopic.name: Search and filter interfaces

UI consistency and visual hierarchy
subTopic.notes:
WHAT IT IS - Consistency: similar things look and behave the same everywhere. - Visual hierarchy: the design guides the eye to the most important thing first. TOOLS FOR HIERARCHY - Size: bigger means more important. - Weight: bold stands out. - Color and contrast: bright or dark stands out from soft or grey. - Spacing: related items are close, unrelated items have more space. - Position: top and left are seen first. CONSISTENCY CHECKLIST - Same button style for the same action. - Same spacing scale (use multiples of 4 or 8). - Same font sizes for headings. - Same icon style. - Same wording (do not use 'Sign in' on one page and 'Login' on another). REAL-WORLD EXAMPLE On a pricing page, the plan name is big and bold, the price is the biggest thing, the feature list is small and grey, and the 'Buy' button is bright. Your eye reads it in the right order without thinking. CODE

Pro Plan

₹499/month

  • Unlimited courses
  • Certificates
TEACHER TIP Squint at your screen. The things you can still see are your real hierarchy. If it is not the right thing, fix the sizes and colors.

subTopic.name: Frontend project documentation
subTopic.notes:
WHAT IT IS
Documentation explains your project so other people (and you after 3 months) can understand, run and use it. For students, a good README is also a big plus for recruiters.

WHAT A GOOD README HAS
1. Project name and one-line description
2. Live demo link and screenshots or GIF
3. Features list
4. Tech stack
5. How to run it locally (install and start commands)
6. Folder structure (short)
7. Challenges you solved or what you learned
8. Future improvements
9. Your contact or links

OTHER DOCS WORTH ADDING
- Comments only for 'why', not for obvious 'what'.
- A components list with their props.
- An .env.example file if you use environment variables.

REAL-WORLD EXAMPLE
A recruiter opens 20 GitHub profiles in one day. The project with screenshots and a clear 'How to run' gets the interview call. The project with an empty README gets closed in 5 seconds.

CODE (README.md template)
# Skillora
A learning path platform to track courses and progress.

## Live Demo
https://your-link.com

## Features
- Course dashboard with progress tracking
- Pending, completed and wishlist projects
- Fully responsive UI

## Tech Stack
React, Tailwind CSS, Context API

## Getting Started
git clone https://github.com/username/skillora.git
cd skillora
npm install
npm run dev

## What I Learned
- Managing shared state with Context
- Building responsive layouts

TEACHER TIP
Write the README as if the reader has never seen your project and has only 2 minutes.

subTopic.name: Creating a React project with Vite
subTopic.notes:
📘 What is it?
Vite (say "veet") is a modern tool that sets up a React project for you and runs it super fast. Think of it as the ready-made kitchen: you just start cooking (coding).

🛠 Steps
```bash
npm create vite@latest my-app -- --template react
cd my-app
npm install
npm run dev
```
Open the link shown in the terminal (usually http://localhost:5173).

📂 Important files
- index.html -> the single HTML page
- src/main.jsx -> starting point, mounts React into the page
- src/App.jsx -> your first component
- package.json -> list of libraries and scripts

🌍 Real-world example
Before building a shopping website, you first create the project folder with Vite. It is like laying the foundation before building a house.

✅ Remember
- Use `npm run dev` while developing, `npm run build` for the final version.
- Saving a file updates the browser instantly (Hot Reload).

subTopic.name: JSX
subTopic.notes:
📘 What is it? JSX is a way to write HTML-like code inside JavaScript. The browser doesn't understand it directly; Vite converts it into normal JavaScript for you. 💻 Example ```jsx function App() { const name = "Anshika"; return (

Hello, {name}!

2 + 2 = {2 + 2}

); } ``` 📏 Rules to remember 1. Return only ONE parent element (wrap with
or <> ). 2. Close every tag: , . 3. Use `className` instead of `class`. 4. Use camelCase: `onClick`, `tabIndex`. 5. Use `{ }` to put JavaScript inside JSX. 🌍 Real-world example On a profile page, you write

{user.name}

. The name changes for every user, but the layout stays the same. ✅ Remember Curly braces `{ }` = "JavaScript zone" inside JSX.

subTopic.name: Function components
Props and component composition
Conditional rendering
Lists and keys
Event handling
State with useState
subTopic.notes:
📘 What is it? State is the memory of a component. When state changes, React updates the screen automatically. `useState` is the hook used to create it. 💻 Example ```jsx import { useState } from "react"; function Counter() { const [count, setCount] = useState(0); return (

Count: {count}

); } ``` 🔍 Understand the line `const [value, setValue] = useState(initialValue);` - value -> current data - setValue -> function to change it - initialValue -> starting data 🌍 Real-world example A like button: state stores whether it is liked. Click it and the heart turns red. Dark mode toggle also uses state. ✅ Remember - Never change state directly (`count = 5` is wrong). Always use the setter. - Call hooks only at the top of the component, not inside if or loops.

subTopic.name: State updates and re-rendering
subTopic.notes:
📘 What happens when state changes?
1. You call the setter (setCount).
2. React schedules a re-render.
3. The component function runs again with the new value.
4. The screen updates.

⏳ State updates are not instant
```jsx
setCount(count + 1);
console.log(count); // still the OLD value
```

🔁 Use the functional update when the new value depends on the old one
```jsx
setCount((prev) => prev + 1);
```

📦 Objects and arrays: make a NEW copy
```jsx
// Wrong: cart.push(item)
setCart([...cart, item]);                 // add
setCart(cart.filter((i) => i.id !== id)); // remove
setUser({ ...user, name: "Anshika" });    // update one field
```

🌍 Real-world example
When you add a product to the cart, a new cart array is created, and the cart icon number updates.

✅ Remember
React only re-renders if it sees a NEW value. Mutating the old array or object will not work.

subTopic.name: Controlled inputs
Lifting state up
Children and composition
Component organization
subTopic.notes:
📘 What is it? Keeping your components in a clean structure so the project stays easy to read as it grows. 📂 Example structure ``` src/ components/ Navbar.jsx CourseCard.jsx Button.jsx pages/ Dashboard.jsx Profile.jsx App.jsx main.jsx ``` 💻 Export and import ```jsx // CourseCard.jsx export default function CourseCard({ title }) { return

{title}

; } // Dashboard.jsx import CourseCard from "../components/CourseCard"; ``` ✂️ When to split a component? - It is getting long (around 100+ lines). - It is used in more than one place. - It does more than one job. 🌍 Real-world example Like a school: classrooms (pages) contain desks (components). Everything has a proper place, so anyone can find it quickly. ✅ Remember - One component per file, file name = component name (PascalCase). - Reusable pieces go in components/, full screens go in pages/.

subTopic.name: React DevTools
subTopic.notes:
📘 What is it?
React DevTools is a free browser extension (Chrome/Edge/Firefox) that lets you look inside your React app: components, props, and state.

🛠 How to use
1. Install "React Developer Tools" from your browser's extension store.
2. Run your app and open Inspect (F12).
3. Use the two new tabs: Components and Profiler.

🔍 Components tab
- See the component tree.
- Click any component to view its props and state.
- Edit state or props live to test changes.

⏱ Profiler tab
- Record interactions and see which components re-rendered and how long they took.

⚙️ Handy setting
Turn on "Highlight updates when components render" to see a colored border flash around re-rendering components.

🌍 Real-world example
The cart count shows the wrong number. Open DevTools, click the Cart component, and check its state. You instantly see whether the data or the display is wrong.

✅ Remember
DevTools is for debugging, not just console.log. Use it whenever something looks wrong.

subTopic.name: React rendering model
subTopic.notes:
📘 What is it?
Rendering means React calling your component functions to find out what the UI should look like.

🔄 Three steps
1. Trigger: first load, or a state change.
2. Render: React runs your component and gets new JSX.
3. Commit: React compares with the old result and updates only the changed parts of the real DOM.

💻 Example
```jsx
function Counter() {
  console.log("Rendered!");
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0);
  return <button onClick={() => setCount(count + 1)}>{count}</button>;
}
```
Each click prints "Rendered!" because state changed.

🔁 When does a component re-render?
- Its own state changes.
- Its props change.
- Its parent re-renders.

🌍 Real-world example
Like a restaurant: you place an order (trigger), the kitchen prepares it (render), the waiter serves only the new dish to your table (commit). The whole restaurant is not rebuilt.

✅ Remember
- Keep components "pure": the same props and state give the same JSX.
- Do not change variables or call APIs directly in the render body.
- In development, Strict Mode may render twice on purpose to catch bugs.

React Router setup
subTopic.notes:
React Router lets your React app show different pages without reloading the browser. This is called a Single Page Application (SPA).

Steps:
1. Install it: npm install react-router-dom
2. Wrap your whole app in <BrowserRouter> (only once, at the top).
3. Inside the app, define which page shows for which URL.

```jsx
// main.jsx
import { BrowserRouter } from 'react-router-dom';

ReactDOM.createRoot(document.getElementById('root')).render(
  <BrowserRouter>
    <App />
  </BrowserRouter>
);
```

Real-world example: On Skillora, when you click 'Dashboard' and then 'Courses', the URL changes and the screen updates instantly with no full page refresh. React Router makes that possible.

Remember: No BrowserRouter = no routing. Routes, Link and useNavigate will all throw errors.

Link and NavLink
subTopic.notes:
Never use a normal <a href> for moving between pages in React. It reloads the whole page. Use Link instead.

```jsx
import { Link, NavLink } from 'react-router-dom';

<Link to='/courses'>Courses</Link>
```

NavLink is a special Link that knows if it is the current page. This is perfect for menus.

```jsx
<NavLink
  to='/dashboard'
  className={({ isActive }) => isActive ? 'text-blue-600 font-bold' : 'text-gray-600'}
>
  Dashboard
</NavLink>
```

Difference:
- Link = simple navigation.
- NavLink = navigation + active styling.

Real-world example: In Skillora's sidebar, the menu item of the page you are currently on is highlighted in blue. That is NavLink using isActive.

Common mistake: Using href instead of to.

404 - Page not found

Go back home

subTopic.name: Fetch and Axios overview

Base URLs and environment variables
subTopic.notes:
A base URL is the common starting part of all your API addresses, like https://api.skillora.com. You write it once and add only the endpoint (/courses) later.

An environment variable (env) stores values that change between development and production, like the API URL or keys. You keep them in a .env file.

.env file (Vite):
VITE_API_URL=http://localhost:5000/api

Using it in code:
const BASE_URL = import.meta.env.VITE_API_URL;
axios.get(`${BASE_URL}/courses`);

Rules to remember:
- Vite variables must start with VITE_. Create React App variables start with REACT_APP_.
- Restart the dev server after changing .env.
- Add .env to .gitignore.
- Never put secret keys in React env files. Anyone can see them in the browser.

Real-world example: On your laptop the API is http://localhost:5000, but after deployment it is https://api.skillora.com. You only change the env value, not your code.

Teacher tip: Hard-coded URLs are the number one reason "it works on my machine but not after deploy".

subTopic.name: Loading and error states
Request cancellation
Avoiding stale responses
Context vs global state
Redux Toolkit overview
Zustand overview
Server state vs client state
subTopic.notes:
Not all state is the same. Knowing the difference makes your code cleaner.

Client state: data that lives only in your browser and you fully control.
Examples: is the modal open, selected tab, dark mode, form input text.

Server state: data that lives on a server database, you only keep a copy. It can become old, can be changed by others, and needs loading/error handling.
Examples: course list, user profile, comments.

Why it matters:
- Client state: useState, Context, Zustand are enough.
- Server state: needs caching, refetching, loading, error and sync. Tools like TanStack Query are made for this.

Example:
const [isMenuOpen, setIsMenuOpen] = useState(false); // client state
const { data: courses } = useQuery({ queryKey: ["courses"], queryFn: getCourses }); // server state

Real-world example: In Skillora, "sidebar open or closed" is client state. "List of courses and progress" is server state because it comes from the database.

Teacher tip: A common mistake is to copy server data into Redux or useState by hand. Let a server-state tool manage it instead.

subTopic.name: TanStack Query overview
Caching and invalidation
Optimistic updates
Pagination and filtering
subTopic.notes:
Pagination means loading data in small pages (10 items at a time) instead of everything at once. Filtering means asking only for the data that matches a condition (like category or search text).

Both are usually sent as query parameters in the URL:
GET /courses?page=2&limit=10&category=frontend

With TanStack Query, put page and filters in the queryKey so each combination is cached separately:

const [page, setPage] = useState(1);
const [category, setCategory] = useState("all");

const { data, isLoading } = useQuery({
  queryKey: ["courses", page, category],
  queryFn: () =>
    axios
      .get("/courses", { params: { page, limit: 10, category } })
      .then((res) => res.data),
  placeholderData: (previous) => previous, // keeps old page visible while loading
});

<button onClick={() => setPage((p) => p - 1)} disabled={page === 1}>Prev</button>
<button onClick={() => setPage((p) => p + 1)}>Next</button>

Real-world example: Skillora may have 100+ courses. Show 10 per page, with a dropdown filter for "Frontend", "Backend", "AI". Only the needed data is loaded.

Teacher tip: Reset page to 1 whenever the filter changes, otherwise you may land on an empty page.

subTopic.name: Authentication state
Benefits of TypeScript
subTopic.notes:
**What is it?**
TypeScript is JavaScript with types. You tell the code what kind of data a variable holds, and TypeScript warns you about mistakes before you run the app.

**Why use it?**
- Catches bugs while you type, not after users find them
- Better autocomplete in VS Code
- Code explains itself, so teams understand it faster
- Safer refactoring (rename something and see everything that breaks)

**Example:**
```ts
function add(a: number, b: number) {
  return a + b;
}

add(5, '10'); // Error: '10' is a string, not a number
```
In plain JavaScript, `5 + '10'` gives `'510'` and nobody warns you.

**Real-world scenario:**
In an e-commerce app, a developer passes the price as the string '499' instead of the number 499. The cart total becomes wrong. TypeScript shows a red line immediately, so the bug never reaches production.

**Remember:** TypeScript is checked at compile time. The browser still runs plain JavaScript.

subTopic.name: TypeScript setup
subTopic.notes:
**Steps to start a TypeScript project:**
```bash
npm init -y
npm install -D typescript
npx tsc --init
```
`tsc --init` creates `tsconfig.json`, the settings file for the compiler.

**Important tsconfig options:**
```json
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "target": "ES2020",
    "module": "ESNext",
    "strict": true,
    "outDir": "./dist",
    "rootDir": "./src"
  }
}
```
- `target`: which JavaScript version to output
- `strict`: turns on all the safety checks (always keep it true)
- `outDir`: where compiled .js files go

**Compile and run:**
```bash
npx tsc          # compiles src/*.ts to dist/*.js
node dist/index.js
```

**Real-world scenario:**
When you create a React app with Vite (`npm create vite@latest my-app -- --template react-ts`), the setup is already done for you. For a Node/Express backend, you set it up yourself like above.

**Tip:** Files use the `.ts` extension (`.tsx` for React components).

subTopic.name: Primitive and inferred types
subTopic.notes:
**Primitive types:** `string`, `number`, `boolean`, `null`, `undefined`, `bigint`, `symbol`.

```ts
let name: string = 'Anshika';
let age: number = 21;
let isStudent: boolean = true;
```

**Type inference:** If you give a value right away, TypeScript guesses the type for you. You do not need to write it.
```ts
let city = 'Delhi';   // inferred as string
city = 42;            // Error
```

**Be careful with `any`:**
```ts
let data: any = 'hello';
data = 100;  // allowed, but you lose all safety
```
Avoid `any`. Use it only as a last option.

**Real-world scenario:**
In a login form: `let email: string`, `let rememberMe: boolean`. If you accidentally assign `rememberMe = 'yes'`, TypeScript stops you.

**Rule of thumb:** Let TypeScript infer when the value is obvious. Write the type yourself for function parameters and when you declare a variable without a value.

subTopic.name: Arrays and tuples
subTopic.notes:
**Arrays:** a list of items of the same type.
```ts
let skills: string[] = ['HTML', 'CSS', 'React'];
let marks: Array<number> = [88, 92, 75];

skills.push('Node');  // ok
skills.push(10);      // Error
```

**Tuples:** a fixed-length array where each position has its own type.
```ts
let user: [string, number] = ['Rahul', 22];
// user[0] is string, user[1] is number

user = [22, 'Rahul']; // Error, wrong order
```

**Real-world scenario:**
React's `useState` returns a tuple: `[value, setValue]`. The first item is the state, the second is a function. That is why you can name them anything.
```ts
const [count, setCount] = useState<number>(0);
```

**Difference in one line:**
- Array = many items, same type, any length
- Tuple = few items, different types, fixed positions

subTopic.name: Interfaces and type aliases
Union and intersection types
Generics
Narrowing and discriminated unions
Utility types
Typing React props and events
Typing Express handlers
Typing API contracts
Shared types across frontend and backend
Runtime validation vs static types
Strict mode and avoiding any
subTopic.notes:
**Strict mode:** In `tsconfig.json`, `"strict": true` turns on a group of safety checks. Always keep it on for new projects.

**What it includes:**
- `noImplicitAny`: you cannot leave a type unknown by accident
- `strictNullChecks`: `null` and `undefined` are not allowed unless you say so
- `strictFunctionTypes`, `strictPropertyInitialization`, and more

**Example (strictNullChecks):**
```ts
function getLength(text: string | null) {
  return text.length;      // Error: text may be null
  return text?.length ?? 0; // safe
}
```

**Why avoid `any`?**
`any` switches off type checking, so you are back to plain JavaScript.
```ts
let value: any = 'hi';
value.toFixed(); // no error, but crashes at runtime
```

**Better choices:**
- `unknown`: safe version of any, you must check the type before using it
- Proper interfaces or generics
- Type guards and narrowing
```ts
function handle(input: unknown) {
  if (typeof input === 'string') {
    console.log(input.toUpperCase()); // safe
  }
}
```

**Real-world scenario:**
A team marks every API response as `any` to finish quickly. Later a renamed field breaks the checkout page and nobody sees it until users complain. With strict mode and real types, the build fails first.

**Teacher's rule:** `any` is a last resort. If you feel the urge to write it, try `unknown` or a proper type first.

subTopic.name: What Node.js is
subTopic.notes:
### Definition
Node.js is an open-source, cross-platform **JavaScript runtime** built on Chrome's V8 engine. It lets you run JavaScript outside the browser (servers, CLIs, tooling, scripts).

### Key Points
- Node.js is a **runtime**, not a language or a framework.
- JavaScript code runs on a **single main thread** using an **event-driven, non-blocking I/O** model.
- **V8** executes JavaScript; **libuv** provides the event loop, async I/O and a thread pool.
- Comes bundled with **npm**, the largest package registry.
- Use **LTS (even-numbered) releases** for production.
- Great for: REST/GraphQL APIs, real-time apps (WebSockets), streaming, CLIs, microservices, build tools.
- Weak at: long CPU-bound work on the main thread (offload with `worker_threads` or child processes).

### Architecture
```
Your JS code
   |
Node.js APIs (fs, http, net, crypto ...)
   |
V8 (JS engine)  +  libuv (event loop, async I/O)
   |
Operating System
```

### Minimal Example
```js
const http = require('node:http');

const server = http.createServer((req, res) => {
  res.writeHead(200, { 'Content-Type': 'text/plain' });
  res.end('Hello from Node.js');
});

server.listen(3000, () => console.log('Listening on http://localhost:3000'));
```

### Mastery Checklist
- Explain why Node handles many concurrent connections with one thread.
- Distinguish I/O-bound vs CPU-bound workloads.
- Know the release lines (Current, Active LTS, Maintenance LTS).
- Check versions: `node -v`, `npm -v`.

subTopic.name: Node.js and V8
subTopic.notes:
### What V8 Is
V8 is Google's open-source JavaScript and WebAssembly engine written in C++. Node.js **embeds** V8 and adds its own APIs (fs, net, http...) through C++ bindings.

### How V8 Runs Code
1. **Parse** source into an AST.
2. **Ignition** (interpreter) generates and runs bytecode.
3. Hot code is **JIT-compiled** by optimizing compilers (Sparkplug / Maglev / TurboFan) into machine code.
4. If assumptions break, V8 **deoptimizes** back to slower code.
5. **Garbage collector** (generational: young + old space) reclaims memory automatically.

### Performance Tips
- Keep object **shapes (hidden classes)** consistent: initialize all properties in the same order.
- Avoid changing a variable's type repeatedly (number -> string).
- Avoid `delete` on object properties in hot paths.
- Prefer typed arrays / Buffers for binary data.

### Memory and Flags
```js
console.log(process.versions.v8); // V8 version bundled with Node
console.log(process.memoryUsage()); // rss, heapTotal, heapUsed, external
```
```bash
# Raise the old-space heap limit to 4 GB
node --max-old-space-size=4096 app.js

# List V8 options
node --v8-options
```

### Mastery Checklist
- Know the difference between V8 (engine) and Node (runtime).
- Understand JIT, deoptimization and GC at a high level.
- Diagnose memory growth with `process.memoryUsage()`, `--inspect` and heap snapshots.

subTopic.name: Browser JavaScript vs Node.js
subTopic.notes:
### Same Language, Different Environment
Both run ECMAScript (same syntax, Promises, async/await, classes), but the **host environment** provides different APIs.

### Key Differences
- **Global object**: browser has `window`; Node has `global`. Use **`globalThis`** for portable code.
- **DOM / BOM**: `document`, `window.location`, `localStorage` exist only in browsers.
- **System access**: Node can use `fs`, `os`, `child_process`, `net`; browsers are sandboxed.
- **Modules**: browsers use ES modules via `<script type="module">`; Node supports CommonJS and ES modules.
- **Process info**: Node has `process`, `__dirname` (CJS), `Buffer`; browsers do not.
- **Fetch**: `fetch` is built in to both (Node 18+).
- **Security model**: browser = untrusted code with same-origin policy/CORS; Node = full OS permissions of the user running it.
- **Version control**: you choose your Node version; browser versions vary per user.

### Portable Code Example
```js
const isNode = typeof process !== 'undefined' && !!process.versions?.node;
const isBrowser = typeof window !== 'undefined';

console.log(isNode ? 'Running in Node' : 'Running in a browser');
console.log(globalThis === (isNode ? global : window)); // true
```

### Mastery Checklist
- Never use `window`/`document` in Node code (ReferenceError).
- Know which Web APIs Node now supports (fetch, URL, AbortController, TextEncoder, structuredClone, WebStreams).
- Understand why CORS does not apply to server-to-server requests.

subTopic.name: Running scripts and using the REPL
subTopic.notes:
### Running Scripts
```bash
node app.js              # run a file
node app.js arg1 arg2    # pass arguments (process.argv)
node -e "console.log(1+1)"   # evaluate a string
node -p "process.version"    # evaluate and print result
node --watch app.js      # restart on file changes (built-in)
node --env-file=.env app.js  # load env variables from a file
node --inspect app.js    # enable debugger (Chrome DevTools / VS Code)
```

### Shebang for Executable Scripts
```js
#!/usr/bin/env node
console.log('I am a CLI script');
```
```bash
chmod +x cli.js && ./cli.js
```

### The REPL (Read-Eval-Print Loop)
Start it by running `node` with no file.
```
> 2 + 3
5
> const a = [1,2,3]
> a.map(x => x * 2)
[ 2, 4, 6 ]
> _            // underscore holds the last result
[ 2, 4, 6 ]
> .help        // list REPL commands
```

### REPL Commands
- `.help` - show commands
- `.editor` - multi-line editor mode (Ctrl+D to run)
- `.load file.js` / `.save file.js` - load or save the session
- `.break` / `.clear` - abort multi-line input / reset context
- `.exit` (or Ctrl+C twice / Ctrl+D) - quit
- **Tab** for autocompletion; built-in modules are available without `require`.

### Mastery Checklist
- Use `process.argv.slice(2)` to read CLI arguments.
- Use REPL for quick experiments and API exploration.
- Know how to attach a debugger with `--inspect` / `--inspect-brk`.

subTopic.name: CommonJS and ES modules
package.json and npm scripts
subTopic.notes:
### package.json
The manifest of a Node project: metadata, dependencies, scripts, entry points.
```bash
npm init -y   # generate a default package.json
```
```json
{
  "name": "my-app",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "description": "Demo app",
  "type": "module",
  "main": "src/index.js",
  "exports": "./src/index.js",
  "scripts": {
    "start": "node src/index.js",
    "dev": "node --watch src/index.js",
    "test": "node --test",
    "lint": "eslint .",
    "prebuild": "npm run lint",
    "build": "tsc"
  },
  "engines": { "node": ">=20" },
  "dependencies": { "express": "^4.19.0" },
  "devDependencies": { "eslint": "^9.0.0" },
  "private": true
}
```

### Important Fields
- `name`, `version` (semver), `description`, `license`
- `main` / `exports` - package entry points
- `type` - `commonjs` (default) or `module`
- `bin` - maps command names to executable files
- `files` - what gets published
- `engines` - supported Node/npm versions
- `private: true` - prevents accidental publishing

### npm Scripts
```bash
npm start          # shortcut for 'npm run start'
npm test           # shortcut for 'npm run test'
npm run dev        # custom scripts need 'run'
npm run build -- --watch   # pass extra args after --
```
- **Lifecycle hooks**: `pre<name>` and `post<name>` run automatically before/after a script (e.g. `prebuild`, `postinstall`).
- Local binaries in `node_modules/.bin` are on the PATH inside scripts.
- Chain commands with `&&` (sequential) or tools like `npm-run-all` for parallel.
- `npx <pkg>` runs a package binary without installing globally.

### Mastery Checklist
- Understand semver: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH.
- Use `exports` to control a package's public API.
- Keep scripts small and composable.

subTopic.name: Dependency management
subTopic.notes:
### Dependency Types
- **dependencies** - needed at runtime.
- **devDependencies** - build/test/lint tools only.
- **peerDependencies** - host app must provide it (common for plugins/libraries).
- **optionalDependencies** - install failure will not break the install.

### Common Commands
```bash
npm install                 # install everything from package.json / lockfile
npm install express         # add a runtime dependency
npm install -D jest         # add a dev dependency
npm install express@4.19.2  # exact version
npm uninstall express       # remove
npm update                  # update within allowed ranges
npm outdated                # show newer versions available
npm ls --depth=0            # list top-level installed packages
npm ci                      # clean, reproducible install from lockfile (CI)
npm audit                   # check for known vulnerabilities
npm audit fix               # auto-fix where safe
```

### Semantic Versioning Ranges
- `^1.2.3` - allows 1.x.x (minor + patch updates)
- `~1.2.3` - allows 1.2.x (patch updates only)
- `1.2.3` - exact version
- `*` / `latest` - avoid in production

### Lockfile
`package-lock.json` pins the exact dependency tree. **Commit it** to version control so every machine and CI run installs identical versions. Use `npm ci` in pipelines.

### Advanced
```json
{
  "overrides": { "lodash": "4.17.21" }
}
```
- `overrides` forces a nested dependency version (fix vulnerabilities in transitive deps).
- **Global vs local**: install tools locally and run with `npx`; reserve `-g` for true CLIs.
- Alternatives: **pnpm** (fast, disk-efficient) and **Yarn**.
- Workspaces (`"workspaces": ["packages/*"]`) manage monorepos.

### Security Best Practices
- Review new packages (maintainers, downloads, last update).
- Run `npm audit` regularly and enable automated dependency updates.
- Never commit `node_modules`; add it to `.gitignore`.

### Mastery Checklist
- Explain `^` vs `~` and lockfile purpose.
- Know when to use `npm ci` vs `npm install`.
- Keep the dependency tree small and audited.

subTopic.name: Built-in modules
process and environment variables
File system and path modules
Events and EventEmitter
Buffers and streams
Asynchronous I/O
Node.js event loop
Graceful process shutdown
Creating a backend project
subTopic.notes:
### What it is
Creating a backend project means building a clean, repeatable baseline (package manifest, dependencies, scripts, version control, folder layout) that every other practice sits on.

### Key points
- `npm init -y` generates `package.json`, the single source of truth for name, scripts and dependencies.
- Use ES modules (set `type` to `module` in package.json) so you can use `import`/`export`.
- Separate `dependencies` (needed at runtime) from `devDependencies` (nodemon, test tools, linters).
- Commit the lockfile (`package-lock.json`) so installs are reproducible; use `npm ci` in CI.
- Pin the Node version with the `engines` field or an `.nvmrc` file.
- Always add a `.gitignore` (node_modules, .env, logs, dist) before the first commit.
- Add a `/health` route early: it proves the project boots and is useful for deployments.

### Quick start
```bash
mkdir my-api && cd my-api
npm init -y
npm i express dotenv
npm i -D nodemon
npm pkg set type=module
npm pkg set scripts.dev='nodemon src/server.js'
npm pkg set scripts.start='node src/server.js'
git init
printf 'node_modules\n.env\nlogs\n' > .gitignore
```

### Typical starting layout
```text
my-api/
  src/
    app.js
    server.js
    config/
    routes/
    controllers/
    services/
    models/
    middleware/
  tests/
  .env.example
  .gitignore
  package.json
```

### Mastery checklist
- Can you go from an empty folder to a running server in under 5 minutes?
- Do `npm run dev` and `npm start` both work for a new teammate with only the README?

subTopic.name: Environment-based configuration
subTopic.notes:
### What it is
Environment-based configuration means the same code runs everywhere (local, test, staging, production) and only the environment variables change. This follows the 12-factor app principle: config lives in the environment, not in the code.

### Key points
- Read values from `process.env`; load a `.env` file locally with `dotenv` (or `node --env-file=.env` on Node 20+).
- All env values are strings. Convert them: `Number(process.env.PORT)`, `process.env.DEBUG === 'true'`.
- Provide safe defaults for non-sensitive values (port, log level), but never for secrets.
- Centralise access in one `config` module. Never scatter `process.env.X` across the codebase.
- Commit `.env.example` (keys, no real values); never commit `.env`.
- Use `NODE_ENV` (`development`, `test`, `production`) to select behaviour.

### Example
```js
// src/config/index.js
import 'dotenv/config';

export const config = {
  env: process.env.NODE_ENV || 'development',
  port: Number(process.env.PORT) || 3000,
  db: { uri: process.env.DATABASE_URL },
  logLevel: process.env.LOG_LEVEL || 'info',
};
```

### .env.example
```bash
NODE_ENV=development
PORT=3000
DATABASE_URL=postgres://user:pass@localhost:5432/app
LOG_LEVEL=debug
JWT_SECRET=change-me
```

### Per-environment files
```bash
# load a specific file
node --env-file=.env.production src/server.js
```

### Common mistakes
- Hard-coding URLs/keys in source files.
- Forgetting that `PORT="3000"` is a string, not a number.
- Importing config before `dotenv` has loaded (import `dotenv/config` first).

subTopic.name: Separating app and server entry points
Routes, controllers, services, and models
Configuration validation
Logging setup
Error handling strategy
Development tools such as nodemon
subTopic.notes:
### What it is
Development tools speed up the feedback loop: auto-restart on changes, linting, formatting, debugging and pre-commit checks. They belong in `devDependencies` and never run in production.

### nodemon
- Watches files and restarts the server when they change.
- Configure it with a `nodemon.json` file using keys such as `watch`, `ext`, `ignore` and `delay`.
- Node 18.11+ also has a built-in alternative: `node --watch src/server.js`.

```bash
npm i -D nodemon
npm pkg set scripts.dev='nodemon src/server.js'
npm run dev
```

### Other essential tools
| Tool | Purpose |
|---|---|
| ESLint | Catch bugs and enforce code rules |
| Prettier | Automatic consistent formatting |
| Husky + lint-staged | Run lint/format/tests before each commit |
| Jest / Vitest + Supertest | Unit and API tests |
| tsx / ts-node | Run TypeScript directly in development |
| cross-env | Set env variables across Windows/macOS/Linux |
| Postman / Bruno / Thunder Client | Manually test APIs |

### Debugging
```bash
# start with the inspector, then attach VS Code or chrome://inspect
node --inspect src/server.js
```

### Recommended script set
```bash
npm pkg set scripts.lint='eslint .'
npm pkg set scripts.format='prettier --write .'
npm pkg set scripts.test='vitest run'
```

### Tips
- Ignore test files, logs and `node_modules` in the watcher to avoid restart loops.
- Keep `start` (plain `node`) separate from `dev` (nodemon) so production never depends on dev tooling.

subTopic.name: Dependency boundaries
Feature-based folder organization
subTopic.notes:
### What it is
Instead of grouping files by technical type (all controllers together, all models together), you group them by business feature (users, orders, payments). Everything about one feature lives in one folder.

### Layer-based (type-based) structure
```text
src/
  controllers/  user.controller.js  order.controller.js
  services/     user.service.js     order.service.js
  models/       user.model.js       order.model.js
  routes/       user.routes.js      order.routes.js
```
Fine for small apps, but adding one feature touches many folders.

### Feature-based structure
```text
src/
  modules/
    users/
      user.routes.js
      user.controller.js
      user.service.js
      user.model.js
      user.schema.js      # validation
      user.test.js
      index.js            # public API of the module
    orders/
      ...
  shared/
    middleware/
    utils/
    errors/
  config/
  app.js
  server.js
```

### Why it scales
- High cohesion: related code sits together, so it is easy to find and change.
- Low coupling: each feature exposes a small public API through `index.js`.
- Easy ownership: teams own features. A feature can later become its own microservice.
- Easy deletion: removing a feature means removing one folder.

### Public API of a module
```js
// modules/users/index.js
export { default as userRoutes } from './user.routes.js';
export { findById } from './user.service.js';
// other modules import ONLY from 'modules/users', never from its internal files
```

### Rules of thumb
- Code used by 2+ features goes to `shared/`.
- Do not let features import each other's internals; go through the public `index.js`.
- Keep the layered separation (route/controller/service/model) INSIDE each feature.

subTopic.name: Managing secrets
subTopic.notes:
### What it is
Secrets are credentials that grant access: database passwords, API keys, JWT signing keys, OAuth client secrets, private certificates. Leaking one can mean a full breach, so how you store and handle them is a core backend skill.

### Golden rules
- **Never commit secrets** to Git (not even in a private repo). Git history keeps them forever.
- Keep secrets in environment variables locally and in a **secret manager** in production.
- Add `.env` to `.gitignore`; commit only `.env.example` with fake placeholders.
- Use **different secrets per environment**; a dev key must never work in production.
- Apply **least privilege**: a key should only be able to do what it needs.
- **Rotate** secrets regularly and immediately after any suspected leak.
- Never log secrets, return them in API responses, or put them in URLs or error messages.

### Generating a strong secret
```bash
openssl rand -hex 32
```

### Where to store them
| Environment | Option |
|---|---|
| Local | `.env` file (git-ignored) |
| CI/CD | Encrypted pipeline secrets (GitHub Actions secrets, GitLab variables) |
| Production | AWS Secrets Manager, GCP Secret Manager, Azure Key Vault, HashiCorp Vault, Doppler, or your host's secret settings |

### Protecting the repo
```bash
# scan for leaked secrets before committing or in CI
gitleaks detect
```
Use GitHub secret scanning and pre-commit hooks as a safety net.

### If a secret leaks
1. Revoke/rotate it immediately.
2. Check access logs for misuse.
3. Remove it from code, then fix the process. Rewriting Git history alone is NOT enough, because the key is already compromised.

### Code habit
```js
// fail fast if a required secret is missing, never fall back to a hard-coded default
if (!process.env.JWT_SECRET) throw new Error('JWT_SECRET is required');
```

subTopic.name: Development vs production settings
subTopic.notes:
### What it is
The same codebase must behave differently depending on where it runs. Development optimises for speed and debugging; production optimises for security, performance, stability and observability.

### Key differences
| Concern | Development | Production |
|---|---|---|
| `NODE_ENV` | `development` | `production` |
| Logging | Pretty, verbose (`debug`) | JSON, `info` or `warn` |
| Errors | Include stack traces | Generic messages only, details in logs |
| Restarts | nodemon auto-reload | Process manager / container orchestrator |
| Database | Local/Docker DB, seed data | Managed DB, backups, migrations |
| Secrets | `.env` file | Secret manager |
| CORS | Open or localhost origins | Strict allowlist |
| Security | Relaxed for convenience | Helmet, rate limiting, HTTPS |
| Dependencies | `npm install` (with dev deps) | `npm ci --omit=dev` |

### Setting NODE_ENV
`NODE_ENV=production` makes Express and many libraries enable optimisations (view caching, less verbose output). Always set it in production.

### Environment-aware code
```js
import helmet from 'helmet';
import cors from 'cors';
import rateLimit from 'express-rate-limit';
import { env } from './config/env.js';

const isProd = env.NODE_ENV === 'production';

app.use(cors({
  origin: isProd ? ['https://myapp.com'] : true,
}));

if (isProd) {
  app.set('trust proxy', 1); // behind a load balancer/reverse proxy
  app.use(helmet());
  app.use(rateLimit({ windowMs: 15 * 60 * 1000, limit: 100 }));
}
```

### Scripts
```bash
npm pkg set scripts.dev='nodemon src/server.js'
npm pkg set scripts.start='NODE_ENV=production node src/server.js'
```

### Best practices
- Avoid scattering `if (env === 'production')` everywhere. Centralise it in config and pass values down.
- Keep staging as close to production as possible to catch issues early.
- Add health checks (`/health`) and graceful shutdown for production.
- Run database migrations as a deploy step, not manually.
- Use a separate `test` environment with its own database so tests never touch real data.
- Containerise (Docker) so dev, CI and production run the same runtime.

subTopic.name: Creating an Express server
Request and response objects
subTopic.notes:
## Overview
Every handler receives `req` (the incoming HTTP request) and `res` (the outgoing response). Both extend Node's native objects with helpers.

## Common `req` properties
| Property | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `req.method` | HTTP verb (GET, POST...) |
| `req.url` / `req.originalUrl` | Requested URL |
| `req.path` | Path without query string |
| `req.params` | Route parameters |
| `req.query` | Parsed query string |
| `req.body` | Parsed body (needs body-parsing middleware) |
| `req.headers` / `req.get('Header')` | Request headers |
| `req.ip` | Client IP |

## Common `res` methods
```js
res.send('text or buffer');        // auto-detects content type
res.json({ ok: true });            // sends JSON
res.status(404).json({ error: 'Not found' });
res.redirect(301, '/new-url');
res.set('X-Custom', 'value');      // set header
res.cookie('sid', 'abc', { httpOnly: true });
res.sendFile('/abs/path/file.pdf');
res.end();                         // end with no body
```

## Key points
- A request must get exactly one response; calling `res.send`/`res.json` twice throws `ERR_HTTP_HEADERS_SENT`.
- `res.status()` is chainable and only sets the code; you still must send something.
- `res.locals` carries per-request data to later middleware/views.
- Add custom data to `req` (e.g. `req.user`) in middleware, and pass it to later handlers.

subTopic.name: Route handlers
Route parameters and query strings
Parsing JSON and form bodies
Express Router
Serving static files
HTTP status codes
subTopic.notes:
## Overview
Status codes tell the client the outcome of a request. Pick the most accurate one, since clients and tools rely on them.

## Classes
- **1xx** Informational
- **2xx** Success
- **3xx** Redirection
- **4xx** Client error
- **5xx** Server error

## Codes you must know
| Code | Name | Use when |
|---|---|---|
| 200 | OK | Successful GET/PUT/PATCH |
| 201 | Created | Resource created (POST); include `Location` header |
| 204 | No Content | Success with no body (DELETE) |
| 301 / 302 | Moved Permanently / Found | Redirects |
| 304 | Not Modified | Cached copy is still valid |
| 400 | Bad Request | Malformed or invalid input |
| 401 | Unauthorized | Not authenticated |
| 403 | Forbidden | Authenticated but not allowed |
| 404 | Not Found | Resource does not exist |
| 405 | Method Not Allowed | Wrong verb for the route |
| 409 | Conflict | Duplicate or state conflict |
| 415 | Unsupported Media Type | Wrong Content-Type |
| 422 | Unprocessable Content | Valid syntax, failed validation |
| 429 | Too Many Requests | Rate limited |
| 500 | Internal Server Error | Unexpected failure |
| 502 / 503 / 504 | Bad Gateway / Unavailable / Timeout | Upstream or overload problems |

## In Express
```js
res.status(201).json(newUser);
res.sendStatus(204);               // sets status and sends its text
res.status(404).json({ error: 'User not found' });
```

## Key points
- Do not return 200 with an error message in the body.
- 401 means 'who are you?', 403 means 'you may not do this'.
- Never leak stack traces on 500 responses in production.

subTopic.name: Response headers
subTopic.notes:
## Overview
Headers carry metadata about the response: content type, caching, security, CORS, cookies and more.

## Setting headers
```js
res.set('X-Request-Id', 'abc123');
res.set({ 'Cache-Control': 'no-store', 'X-Powered-By-Me': 'api' });
res.type('json');                       // sets Content-Type
res.location('/api/users/42');          // Location header
res.append('Set-Cookie', 'a=1');        // add without overwriting
```

## Important headers
| Header | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `Content-Type` | Format of body (`application/json; charset=utf-8`) |
| `Cache-Control` | Caching rules (`public, max-age=3600`, `no-store`) |
| `ETag` | Validator for conditional requests (Express adds it automatically) |
| `Location` | URL of created/redirected resource |
| `Set-Cookie` | Sends cookies |
| `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` | CORS |
| `Retry-After` | When to retry (429/503) |
| `Content-Disposition` | Trigger a file download |

## Security headers with Helmet
```js
import helmet from 'helmet';
app.use(helmet());
app.disable('x-powered-by');
```

## CORS
```js
import cors from 'cors';
app.use(cors({ origin: 'https://myapp.com', credentials: true }));
```

## File download
```js
res.download('/abs/path/report.pdf', 'report.pdf');
```

## Key points
- Headers must be set before the body is sent.
- Header names are case-insensitive.
- Disable `X-Powered-By` and add Helmet to reduce fingerprinting and common attacks.
- Cache static and public data, but use `no-store` for private data.

subTopic.name: Building REST endpoints
CRUD API design
Pagination and filtering
API versioning
Consistent response contracts
Testing with Postman or Bruno
Middleware lifecycle
Built-in and third-party middleware
Custom middleware
Middleware ordering
Request logging
CORS configuration
subTopic.notes:
CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) is a browser security mechanism that controls whether a web application running on one origin can access resources from another origin. An origin consists of the protocol, hostname, and port. For example, http://localhost:5173 and http://localhost:5000 are different origins.

Important CORS headers:
1. Access-Control-Allow-Origin: Specifies permitted origins.
2. Access-Control-Allow-Methods: Specifies permitted HTTP methods.
3. Access-Control-Allow-Headers: Specifies permitted request headers.
4. Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: Allows credentials in cross-origin requests.
5. Access-Control-Expose-Headers: Specifies response headers accessible to browser JavaScript.

Preflight requests: Browsers may send an OPTIONS request before the actual request to check whether the server permits the requested origin, method, and headers.

Installation:
npm install cors

Implementation (JavaScript - Express.js):
const cors = require('cors');

app.use(cors({
  origin: 'http://localhost:5173',
  methods: ['GET', 'POST', 'PUT', 'PATCH', 'DELETE'],
  allowedHeaders: ['Content-Type', 'Authorization'],
  credentials: true
}));

Frontend (JavaScript - Fetch API):
fetch('http://localhost:5000/api/users', {
  method: 'GET',
  credentials: 'include'
});

Important concepts:
1. CORS is enforced by browsers, not a replacement for server-side authentication or authorization.
2. Never use wildcard origin (*) when credentialed requests are required.
3. The server must explicitly allow the frontend origin when using credentials.
4. Cookies may require appropriate SameSite and Secure attributes.
5. Configure OPTIONS preflight handling correctly.
6. CORS errors frequently occur when frontend and backend run on different ports during development.

subTopic.name: Cookie parsing
Authentication middleware
Validation middleware
Centralized error handling
Custom error classes
Async errors
404 handling
Avoiding sensitive error details
Structured error responses
subTopic.notes:
Structured error responses follow a consistent JSON format for communicating failures from the backend to the frontend. They make error handling predictable and allow frontend applications to display meaningful messages based on status codes and error categories.

Recommended response properties:
1. success: Indicates whether the operation succeeded or failed.
2. status: A short error classification such as fail or error.
3. statusCode: HTTP response status code.
4. message: Human-readable error message.
5. errorCode: Application-specific error identifier.
6. errors: Optional field containing validation or field-level errors.
7. timestamp: Time at which the error occurred.
8. path: Request path associated with the error.
9. requestId: Identifier used to trace the request in server logs.

Implementation (JavaScript - Express.js):
const errorHandler = (err, req, res, next) => {
  const statusCode = err.statusCode || 500;

  const response = {
    success: false,
    status: err.status || 'error',
    statusCode,
    message: err.isOperational
      ? err.message
      : 'Internal Server Error',
    errorCode: err.code || 'INTERNAL_ERROR',
    timestamp: new Date().toISOString(),
    path: req.originalUrl,
    requestId: req.id || null
  };

  if (err.errors) {
    response.errors = err.errors;
  }

  res.status(statusCode).json(response);
};

Example JSON response:
{
  "success": false,
  "status": "fail",
  "statusCode": 400,
  "message": "Validation failed",
  "errorCode": "VALIDATION_ERROR",
  "errors": [
    {
      "field": "email",
      "message": "Invalid email address"
    }
  ],
  "timestamp": "2026-11-16T10:30:00.000Z",
  "path": "/api/register",
  "requestId": "req-12345"
}

Important concepts:
1. Maintain the same response structure across all API endpoints.
2. Use appropriate HTTP status codes (400, 401, 403, 404, 409, 422, 429, and 500).
3. Use application-specific error codes for frontend error handling.
4. Return field-level validation errors when appropriate.
5. Use timestamps and request IDs for debugging and monitoring.
6. Never expose internal stack traces, credentials, or database implementation details.
7. Ensure the frontend can reliably distinguish between validation, authentication, authorization, and server errors.
8. Use a consistent API response contract for both successful and unsuccessful operations.

subTopic.name: REST principles
Resource modeling
subTopic.notes:
## Resource Modeling in REST APIs

Resource modeling is the process of identifying application entities and representing them as resources accessible through API endpoints.

A resource represents an object or collection of objects, such as users, products, orders, courses, or payments.

### 1. Identify Resources

Start by identifying the main entities in your application.

Example: E-commerce application.
- Users
- Products
- Categories
- Orders
- Payments
- Reviews

### 2. Design Resource URLs

Use meaningful, plural nouns to represent collections.

```http
GET    /api/products
GET    /api/products/101
POST   /api/products
PUT    /api/products/101
DELETE /api/products/101
```

### 3. Model Relationships

Resources can have one-to-one, one-to-many, or many-to-many relationships.

Example: One user can have multiple orders.

```http
GET /api/users/101/orders
GET /api/orders/501
```

### 4. Nested Resources

Use nested endpoints when a child resource is meaningfully scoped by its parent.

```http
GET /api/courses/10/lessons
GET /api/courses/10/lessons/5
```

Avoid deeply nested URLs. Two or three levels are generally sufficient.

### 5. Resource Representation

A resource can be represented using JSON.

**Language: JSON**

```json
{
  "id": 101,
  "name": "Anshika",
  "email": "anshika@example.com",
  "orders": [501, 502]
}
```

### Best Practices
- Design URLs around business entities.
- Use consistent naming conventions.
- Keep resource relationships understandable.
- Avoid exposing internal database structures unnecessarily.
- Use stable resource identifiers.
- Separate resources from their database implementation.

### Important Concepts
Understand entity relationships, resource identifiers, collection versus individual resources, nested resources, URI design, and resource representation.

subTopic.name: HTTP methods and idempotency
subTopic.notes:
## HTTP Methods

HTTP methods define the action a client wants to perform on a server resource.

### Common HTTP Methods

1. **GET:** Retrieves a resource without modifying server state.
2. **POST:** Creates a resource or submits data for processing.
3. **PUT:** Creates or completely replaces a resource at a specified URI.
4. **PATCH:** Partially updates an existing resource.
5. **DELETE:** Removes a resource.
6. **HEAD:** Retrieves response headers without the response body.
7. **OPTIONS:** Identifies supported communication options for a resource.

### HTTP Method Comparison

| Method | Purpose | Safe | Idempotent |
|---|---|---|---|
| GET | Read data | Yes | Yes |
| POST | Create/process | No | No (generally) |
| PUT | Replace data | No | Yes |
| PATCH | Partial update | No | Not necessarily |
| DELETE | Delete resource | No | Yes |
| HEAD | Read headers | Yes | Yes |
| OPTIONS | Check capabilities | Yes | Yes |

### What Is Idempotency?

An operation is idempotent when performing the same request multiple times produces the same intended server state as performing it once.

Example:

```http
PUT /api/users/101
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "name": "Anshika"
}
```

Sending this request multiple times leaves the resource with the same name.

### Non-idempotent Example

```http
POST /api/orders
```

Repeated requests may create multiple orders unless the API implements an idempotency mechanism.

### Implementing Idempotency Keys

**Language: JavaScript**

```javascript
app.post('/api/payments', async (req, res) => {
  const key = req.headers['idempotency-key'];

  if (!key) {
    return res.status(400).json({
      message: 'Idempotency key required'
    });
  }

  // Check persistent storage for an existing result.
  // If found, return the previously stored response.
  // Otherwise process and store the payment result.
});
```

A production implementation should store keys with unique constraints, request fingerprints, results, and expiration policies.

### Best Practices
- Use GET for retrieving resources.
- Use POST for creation and non-idempotent operations.
- Use PUT for complete replacement.
- Use PATCH for partial updates.
- Implement idempotency keys for payment and retry-sensitive operations.
- Never assume that every PATCH request is idempotent.

### Important Concepts
Understand safe methods, idempotent methods, HTTP semantics, retry behavior, duplicate submissions, and payment API reliability.

subTopic.name: Request and response schemas
Consistent error formats
subTopic.notes:
## Consistent API Error Formats

An API error format defines how the server communicates failures to clients. A consistent error structure makes frontend error handling predictable and simplifies debugging.

### 1. HTTP Status Codes

Common HTTP error status codes:

| Status | Meaning |
|---|---|
| 400 | Bad Request |
| 401 | Unauthorized |
| 403 | Forbidden |
| 404 | Resource Not Found |
| 405 | Method Not Allowed |
| 409 | Conflict |
| 422 | Unprocessable Content |
| 429 | Too Many Requests |
| 500 | Internal Server Error |
| 502 | Bad Gateway |
| 503 | Service Unavailable |

### 2. Standard Error Response

**Language: JSON**

```json
{
  "success": false,
  "error": {
    "code": "USER_NOT_FOUND",
    "message": "The requested user does not exist",
    "details": null,
    "timestamp": "2026-11-16T10:00:00Z",
    "path": "/api/users/101"
  }
}
```

### 3. Centralized Error Handling

Instead of handling every server error independently, use centralized error middleware.

**Language: JavaScript (Express.js)**

```javascript
app.use((err, req, res, next) => {
  const statusCode = err.statusCode || 500;

  res.status(statusCode).json({
    success: false,
    error: {
      code: err.code || 'INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR',
      message: statusCode === 500
        ? 'Something went wrong'
        : err.message
    }
  });
});
```

### 4. Error Categories

- Client errors: Invalid input, missing resources, authentication failures.
- Server errors: Database failures, unexpected exceptions, unavailable dependencies.
- Business errors: Insufficient balance, duplicate order, unavailable product.

### Best Practices
- Maintain one consistent error response structure.
- Use meaningful machine-readable error codes.
- Return appropriate HTTP status codes.
- Do not expose stack traces or internal server details in production.
- Log detailed errors securely on the server.
- Include request IDs for distributed debugging.
- Keep error messages understandable to API consumers.

### Important Concepts
Understand HTTP error codes, custom error classes, centralized middleware, exception handling, structured logging, and correlation IDs.

subTopic.name: Validation errors
Pagination and sorting patterns
Filtering and search endpoints
OpenAPI and Swagger
subTopic.notes:
## OpenAPI and Swagger

OpenAPI is a language-independent specification for describing HTTP APIs. It defines endpoints, methods, parameters, request bodies, response schemas, authentication, and other API details.

Swagger is a collection of tools that work with OpenAPI documents, including Swagger UI and Swagger Editor.

### 1. Why OpenAPI Is Important

- Provides machine-readable API documentation.
- Helps frontend and backend developers agree on API contracts.
- Supports automatic client SDK generation.
- Enables interactive API testing through Swagger UI.
- Helps validate API specifications.
- Improves collaboration between development teams.

### 2. OpenAPI Specification Example

**Language: YAML (OpenAPI 3.0)**

```yaml
openapi: 3.0.3
info:
  title: User API
  version: 1.0.0
  description: API for managing users

servers:
  - url: http://localhost:3000

paths:
  /api/users:
    get:
      summary: Get all users
```
