subTopic.name: REST principles and resource modeling
subTopic.notes: REST models application data as resources identified by URLs and manipulated through standard HTTP methods. Aim for stateless requests, consistent representations, cache-aware behavior, and clear resource relationships.

subTopic.name: Choosing resource-oriented URLs
subTopic.notes: Prefer nouns and resource hierarchies such as `/users/:userId/orders` rather than action-heavy URLs. Use HTTP methods to express the operation and keep URL naming consistent.

subTopic.name: HTTP methods and idempotency
subTopic.notes: Use GET to read, POST to create/process, PUT to replace, PATCH to partially update, and DELETE to remove. Match method semantics to the operation and avoid state-changing GET endpoints.

subTopic.name: Status codes and error semantics
subTopic.notes: Use 2xx for success, 3xx for redirects, 4xx for client/request problems, and 5xx for server failures. Common API codes: 200, 201, 204, 400, 401, 403, 404, 409, 422, and 500.

subTopic.name: Request and response schemas
subTopic.notes: `req` contains method, path, params, query, headers, body, and authenticated context; `res` sends status, headers, and response data. Send exactly one response per request and return after sending it.

subTopic.name: Pagination patterns
Filtering and sorting
subTopic.notes: Accept allowlisted filter and sort parameters, validate types, and map them to database queries. Add indexes for frequent combinations; never pass arbitrary client-supplied MongoDB operators or field names unchecked.

subTopic.name: Search endpoints
subTopic.notes: Define searchable fields, normalization, matching behavior, and limits. Use indexed search strategies appropriate to scale; debounce user input and paginate results. Escape or validate user-provided search expressions.

subTopic.name: API versioning
subTopic.notes: Version APIs when changes would break existing clients, commonly with `/api/v1`. Prefer backward-compatible additive changes and document deprecation/migration timelines.

subTopic.name: Consistent response formats
subTopic.notes: Use a stable response contract, such as `{data, meta}` for success and `{error:{code,message,details}}` for failures. Keep field names, status codes, and pagination metadata consistent.

subTopic.name: Validation errors and API error contracts
subTopic.notes: Validation errors and API error contracts: Design this as part of a predictable HTTP contract: define URL, method, inputs, output, status codes, validation, and authorization. Keep behavior consistent for all clients.

subTopic.name: Date, time, and serialization conventions
subTopic.notes: Store timestamps in UTC (typically ISO 8601) and convert to the user's timezone for display. Distinguish date-only values from instants; validate parsing and avoid locale-dependent server formats.

subTopic.name: Designing CRUD endpoints
subTopic.notes: Designing CRUD endpoints: Design this as part of a predictable HTTP contract: define URL, method, inputs, output, status codes, validation, and authorization. Keep behavior consistent for all clients.

subTopic.name: OpenAPI and API documentation overview
subTopic.notes: OpenAPI describes endpoints, parameters, schemas, authentication, and responses in a machine-readable contract. Swagger UI can render interactive docs; keep the specification synchronized with implementation.

subTopic.name: What MongoDB is and when to use it
subTopic.notes: MongoDB is a document-oriented NoSQL database suited to flexible, nested records and evolving schemas. Choose it based on access patterns and consistency needs, not simply because the data is JSON-shaped.

subTopic.name: Relational databases vs document databases
subTopic.notes: Relational databases organize normalized data into tables with foreign keys and joins; document databases store related data in BSON documents and may embed it. Compare transaction needs, query patterns, relationships, and schema evolution.

subTopic.name: Documents, collections, and databases
subTopic.notes: A database contains collections; a collection contains documents; a document contains fields and values. Documents are similar to JSON objects but stored as BSON and normally have a unique `_id`.

subTopic.name: BSON and JSON relationship
subTopic.notes: JSON is a text interchange format; BSON is MongoDB's binary serialization with additional types such as ObjectId, Date, and binary data. BSON is not simply identical to JSON.

subTopic.name: Installing MongoDB or using Atlas
subTopic.notes: MongoDB is a document-oriented NoSQL database suited to flexible, nested records and evolving schemas. Choose it based on access patterns and consistency needs, not simply because the data is JSON-shaped.

subTopic.name: Connecting with mongosh and Compass
subTopic.notes: `mongosh` is a command-line shell for running database commands; Compass is a graphical tool for inspecting collections, documents, indexes, and query plans. Both connect using a MongoDB URI and appropriate credentials.

subTopic.name: CRUD operations
subTopic.notes: CRUD means Create, Read, Update, Delete. Know the matching MongoDB methods (`insertOne`, `find`, `updateOne`, `deleteOne`) and their filters, options, and returned result metadata.

subTopic.name: Insert one and insert many
subTopic.notes: `insertOne(document)` inserts one document; `insertMany([...])` inserts multiple documents. Understand generated `_id`, ordered vs unordered bulk behavior, validation, and duplicate-key failures.

subTopic.name: Find and query filters
Update and replace operations
subTopic.notes: `updateOne`/`updateMany` apply operators such as `$set` and `$inc`; `replaceOne` replaces the document except `_id`. Always use a selective filter and inspect matched/modified counts.

subTopic.name: Delete operations
subTopic.notes: `deleteOne` removes the first matching document; `deleteMany` removes all matches. Verify the filter before destructive operations and use authorization/soft-delete policies where recovery or auditability is required.

subTopic.name: Projection and field selection
subTopic.notes: Projection selects fields to return and reduces network payload. Include or exclude fields (except `_id` special handling); do not mix inclusion and exclusion arbitrarily in one projection.

subTopic.name: Sorting and limiting results
subTopic.notes: Use `.sort({createdAt:-1}).limit(20)` to order and cap results. Add a unique tie-breaker for stable ordering and index the sort/filter pattern for performance.

subTopic.name: ObjectId fundamentals
subTopic.notes: ObjectId is MongoDB's default unique identifier type, commonly represented as a 24-character hexadecimal string. Convert validated route IDs to ObjectId/Mongoose IDs and handle malformed IDs separately from missing records.

subTopic.name: Comparison query operators
subTopic.notes: Comparison operators include `$eq`, `$ne`, `$gt`, `$gte`, `$lt`, `$lte`, and `$in`/`$nin`. Use them to express typed comparisons and validate values before building filters.

subTopic.name: Logical query operators
subTopic.notes: Logical operators `$and`, `$or`, `$nor`, and `$not` combine conditions. MongoDB often supports implicit AND by listing multiple fields; understand precedence when composing nested filters.

subTopic.name: Array query operators
subTopic.notes: Use `$all`, `$elemMatch`, `$size`, and array membership queries to match array contents. `$elemMatch` ensures multiple conditions apply to the same array element.

subTopic.name: Embedded documents and arrays
subTopic.notes: Embedded documents and arrays: Understand the MongoDB document/query behavior, its data-modeling implications, and performance or correctness trade-offs. Practice with representative documents and inspect query results.

subTopic.name: Embedding vs referencing
subTopic.notes: Embedding stores related data inside one document, enabling single-read access and atomic updates but increasing document size/duplication. Referencing stores related records separately, reducing duplication but requiring additional queries or `$lookup`/populate.

subTopic.name: One-to-one relationships
subTopic.notes: For one-to-one data, embed when the child is small, bounded, and usually read with its parent; reference when independently accessed, large, or separately secured. Enforce uniqueness where the relationship requires it.

subTopic.name: One-to-many relationships
subTopic.notes: For one-to-many relationships, embed bounded child arrays when read/updated together; reference children when the set can grow without bound or children are independently queried. Avoid unbounded arrays.

subTopic.name: Many-to-many relationships
subTopic.notes: Many-to-many relationships can use arrays of references or a join/association collection. Choose based on cardinality, update frequency, query direction, and whether the relationship itself has attributes.

subTopic.name: Schema design around access patterns
subTopic.notes: Schema design around access patterns: Understand the MongoDB document/query behavior, its data-modeling implications, and performance or correctness trade-offs. Practice with representative documents and inspect query results.

subTopic.name: Atomic updates
subTopic.notes: A single-document MongoDB write is atomic. Prefer conditional updates with operators (e.g. decrement stock only when stock is sufficient) to prevent read-modify-write races; use transactions for multi-document invariants.

subTopic.name: Update operators
subTopic.notes: Common operators: `$set` assigns, `$unset` removes, `$inc` increments, `$min`/`$max` bound values, `$rename` changes field names, and `$currentDate` sets a timestamp. Use targeted updates rather than replacing whole documents unnecessarily.

subTopic.name: Array update operators
subTopic.notes: Common operators: `$set` assigns, `$unset` removes, `$inc` increments, `$min`/`$max` bound values, `$rename` changes field names, and `$currentDate` sets a timestamp. Use targeted updates rather than replacing whole documents unnecessarily.

subTopic.name: Aggregation pipeline fundamentals
Grouping, projection, sorting, and lookup
subTopic.notes: Projection selects fields to return and reduces network payload. Include or exclude fields (except `_id` special handling); do not mix inclusion and exclusion arbitrarily in one projection.

subTopic.name: Data validation rules
subTopic.notes: MongoDB schema validation can enforce required fields, BSON types, and allowed values at the database boundary. Pair it with application validation; database validation protects against writes from other clients or scripts.

subTopic.name: What indexes do
subTopic.notes: An index is an auxiliary data structure that speeds reads by reducing scanned documents, at the cost of storage and slower writes. Index fields used in filters, sorts, and joins; verify with `explain()` rather than adding indexes blindly.

subTopic.name: Single-field indexes
subTopic.notes: An index is an auxiliary data structure that speeds reads by reducing scanned documents, at the cost of storage and slower writes. Index fields used in filters, sorts, and joins; verify with `explain()` rather than adding indexes blindly.

subTopic.name: Compound indexes
subTopic.notes: An index is an auxiliary data structure that speeds reads by reducing scanned documents, at the cost of storage and slower writes. Index fields used in filters, sorts, and joins; verify with `explain()` rather than adding indexes blindly.

subTopic.name: Multikey indexes
subTopic.notes: An index is an auxiliary data structure that speeds reads by reducing scanned documents, at the cost of storage and slower writes. Index fields used in filters, sorts, and joins; verify with `explain()` rather than adding indexes blindly.

subTopic.name: Unique and sparse indexes
subTopic.notes: An index is an auxiliary data structure that speeds reads by reducing scanned documents, at the cost of storage and slower writes. Index fields used in filters, sorts, and joins; verify with `explain()` rather than adding indexes blindly.

subTopic.name: Text and geospatial index overview
subTopic.notes: Text indexes support basic text search over selected string fields; geospatial indexes (`2dsphere`) support location queries on GeoJSON coordinates. For advanced relevance/search needs, evaluate Atlas Search.

subTopic.name: Index order and prefix rules
subTopic.notes: Compound index prefix rules mean an index on `{a:1,b:1,c:1}` can support queries beginning with `a` and `a+b`, but generally not `b` alone. Sort direction and equality/range predicates also matter.

subTopic.name: Query plans and explain()
subTopic.notes: `explain('executionStats')` reveals winning plan, index use, documents/keys examined, and execution time. Compare `COLLSCAN` with `IXSCAN`; use representative data and query shapes.

subTopic.name: Covered queries
subTopic.notes: A query is covered when the index contains every field needed for matching and returned projection, so MongoDB need not fetch documents. Confirm coverage in the explain plan and account for `_id` projection.

subTopic.name: Index selectivity
subTopic.notes: Selectivity measures how narrowly a predicate filters records. Highly selective fields often make useful index prefixes; low-selectivity fields may provide little benefit alone. Test with real distributions.

subTopic.notes: Slow query diagnosis: Understand the MongoDB document/query behavior, its data-modeling implications, and performance or correctness trade-offs. Practice with representative documents and inspect query results.

subTopic.name: Pagination with skip/limit vs cursor patterns
subTopic.notes: Pagination limits response size. Offset pagination uses `page`/`limit` or `skip`/`limit`; cursor pagination uses a stable indexed key and is more efficient for large/changing datasets. Return metadata such as next cursor or total when appropriate.

subTopic.name: Connection pooling overview
subTopic.notes: A connection pool reuses database connections instead of opening one per request. Configure pool limits and timeouts based on application concurrency; create one shared client/connection per process.

subTopic.notes: MongoDB is a document-oriented NoSQL database suited to flexible, nested records and evolving schemas. Choose it based on access patterns and consistency needs, not simply because the data is JSON-shaped.

subTopic.name: Database users and least privilege
subTopic.notes: Create separate database users with only the roles required by the application or operator. Avoid broad admin credentials in application configuration and rotate credentials periodically.

subTopic.name: Network access and IP allowlists
subTopic.notes: Atlas network access rules restrict which IP addresses can connect. Prefer fixed application egress addresses or private networking; avoid unrestricted `0.0.0.0/0` outside tightly controlled temporary testing.

subTopic.name: Connection strings and URI encoding
subTopic.notes: A MongoDB URI identifies hosts, database, options, and credentials. Percent-encode reserved characters in usernames/passwords, keep the URI secret, and use TLS for remote connections.

subTopic.name: Connecting an application to Atlas
subTopic.notes: Atlas operations include cluster provisioning, access control, network rules, backups, monitoring, and scaling. Separate development and production clusters and verify region, tier, and backup policy.

subTopic.name: Database backups and restore
subTopic.notes: Backups protect against accidental deletion, corruption, and infrastructure failure. Define retention and recovery-point/recovery-time objectives, test restores regularly, and do not assume a backup is usable until restoration is verified.

subTopic.notes: A liveness check indicates the process is running; readiness indicates it can safely receive traffic (for example, required dependencies are available). Keep checks fast and avoid leaking infrastructure details.

subTopic.name: What Mongoose is and why use it
subTopic.notes: Mongoose is an ODM that maps MongoDB documents to JavaScript objects with schemas, casting, validation, middleware, and query helpers. It adds application-level structure but does not replace database indexes or server-side security.

subTopic.name: Connecting Mongoose to MongoDB
Schemas and models
Field types and schema options
subTopic.notes: Mongoose supports String, Number, Boolean, Date, ObjectId, Array, Map, Mixed, and nested schemas. Use appropriate types, `ref` for relationships, and options such as `trim`, `lowercase`, `min`, and `max`.

subTopic.name: Required fields and validation
subTopic.notes: Schema validators enforce constraints during document validation/save. Use `required`, length/range validators, and custom validators; remember update operations may need `runValidators: true`.

subTopic.name: Default values
subTopic.notes: A schema `default` is applied when a field is `undefined`, not necessarily when it is explicitly `null`. Use functions for per-document dynamic defaults such as timestamps or generated values.

subTopic.name: Enums and custom validators
subTopic.notes: An enum restricts a field to an allowed set, e.g. `enum: ['pending','paid','cancelled']`. Custom validators handle domain rules; validation errors should be translated into safe client responses.

subTopic.name: Timestamps
subTopic.notes: Set `{timestamps:true}` to maintain `createdAt` and `updatedAt`. Use these fields for audit trails and sorting; do not let clients freely overwrite system-managed timestamps.

subTopic.name: Create, read, update, and delete with Mongoose
subTopic.notes: Mongoose is an ODM that maps MongoDB documents to JavaScript objects with schemas, casting, validation, middleware, and query helpers. It adds application-level structure but does not replace database indexes or server-side security.

subTopic.name: findById and query methods
subTopic.notes: `findById(id)` queries by `_id`; `findOne(filter)` and `find(filter)` support other query shapes. Know when a method returns one document, an array, or a query, and handle `null` results.

subTopic.name: lean() and document behavior
subTopic.notes: `lean()` returns plain JavaScript objects instead of hydrated Mongoose documents, reducing overhead for read-only responses. Lean results do not have document methods, getters, setters, or `save()`.

subTopic.name: Middleware and hooks
subTopic.notes: Mongoose middleware runs before/after operations such as save or query. Use hooks for cross-cutting model behavior, but avoid hiding complex business workflows in hooks; distinguish document and query middleware.

subTopic.name: Instance and static methods
subTopic.notes: Instance methods operate on a document (e.g. `user.comparePassword()`); static methods operate on the model (e.g. `User.findActive()`). Keep methods cohesive and avoid duplicating service-layer logic.

subTopic.name: Virtual properties
subTopic.notes: Virtuals are computed properties not persisted as document fields, useful for derived values or relationships. Configure virtual serialization if they must appear in JSON output.

subTopic.name: References and populate()
subTopic.notes: `populate()` replaces referenced ObjectId fields with related documents. Select only needed fields, understand query cost, and avoid deep/unbounded population that creates N+1 or oversized responses.

subTopic.name: Subdocuments and nested schemas
subTopic.notes: Subdocuments are nested schema instances with their own validation and middleware. Use them for bounded data owned by the parent; understand `_id` behavior and update nested paths safely.

subTopic.name: Indexes in Mongoose
subTopic.notes: An index is an auxiliary data structure that speeds reads by reducing scanned documents, at the cost of storage and slower writes. Index fields used in filters, sorts, and joins; verify with `explain()` rather than adding indexes blindly.

subTopic.name: Update validators
subTopic.notes: Mongoose update validators are not always enabled by default. Pass `{runValidators:true}` for update operations and understand that validators may run only on updated paths and supported operators.

subTopic.name: Handling validation and cast errors
subTopic.notes: A ValidationError means a schema rule failed; a CastError means a value could not be converted to the declared type. Map these to client errors while logging internal details safely.

subTopic.name: Avoiding duplicate database connections
subTopic.notes: Avoiding duplicate database connections: Understand the Mongoose schema/model/document behavior and its interaction with MongoDB. Know relevant options, validation behavior, query return types, and performance implications.

subTopic.name: Why server-side validation is mandatory
subTopic.notes: Client validation improves UX but is bypassable. Validate every untrusted value on the server, including route params, query strings, request bodies, file metadata, and authorization-sensitive fields.

subTopic.name: Validating params, query, and body
subTopic.notes: Validate `req.params`, `req.query`, and `req.body` independently. Parse strings into expected types, enforce bounds/enums, reject unknown fields when appropriate, and never trust client-supplied ownership or role fields.

subTopic.name: Schema validation with Zod, Joi, or express-validator
subTopic.notes: Schema libraries such as Zod, Joi, and express-validator define reusable input contracts. Parse at the API boundary, return field-level errors, and use validated output—not the original untrusted object—in business logic.

subTopic.name: Sanitization and normalization
subTopic.notes: Normalization makes equivalent inputs consistent (trim whitespace, canonicalize email case where appropriate); sanitization removes or rejects unsafe forms. Prefer context-aware output encoding over attempting to strip every dangerous character.

subTopic.name: Centralized async error handling
subTopic.notes: Use `try/catch/finally` for synchronous code and awaited promises; throw meaningful errors and handle them at the correct boundary. Do not silently swallow errors or expose internal details to users.

subTopic.name: Custom application error classes
subTopic.notes: Create an application error class with a safe message, HTTP status, and machine-readable code. Central middleware maps known errors to responses and treats unknown errors as 500 without exposing stack traces.

subTopic.name: Not found errors
subTopic.notes: Return 404 when the requested resource or route does not exist. Distinguish a malformed identifier (often 400) from a valid ID with no matching record (404).

subTopic.name: Conflict and duplicate-key errors
subTopic.notes: MongoDB duplicate-key error (commonly code 11000) occurs when a unique constraint is violated. Return 409 Conflict with a field-safe message; do not rely only on a pre-check because concurrent requests can race.

subTopic.name: Validation error responses
subTopic.notes: Return 400 or 422 consistently with a stable error code and field details, e.g. `{error:{code:'VALIDATION_ERROR',message:'Invalid input',fields:{email:'Invalid email'}}}`. Avoid returning raw stack traces or database messages.

subTopic.name: Avoiding leaking stack traces
subTopic.notes: Read the error type and message first, then the first stack frame in your own code; follow the call chain to the origin. Distinguish the root cause from downstream errors and inspect relevant logs, inputs, and environment configuration.

subTopic.name: Consistent error response structure
subTopic.notes: Consistent error response structure: Treat all input as untrusted. Define validation, failure conditions, safe status codes, logging, and a consistent response contract; test malformed and adversarial inputs.

subTopic.name: Handling rejected promises
subTopic.notes: Handling rejected promises: Treat all input as untrusted. Define validation, failure conditions, safe status codes, logging, and a consistent response contract; test malformed and adversarial inputs.

subTopic.name: Logging errors with request context
subTopic.notes: Structured logs use consistent fields (timestamp, level, message, requestId, user-safe context) so they can be searched and aggregated. Never log passwords, tokens, payment data, or full sensitive request bodies.

subTopic.name: Graceful failure behavior
subTopic.notes: Graceful failure behavior: Treat all input as untrusted. Define validation, failure conditions, safe status codes, logging, and a consistent response contract; test malformed and adversarial inputs.

subTopic.name: Authentication vs authorization
subTopic.notes: Authentication establishes who the caller is; authorization determines what that identity may do. A logged-in user is not automatically permitted to access every resource or operation.

subTopic.name: Registration and login flows
subTopic.notes: Registration validates input, checks uniqueness, hashes the password, and stores the user. Login verifies the password hash, then issues a session or token; apply rate limits and generic failure messages.

subTopic.name: Password hashing with bcrypt or Argon2
subTopic.notes: Hash passwords with a password-hashing algorithm such as Argon2id or bcrypt using a suitable work factor and unique salt. Never store plaintext or reversible encryption; compare using the library's verification function.

subTopic.name: Password reset flow
subTopic.notes: Use a cryptographically random, single-use, short-lived reset token; store a hash of it, bind it to the account, and invalidate it after use. Avoid revealing whether an email address is registered.

subTopic.name: Email verification concepts
subTopic.notes: Send a time-limited, single-use verification token or link and mark the account verified only after server-side validation. Rate-limit resends and avoid placing long-lived credentials in URLs.

subTopic.name: Session-based authentication
subTopic.notes: A session stores authentication state server-side; the browser holds an opaque session ID, usually in a cookie. Sessions can be revoked centrally, but require secure storage and appropriate scaling strategy.

subTopic.name: Cookie-based sessions
subTopic.notes: Cookies automatically accompany matching requests. Configure `HttpOnly`, `Secure`, `SameSite`, path, domain, and expiry; rotate session IDs after login and protect state-changing requests against CSRF.

subTopic.name: JWT structure and claims
Access tokens and refresh tokens
subTopic.notes: Access tokens are short-lived credentials for API calls; refresh tokens obtain new access tokens and should be stored/rotated more carefully. Revoke or detect reuse of refresh tokens and bind them to a session/device as appropriate.

subTopic.name: Token expiry and rotation
subTopic.notes: Set short access-token lifetimes and rotate refresh tokens. Verify expiry, issuer, audience, and allowed algorithm; handle clock skew and revoke compromised sessions.

subTopic.name: Secure cookie attributes
subTopic.notes: Use `HttpOnly` to block JavaScript access, `Secure` for HTTPS-only transmission, and an appropriate `SameSite` policy. Cookie settings must match cross-site frontend/API deployment and CSRF strategy.

subTopic.name: Logout and token invalidation
subTopic.notes: Logout should invalidate the server session or refresh-token family and clear the browser cookie using matching path/domain attributes. Deleting a token only in frontend state does not revoke a stolen token.

subTopic.name: Role-based access control
subTopic.notes: RBAC assigns permissions to roles such as admin, editor, and user. Enforce roles on the server for every protected operation; frontend hiding is only a UX measure.

subTopic.name: Resource ownership checks

subTopic.name: Account lockout and rate limiting
subTopic.notes: Limit requests by account, IP, and/or endpoint to reduce brute force and abuse. Use progressive delays or temporary lockouts carefully, avoid account-enumeration leaks, and consider distributed rate-limit storage.

subTopic.name: Multi-factor authentication overview
subTopic.notes: MFA combines independent factors such as knowledge (password), possession (authenticator/security key), and inherence (biometric). Prefer phishing-resistant passkeys/security keys where supported; protect recovery codes.

subTopic.name: OWASP Top 10 overview
subTopic.notes: OWASP Top 10 summarizes prevalent web application risk classes, including broken access control, injection, cryptographic failures, and security misconfiguration. Use it as a threat-review checklist, not a complete security standard.

subTopic.name: NoSQL injection prevention
subTopic.notes: NoSQL injection occurs when untrusted input is interpreted as query operators or expressions. Validate types and allowlisted fields, construct filters explicitly, and never pass raw request objects directly into MongoDB queries.

subTopic.name: Cross-site scripting (XSS)
subTopic.notes: XSS executes attacker-controlled script in a trusted page. Use framework escaping, avoid unsafe HTML insertion, sanitize trusted rich text, apply CSP, and encode output for its context.

subTopic.name: Cross-site request forgery (CSRF)
subTopic.notes: CSRF tricks an authenticated browser into sending an unwanted state-changing request. Use SameSite cookies, CSRF tokens or origin checks as appropriate, and never mutate state through GET requests.

subTopic.name: CORS is not authentication
subTopic.notes: CORS is a browser-enforced cross-origin access policy, not authentication or authorization. Allow only trusted origins, configure credentials deliberately, and remember non-browser clients are not constrained by CORS.

subTopic.name: Helmet and security headers
subTopic.notes: Helmet configures HTTP security headers such as CSP and frame/content-type protections. Review each header for application compatibility; headers complement, but do not replace, input validation and access control.

subTopic.name: Secure password storage

subTopic.name: JSX and component syntax
subTopic.notes: JSX is syntax for describing React elements; expressions go inside `{}` and components use PascalCase. Return one parent/fragment, use `className`, and provide stable keys for lists.

Props and component composition
subTopic.notes: Props are read-only inputs passed from parent to child. Use composition and explicit interfaces rather than mutating props; pass callbacks when children need to request parent state changes.

subTopic.name: Rendering lists and keys
subTopic.notes: Render collections with `map()` and provide a stable, unique `key` (usually a database ID). Keys let React preserve item identity across insertions, removals, and reordering; avoid array indices for changing lists.

subTopic.name: Conditional rendering
subTopic.notes: Render UI conditionally with `if`, ternaries, `&&`, or early returns. Handle loading, empty, error, and success states explicitly; avoid rendering unintended `0` values from numeric `&&` expressions.

subTopic.name: Event handling
subTopic.notes: Attach handlers such as `onClick` and `onChange` as functions, not strings. Pass arguments through callbacks and avoid invoking a handler during render. Use event delegation patterns only when appropriate.

subTopic.name: State with useState
subTopic.notes:
`useState` stores component state and returns `[value, setter]`. Setters schedule a render; use functional updates when next state depends on previous state: `setCount(c => c + 1)`. Never mutate state directly.

```jsx
const [count, setCount] = useState(0);

<button onClick={() => setCount(current => current + 1)}>
  Count: {count}
</button>
```

subTopic.name: State updates and re-rendering
subTopic.notes: React state is a render snapshot; updates are queued and may be batched. Replace objects/arrays immutably and use functional setters to avoid stale values when updates depend on prior state.

subTopic.name: Controlled inputs
subTopic.notes: A controlled input gets its value from React state and updates through `onChange`. Keep value types consistent and provide an initial value to avoid switching between controlled and uncontrolled modes.

subTopic.name: Lifting state up
subTopic.notes: Lift state to the nearest common parent when multiple components need the same source of truth. Pass values and callbacks down; avoid duplicating synchronized state in siblings.

subTopic.name: Reusable components

3.name: Hyper Text Markup Language
3.desc: Start your web development journey by learning how websites are structured. Understand HTML elements, semantic markup, forms, links, media, and accessibility while gradually progressing from simple pages to complete multi-page website structures.

subTopic.name: Introduction to HTML
subTopic.notes:
HTML (HyperText Markup Language) defines a page's structure and meaning; it is not a programming language. The browser parses HTML into the DOM (Document Object Model), then combines it with CSS for presentation and JavaScript for behavior. Learn the roles of elements, attributes, the DOM tree, and how HTML content is requested and rendered. ```html

Welcome

A page starts with structured content.

```
subTopic.practice: Identify HTML elements in a sample page and explain the role of HTML.

subTopic.name: HTML Document Structure
subTopic.notes:
A document has one root element, metadata in , and visible page content in . Set the character encoding, responsive viewport, document title, and page language. The browser builds a DOM tree from this structure. ```html My Page

Hello

```
subTopic.practice: Create a valid HTML document from scratch.

subTopic.name: DOCTYPE Declaration
subTopic.notes: Place <!doctype html> before the root element. It identifies an HTML document and makes browsers use standards mode rather than quirks mode. It is a declaration, not an HTML element or a version-specific tag. Missing or malformed doctypes can trigger legacy layout behavior.
subTopic.practice: Add the correct DOCTYPE and identify an incorrect document setup.

subTopic.name: Elements and Tags
subTopic.notes:
A tag is markup such as

; an element includes its opening tag, content, and closing tag. Most elements have start and end tags; void elements (img, br, input, meta, link) have no closing tag. Use lowercase names, close elements correctly, and do not place block structure where the content model forbids it.
subTopic.practice: Identify and correct incorrectly nested elements.

subTopic.name: HTML Attributes
subTopic.notes: Attributes configure an element and are written in its start tag as name="value". Learn global versus element-specific attributes, boolean attributes (required, disabled, checked), and valid quoting. Boolean attributes are true by presence; writing disabled="false" still disables the control. Avoid duplicate attributes.
subTopic.practice: Add appropriate attributes to links, images, buttons, and inputs.

subTopic.name: Comments
subTopic.notes: HTML comments use <!-- comment --> and are ignored as rendered content, though users can inspect source. Use them to explain non-obvious structure or mark sections; remove stale comments. Never place passwords, API keys, private data, or security-sensitive information in comments.
subTopic.practice: Add useful comments to a sample document.

subTopic.name: Nesting and Hierarchy
subTopic.notes: HTML forms a tree: an element can have parent, child, and sibling nodes. Nest elements according to their content models and close them in the correct order. Invalid nesting can cause browser error recovery and a DOM different from the intended structure. Indentation helps reveal hierarchy.
subTopic.practice: Repair invalid nesting and hierarchy in a document.

subTopic.name: Entities and Special Characters
subTopic.notes: Character references display reserved characters and symbols. Common named references include & (&), < (<), > (>), " (") and   (non-breaking space). Numeric references use decimal (©) or hexadecimal (©). Use UTF-8 for normal Unicode text; escape markup-significant characters in text and attribute values.
subTopic.practice: Display reserved characters and symbols correctly.

subTopic.name: Global Attributes
subTopic.notes: Global attributes apply to most HTML elements: id (unique identifier), class (reusable grouping), title (advisory text), lang (language), dir (text direction), hidden, tabindex, contenteditable, draggable, and data-* (custom data). IDs must be unique; use tabindex="0" for natural keyboard inclusion and avoid positive tabindex values. data-* is exposed through JavaScript dataset.
subTopic.practice: Use suitable global attributes in a sample page.

subTopic.name: HTML Validation
subTopic.notes: Validate markup against HTML conformance rules using the Nu HTML Checker or browser developer tools. Check missing required attributes, invalid nesting, duplicate IDs, obsolete elements, malformed attributes, and semantic misuse. A validator finds markup issues but cannot prove accessibility, usability, security, or correct application behavior.
subTopic.practice: Validate a page and fix reported errors.

subTopic.name: Headings
subTopic.notes: Use h1–h6 to express nested section hierarchy, not merely visual size. Keep heading levels logically ordered and do not skip levels without a structural reason. A page normally has one clear main heading; use CSS for appearance. Screen-reader users often navigate by headings, so labels should describe the section.
subTopic.practice: Structure an article using hierarchical headings.

subTopic.name: Paragraphs and Separators
subTopic.notes:
Use

for a paragraph,
only for a meaningful line break (such as an address or poem), and

for a thematic change between sections. Do not use repeated br elements or hr as spacing tools; use CSS margins and layout for presentation.
subTopic.practice: Format an article into paragraphs and meaningful section breaks.

subTopic.name: Text Emphasis and Importance
subTopic.notes: <strong> conveys importance or seriousness; <em> conveys stress emphasis. <b> draws attention without adding importance, while <i> marks alternate voice or convention (such as a technical term). Choose by meaning, not default bold/italic appearance; style with CSS when appearance alone is intended.
subTopic.practice: Mark important and emphasized text appropriately.

subTopic.name: Inline Text Semantics
subTopic.notes: Use <mark> for highlighted relevance, <small> for side comments, <del>/<ins> for edits, <s> for no-longer-accurate text, <sub>/<sup> for subscripts/superscripts, and <abbr title="..."> for abbreviations. These elements communicate meaning; do not choose them solely for styling.
subTopic.practice: Create content with abbreviations, edits, highlights, and mathematical notation.

subTopic.name: Quotes and Citations
subTopic.notes: Use <blockquote> for an extended quotation and <q> for a short inline quotation. The cite attribute can identify a source URL; <cite> represents the title of a creative work, not generally a person's name. Provide visible attribution where appropriate and quote accurately.
subTopic.practice: Create a quotation section with source information.

subTopic.name: Code and Preformatted Text
subTopic.notes:
Use for inline code, 
 for whitespace-preserving blocks,  for program output,  for user input, and  for variables. Combine pre and code for code listings and escape <, >, and & so examples render as text.

```html

const total = 2 + 3;

```
subTopic.practice: Create a tutorial containing code and keyboard instructions.

subTopic.name: Generic Containers
subTopic.notes: <div> is a generic block container and <span> a generic inline container; neither adds meaning. Use them when no semantic element fits, usually for CSS or scripting hooks. Prefer main, section, article, nav, header, footer, or other semantic elements when their meaning matches the content.
subTopic.practice: Replace generic containers with semantic elements where appropriate.

subTopic.name: Address and Contact Information
subTopic.notes: <address> identifies contact information for the nearest article or page owner, such as an author or organization. It is not a generic wrapper for every postal address. Use readable text and appropriate links (mailto:, tel:); keep unrelated contact details outside the element.
subTopic.practice: Create a contact section using suitable markup.

subTopic.name: Anchor Elements
subTopic.notes: An <a> element with href creates a hyperlink. URLs may be absolute, relative to the current document, or fragment references such as #pricing (matching an element id). Use href for navigation and a button for actions. Check URL encoding and ensure fragment targets exist.
subTopic.practice: Create internal, external, and section-anchor links.

subTopic.name: Link Targets
subTopic.notes: The target attribute controls the browsing context: _self is default, _blank opens a new context, and named targets can reuse one. For untrusted/new-tab destinations, use rel="noopener" (modern browsers imply it for _blank) and consider noreferrer when referrer suppression is required. Do not force new tabs without a user benefit.
subTopic.practice: Create external links that open safely in a new tab.

subTopic.name: Email and Telephone Links
subTopic.notes: Use mailto: for email composition and tel: for telephone dialing. Encode query values when adding subject/body parameters, and format phone numbers with country codes where appropriate. These links depend on a configured mail or phone handler and do not send messages themselves. ```html Email support Call us ```
subTopic.practice: Create clickable email addresses and telephone numbers.

subTopic.name: Navigation Menus
subTopic.notes: Place major navigation links in <nav>, commonly as a list of anchors. Give multiple nav landmarks distinct accessible names (for example, aria-label="Primary"). Use a list for related destinations, indicate the current page with aria-current="page", and ensure keyboard focus is visible.
subTopic.practice: Build a primary navigation menu.

subTopic.name: Download Links
subTopic.notes: The download attribute suggests that a linked resource should be downloaded and may provide a filename. It generally works for same-origin URLs and blob/data URLs; cross-origin behavior can be restricted. The server's Content-Disposition header and browser settings may affect the result.
subTopic.practice: Create links to downloadable files.

subTopic.name: Accessible Link Text
subTopic.notes: Link text should communicate destination or purpose without relying on surrounding visual context. Avoid vague labels such as “click here”; use concise descriptive text, meaningful image alt text for image-only links, and distinguish repeated links when their destinations differ. Links must be keyboard accessible.
subTopic.practice: Rewrite ambiguous links to make their destinations clear.

subTopic.name: Unordered Lists
subTopic.notes: Use <ul> with <li> for items whose order is not meaningful, such as features or ingredients. Each list item belongs directly to a list (or nested list). Do not create lists using manual bullets or line breaks; CSS controls marker style and spacing.
subTopic.practice: Create a list of features or product benefits.

subTopic.name: Ordered Lists
subTopic.notes: Use <ol> with <li> when sequence or ranking matters. start sets the starting number, reversed counts down, and type selects marker style (1, A, a, I, i). The value attribute on li can reset an item's number. Use CSS list-style for presentation where possible.
subTopic.practice: Create a numbered tutorial with a custom starting number.

subTopic.name: Description Lists
subTopic.notes: Use <dl> to associate terms (<dt>) with descriptions (<dd>), such as glossaries, metadata, or key-value details. A term may have one or more descriptions and vice versa. Do not use description lists merely to create indentation or layout.
subTopic.practice: Create a glossary of web development terms.

subTopic.name: Nested Lists
subTopic.notes: Place a nested <ul> or <ol> inside the relevant parent <li>, not beside it. The nested list expresses hierarchy beneath that item. Keep nesting meaningful and avoid excessive depth; use headings or separate sections for complex information architecture.
subTopic.practice: Create a curriculum outline with topics and subtopics.

subTopic.name: Image Element
subTopic.notes: Use to embed an image. Provide meaningful alternative text for informative images and alt="" for decorative images. Set intrinsic width and height to reserve layout space and reduce layout shift; use CSS for responsive sizing. ```html ```
subTopic.practice: Add informative and decorative images with appropriate alternative text.

subTopic.name: Image Accessibility
subTopic.notes: Choose alt text by the image's purpose in context: describe essential information for informative images, use empty alt for decoration, and describe an action/destination for linked images. Avoid “image of” unless relevant, and do not repeat nearby text. Complex charts need a complete text explanation or data table.
subTopic.practice: Write suitable alt text for product and informational images.

subTopic.name: Responsive Images
subTopic.notes: Use srcset and sizes to let the browser select a suitable resolution based on viewport and pixel density. Use with or type for art direction and format alternatives; keep as the fallback and alt-text source. Test crop, aspect ratio, and quality across breakpoints.
subTopic.practice: Build a responsive image example using alternate image sources.

subTopic.name: Image Formats and Loading
subTopic.notes: Choose formats by content and support: AVIF/WebP often reduce size; JPEG suits photos; PNG suits lossless transparency; SVG suits scalable vector graphics. Use loading="lazy" for offscreen images, not the likely LCP hero; consider fetchpriority="high" for the main image and decoding="async" where appropriate. Compress and size assets correctly.
subTopic.practice: Improve image markup for a page with multiple images.

subTopic.name: Figure and Figcaption
subTopic.notes: Use <figure> for self-contained content such as an image, diagram, code listing, or chart that can be referenced independently. <figcaption> supplies its caption and may appear before or after the content. Do not use figure solely as a styling wrapper.
subTopic.practice: Create an article image with a caption.

subTopic.name: Audio Element
subTopic.notes: Use <audio controls> to provide native playback UI; add one or more <source> elements with accurate type values and fallback text. Common attributes include loop, muted, preload, and autoplay; autoplay with sound is commonly blocked. Provide transcripts for meaningful spoken content and do not rely on audio alone.
subTopic.practice: Embed audio with accessible playback controls.

subTopic.name: Video Element
subTopic.notes: Use <video controls> with source files, a poster image, and fallback text. Configure width/height or aspect ratio to prevent layout shift; preload can be none, metadata, or auto. playsinline supports inline mobile playback; autoplay is commonly restricted unless muted. Provide captions and accessible controls.
subTopic.practice: Embed a video with a poster image and controls.

subTopic.name: Captions and Transcripts
subTopic.notes: Use <track kind="captions" src="..." srclang="en" label="English"> for synchronized dialogue and relevant sounds; subtitles translate dialogue, while descriptions convey visual information. A transcript provides a text equivalent and supports search and accessibility. Ensure WebVTT timing and language metadata are correct.
subTopic.practice: Add captions and a transcript to a sample video.

subTopic.name: Iframes and External Content
subTopic.notes: An <iframe> embeds another browsing context. Give it a descriptive title; use loading="lazy" for offscreen embeds and sandbox to restrict capabilities, granting only required tokens. Configure allow and referrerpolicy deliberately. Embed only trusted sources and consider privacy, third-party tracking, and responsive dimensions.
subTopic.practice: Embed an external resource with a descriptive title and suitable restrictions.

subTopic.name: Object and Embed
subTopic.notes: <object> can embed external resources and provide fallback content; <embed> is a void element for external content. Browser/plugin support varies, and these are less common for modern media than img, audio, video, or iframe. Prefer a direct link or supported native element when possible.
subTopic.practice: Compare embedding approaches for a document or external resource.

subTopic.name: Semantic HTML Fundamentals
subTopic.notes: Semantic elements communicate purpose to browsers, assistive technology, search engines, and developers. Use landmarks and content elements according to their meaning rather than choosing tags for default styling. Good semantics improve navigation, maintainability, and accessibility but do not replace labels, keyboard support, or testing.
subTopic.practice: Replace a generic div-based layout with semantic HTML.

subTopic.name: Header and Footer
subTopic.notes: <header> contains introductory content or navigation for a page or section; <footer> contains related closing information such as author, copyright, or related links. They may appear at page or section level. They are not automatically landmark regions when nested inside sectioning content.
subTopic.practice: Build a page with a site header and article footer.

subTopic.name: Main Element
subTopic.notes: <main> identifies the document's dominant content and usually appears once per page, outside repeated site-wide headers, navigation, and footers. It helps assistive technology jump to primary content. Do not use multiple simultaneously exposed main elements; hidden alternatives require careful handling.
subTopic.practice: Identify and correct multiple main elements in a page.

subTopic.name: Section and Article
subTopic.notes: <section> groups a thematic part of a page and generally has a heading. <article> is self-contained content that could be distributed or reused independently, such as a post or news story. Use div when no semantic grouping applies; do not select section merely to obtain styling hooks.
subTopic.practice: Structure a blog page with articles and thematic sections.

subTopic.name: Aside Element
subTopic.notes: <aside> marks complementary content tangentially related to surrounding content, such as a sidebar, glossary note, or related links. Its meaning depends on context. It is not synonymous with every visually positioned sidebar; use CSS for placement and a suitable heading when helpful.
subTopic.practice: Add related articles to a main article page.

subTopic.name: Semantic Navigation
subTopic.notes: Use <nav> for a major block of navigation links, not every group of links. A page can have multiple nav landmarks, each with a unique accessible label. Structure links in lists where appropriate, identify the current destination, and preserve logical keyboard order.
subTopic.practice: Create primary and secondary navigation regions.

subTopic.name: Time and Date Semantics
subTopic.notes: <time datetime="..."> presents human-readable date/time while exposing a machine-readable value. Use valid date, time, or duration formats (for example, 2026-11-16 or PT30M). The visible text should agree with datetime, including timezone meaning when relevant.
subTopic.practice: Mark publication dates and event schedules.

subTopic.name: Details and Summary
subTopic.notes: <details> creates a native disclosure widget; its first <summary> child is the visible label. The open attribute sets the initial expanded state, and name can group related disclosures in supporting browsers. Native keyboard behavior is provided; ensure summary text clearly describes the hidden content.
subTopic.practice: Create an FAQ using details and summary.

subTopic.name: Dialog Element
subTopic.notes: <dialog> represents a dialog; show() opens it non-modally and showModal() opens it modally with background interaction blocked. close() closes it, and the close event can observe closure. Provide a clear title, accessible focus management, a close/cancel path, and restore focus to the invoker.
subTopic.practice: Create a confirmation dialog using dialog.

subTopic.name: Table Fundamentals
subTopic.notes: Use <table> only for data with meaningful row/column relationships, not page layout. Rows use <tr>, header cells use <th>, and data cells use <td>. Provide clear headers and, where useful, a caption. Keep the source order logical for screen readers and narrow screens.
subTopic.practice: Create a course table with names, durations, and statuses.

subTopic.name: Table Structure
subTopic.notes: Use <caption> to name the table, <thead> for column headings, <tbody> for data rows, and <tfoot> for summary/footer rows. These groups clarify structure and support styling and scripting. A table can contain multiple tbody sections; use valid row/cell nesting.
subTopic.practice: Organize a data table into meaningful sections.

subTopic.name: Headers and Accessibility
subTopic.notes: Use <th scope="col"> for column headers and <th scope="row"> for row headers so assistive technology can associate data with headings. For complex multi-level tables, use id on headers and headers on data cells. Include a useful caption and avoid using tables for layout.
subTopic.practice: Build an accessible student-results table.

subTopic.name: Complex Tables
subTopic.notes: colspan merges cells across columns and rowspan across rows. Ensure the resulting grid remains coherent and header relationships remain explicit. Multi-level headers may need id/headers associations; do not rely on visual position alone. Validate that every row has the intended number of columns.
subTopic.practice: Create a timetable with merged cells and meaningful headers.

subTopic.name: Responsive Tables
subTopic.notes: Wide data tables may need a horizontally scrollable wrapper, a deliberate minimum width, or a simplified mobile presentation. Preserve table semantics and keyboard access; provide a visible cue when horizontal scrolling is available. Do not convert tabular relationships into inaccessible visual-only cards.
subTopic.practice: Create a wide data table that remains usable on mobile.

subTopic.name: Form Fundamentals
subTopic.notes: <form> groups controls for submission. action specifies the destination URL and method is usually GET (query parameters) or POST (request body). Controls need name attributes to be submitted. Server-side code must validate all data; client-side validation improves usability but is not a security boundary.
subTopic.practice: Create a form that submits to a test endpoint.

subTopic.name: Input Types
subTopic.notes: Choose input types to match data: text, email, password, number, checkbox, radio, date, file, hidden, search, url, tel, and others. Type affects browser UI, validation, keyboard, and submitted value. Radio controls share a name for one choice; checkboxes allow independent selections.
subTopic.practice: Create a form using appropriate input types.

subTopic.name: Input Attributes
subTopic.notes: name determines the submitted key; value sets the current/default value; placeholder is a hint, not a label. required enables constraint validation; readonly values submit while disabled controls do not. autocomplete improves entry, autofocus should be used sparingly, and inputmode hints the virtual keyboard.
subTopic.practice: Configure inputs with appropriate attributes.

subTopic.name: Labels and Field Groups
subTopic.notes: Associate <label for="email"> with an input id="email"; wrapping the control in label is an alternative. Labels provide accessible names and larger click targets. Use <fieldset> and <legend> to group related controls, especially radio buttons and checkboxes.
subTopic.practice: Create an accessible registration form with grouped fields.

subTopic.name: Textarea and Select
subTopic.notes: <textarea> accepts multiline text and uses its text content as the initial value. <select> contains <option> elements; optgroup groups options and selected sets an initial choice. multiple permits several selections. Always provide a label and meaningful option values.
subTopic.practice: Create a feedback form with a message field and grouped options.

subTopic.name: Buttons in Forms
subTopic.notes: A button inside a form defaults to submit unless its type is specified. Use type="submit" to submit, type="button" for custom actions, and type="reset" only when reset is genuinely useful. Explicit types prevent accidental form submission from unrelated controls.
subTopic.practice: Build a form with submit and non-submit buttons.

subTopic.name: Native Form Validation
subTopic.notes: HTML constraints include required, minlength, maxlength, min, max, step, and pattern. The browser blocks invalid submission and exposes validity states; :valid and :invalid can style controls. Use clear instructions and error messages, and repeat validation on the server because client checks can be bypassed.
subTopic.practice: Create a form with native validation constraints.

subTopic.name: Form Submission Data
subTopic.notes: Submission serializes successful named controls as key-value pairs; disabled controls and unnamed controls are omitted. GET appends data to the URL and suits retrieval; POST sends a request body. enctype controls encoding, including multipart/form-data for file uploads and application/x-www-form-urlencoded by default.
subTopic.practice: Inspect submitted form data and compare encodings.

subTopic.name: File Upload Inputs
subTopic.notes: Use <input type="file"> with accept as a chooser hint and multiple to allow several files. The server must independently verify file type, size, content, and authorization; accept is not security validation. Use multipart/form-data and provide clear upload limits and feedback.
subTopic.practice: Build a document upload form with file-type restrictions.

subTopic.name: Specialized Form Controls
subTopic.notes: Use range for sliders, color for color selection, date/time/datetime-local/month/week for temporal values, and search for search terms. Browser support and UI vary. Read submitted values in their defined formats and do not assume the user's timezone for datetime-local values.
subTopic.practice: Create a booking form using specialized inputs.

subTopic.name: Datalist and Output
subTopic.notes: <datalist id="choices"> provides suggestions for an input with a matching list attribute; users can usually enter values beyond suggestions. <output> represents a calculation or action result and can be associated with controls using for. Validate entered values even when suggestions exist.
subTopic.practice: Create a form with suggestions and a calculation result.

subTopic.name: Form Accessibility
subTopic.notes: Every control needs an accessible name, usually a visible label. Provide instructions, required-state indicators, grouped controls, and programmatically associated error descriptions (for example, aria-describedby). Ensure keyboard operation, visible focus, logical tab order, and errors that identify how to fix the issue.
subTopic.practice: Audit and improve a registration form's accessibility.

subTopic.name: Semantic Markup for SEO
subTopic.notes: Search engines use page content and links to understand a page; semantic HTML clarifies structure but does not guarantee ranking. Use descriptive titles, meaningful headings, crawlable anchors, useful alt text, and content that matches user intent. Avoid keyword stuffing and empty semantic wrappers.
subTopic.practice: Improve a poorly structured article page.

subTopic.name: Search Metadata
subTopic.notes: Set a unique, descriptive <title> and concise meta name="description" for each page. Use rel="canonical" to indicate the preferred URL when duplicate/near-duplicate URLs exist, and robots metadata to control indexing/snippet behavior. Metadata guides crawlers; search engines may choose different titles or snippets.
subTopic.practice: Prepare metadata for a product page and blog article.

subTopic.name: Structured Data Concepts
subTopic.notes:
Structured data expresses page entities and properties in a machine-readable vocabulary, commonly Schema.org JSON-LD. Mark up only visible, accurate content and choose a type that matches the page. Valid markup can make a page eligible for rich results, but eligibility does not guarantee display.

```html
<script type="application/ld+json">
{"@context":"https://schema.org","@type":"Article","headline":"HTML Basics"}
</script>
```
subTopic.practice: Add appropriate structured data to a sample article and validate its format.

subTopic.name: Heading and Link Optimization
subTopic.notes: Create a logical heading outline with descriptive section titles and natural language. Use concise anchor text that explains the linked page or resource, and connect related pages with contextual internal links. Avoid repetitive exact-match keywords, generic anchors, and heading levels chosen only for visual size.
subTopic.practice: Improve heading hierarchy and internal links.

subTopic.name: Crawlability and Indexing
subTopic.notes: Ensure important pages are reachable through crawlable <a href> links, return appropriate HTTP status codes, and avoid accidental noindex directives. robots.txt controls crawling, not reliable de-indexing; meta robots controls indexing instructions when crawlers can access the page. Canonicals consolidate duplicate URL signals but are hints, not guarantees.
subTopic.practice: Review a page for indexing and canonicalization mistakes.

subTopic.name: HTML Fundamentals Quiz
subTopic.notes: Review document skeleton, doctype, elements versus tags, void elements, attributes, entities, and valid nesting. Be able to predict the DOM for short snippets, identify browser-recovered markup errors, and explain semantic choices. Test understanding with MCQs, code-reading, and correction exercises.
subTopic.practice: Complete MCQs, output-prediction questions, and error-identification tasks.

subTopic.name: Semantic HTML Challenge
subTopic.notes: Convert a generic layout into meaningful header, nav, main, article, section, aside, and footer regions. Add a logical heading hierarchy, descriptive links, and accessible landmarks. Verify that the page remains understandable without CSS and can be navigated by headings and landmarks.
subTopic.practice: Convert a generic webpage into a semantic HTML document.

subTopic.name: Forms Challenge
subTopic.notes: Build a complete form with appropriate input types, associated labels, fieldset/legend groups, constraints, and useful error guidance. Test keyboard-only interaction, required and invalid states, and actual submitted name-value pairs. Remember to validate and sanitize again on the server.
subTopic.practice: Build a complete registration form with native validation.

subTopic.name: Tables and Media Challenge
subTopic.notes: Create a data table with caption, header associations, and responsive handling; add responsive images, audio/video controls, captions, and a properly titled iframe where relevant. Verify alternatives and transcripts, test media fallback, and check that the page works on small screens.
subTopic.practice: Build a report page with an accessible table and multimedia.

subTopic.name: Accessibility Audit
subTopic.notes: Audit semantic landmarks, heading order, keyboard navigation, visible focus, link purpose, image alternatives, form labels, error associations, and table headers. Use automated tools such as axe or Lighthouse as aids, then perform manual keyboard and screen-reader checks; automated scores alone are insufficient.
subTopic.practice: Audit a webpage and correct its accessibility issues.

subTopic.name: SEO Markup Challenge
subTopic.notes: Prepare a meaningful title, description, canonical URL where needed, robots directives, semantic article structure, and appropriate JSON-LD. Confirm metadata is page-specific, structured data matches visible content, and internal links are crawlable. Validate JSON syntax and test eligibility with search-engine tools.
subTopic.practice: Prepare a document head and semantic body for an article page.

subTopic.name: HTML Debugging Challenge
subTopic.notes: Inspect a deliberately broken document for missing doctype, malformed tags, invalid nesting, duplicate IDs, missing alt/labels, incorrect form attributes, and semantic misuse. Use browser DevTools and an HTML validator, fix the underlying markup, then retest keyboard behavior and submission.
subTopic.practice: Fix a deliberately broken HTML document and validate it.

subTopic.name: Project 1: Personal Profile Page
subTopic.notes: Build a profile page using a valid document skeleton, one clear h1, section headings, paragraphs, a profile image with suitable alt text, skills/interests lists, and contact links. Keep content semantic and readable without CSS; then validate markup and test links.
subTopic.practice: Build a personal profile page with biography, skills, interests, and contact links.

subTopic.name: Project 2: Course Catalog Page
subTopic.notes: Create a catalog with semantic header/nav/main, course cards grouped by category, descriptive titles and summaries, images with useful alternatives, and links to details. Use lists or articles appropriately, make navigation keyboard accessible, and ensure each course link has a clear purpose.
subTopic.practice: Build a catalog page containing course cards, descriptions, categories, and navigation.

subTopic.name: Project 3: Registration and Feedback Forms
subTopic.notes: Build registration and feedback forms with labels, suitable input types, fieldsets, select, textarea, required constraints, and submit controls. Test valid/invalid cases and inspect FormData or network submissions. Document that backend validation and secure handling are still required.
subTopic.practice: Build accessible registration and feedback forms with native validation.

subTopic.name: Project 4: Blog Article and Media Page
subTopic.notes: Create an article with title and metadata, semantic sections, author/date information, figures and captions, an accessible data table, and embedded audio/video with captions or transcripts. Add descriptive internal links and page-specific SEO metadata; verify responsive behavior.
subTopic.practice: Build a complete article page with images, a data table, embedded media, and metadata.

subTopic.name: Project 5: Accessible Multi-Page Website
subTopic.notes: Build linked home, course-listing, course-detail, and contact pages with consistent semantic navigation, unique titles/descriptions, responsive images, accessible forms, and clear heading hierarchy. Test all routes and links, keyboard navigation, mobile layouts, validation, and HTML conformance.
subTopic.practice: Build a multi-page educational website with a homepage, course listing, course detail, contact form, and accessible navigation.

4.name: Cascading Styling Sheet
4.desc: Turn basic HTML structures into attractive, responsive web experiences. Learn how to control layouts, typography, colors, spacing, animations, and visual hierarchy, then apply those skills to real-world interfaces that work across screen sizes.

subTopic.name: Introduction to CSS
subTopic.notes: CSS (Cascading Style Sheets) controls the presentation of HTML: colors, typography, spacing, layout and responsive behavior. The browser parses CSS, matches selectors to elements, resolves the cascade, computes styles and renders the result. Keep content/meaning in HTML and presentation in CSS.
subTopic.practice: Explain the role of CSS and identify CSS rules in a sample stylesheet.

subTopic.name: Ways to Apply CSS
subTopic.notes: Inline CSS uses the style attribute and is best kept for exceptional, dynamic cases; internal CSS uses a style element; external CSS uses a separate .css file linked with link rel="stylesheet". External files are easiest to reuse, cache and maintain. @import loads another stylesheet but can delay discovery; link is generally preferred. When rules conflict, cascade rules and source order matter.
subTopic.practice: Connect an external stylesheet and compare the three ways of applying CSS.

subTopic.name: CSS Syntax and Rules
subTopic.practice: Write CSS rules for sample elements and correct syntax errors.

subTopic.name: CSS Selectors
subTopic.practice: Write selectors that target specified elements without affecting unrelated elements.

subTopic.name: Combinators
subTopic.practice: Style nested and sibling elements using the appropriate combinator.

subTopic.name: Attribute Selectors
subTopic.practice: Style links and form controls according to their attributes.

subTopic.name: CSS Cascade
subTopic.notes: The cascade resolves competing declarations by origin and importance, cascade layer, specificity, scoping proximity where applicable, and source order. Inheritance passes selected properties from parent to child; computed values resolve relative values and variables. Do not assume the last rule wins unless earlier cascade criteria tie.
subTopic.practice: Resolve conflicting declarations and explain which rule wins.

subTopic.name: Specificity and Inheritance
subTopic.notes: Specificity is commonly compared as ID, class/attribute/pseudo-class, then type/pseudo-element components; compare each column from left to right, not by adding arbitrary scores. Inline styles and !important have special cascade treatment. Text and color often inherit; box-model properties generally do not. Keep selectors shallow.
subTopic.practice: Debug conflicting styles and reduce unnecessary specificity.

subTopic.name: Cascade Layers
subTopic.practice: Organize base, component, utility, and override styles into layers.

subTopic.name: CSS Units and Values
subTopic.notes: Absolute px units are useful for fine details; %, em and rem scale relative to containing dimensions or font sizes; vw/vh and svh/lvh/dvh relate to viewport dimensions; container units relate to a query container. Choose units based on what should scale. Intrinsic keywords such as min-content and max-content size from content.
subTopic.practice: Choose appropriate units for text, spacing, and responsive dimensions.

subTopic.name: CSS Math Functions
subTopic.practice: Create fluid spacing and typography with CSS math functions.

subTopic.name: CSS Reset and Normalize Concepts
subTopic.practice: Create an intentional base stylesheet for a new project.

subTopic.name: CSS Color Formats
subTopic.notes: Understand css color formats as part of practical CSS authoring. Core concepts: Named colors, hex, RGB, RGBA, HSL, HSLA, and modern color syntax. Know the syntax, what each option changes, when to use it, and its interaction with normal document flow, the cascade, responsive behavior and accessibility. Verify the result in browser DevTools and test keyboard, narrow-screen and long-content cases where relevant.
subTopic.practice: Recreate a supplied palette using several CSS color formats.

subTopic.name: Transparency and Color Mixing
subTopic.notes: Understand transparency and color mixing as part of practical CSS authoring. Core concepts: Alpha channels, color-mix(), color interpolation, and transparency trade-offs. Know the syntax, what each option changes, when to use it, and its interaction with normal document flow, the cascade, responsive behavior and accessibility. Verify the result in browser DevTools and test keyboard, narrow-screen and long-content cases where relevant.
subTopic.practice: Create a palette with mixed colors and translucent surfaces.

subTopic.name: CSS Gradients

subTopic.name: Background Shorthand
subTopic.notes: Understand background shorthand as part of practical CSS authoring. Core concepts: Combining background properties and understanding shorthand resets. Know the syntax, what each option changes, when to use it, and its interaction with normal document flow, the cascade, responsive behavior and accessibility. Verify the result in browser DevTools and test keyboard, narrow-screen and long-content cases where relevant.
subTopic.practice: Refactor background declarations into correct shorthand.

subTopic.name: Color Contrast Basics
subTopic.notes: Contrast is the luminance difference between foreground and background. WCAG guidance commonly targets 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text; UI components and graphical objects have their own requirements. Check real rendered combinations and never communicate status by color alone.
subTopic.practice: Audit a color palette for readable text combinations.

subTopic.name: Font Families
subTopic.notes:
Understand font families as part of practical CSS authoring. Core concepts: Font-family stacks, generic families, system fonts, and fallback behavior. Know the syntax, what each option changes, when to use it, and its interaction with normal document flow, the cascade, responsive behavior and accessibility. Verify the result in browser DevTools and test keyboard, narrow-screen and long-content cases where relevant.

```css
body { font-family: Inter, system-ui, sans-serif; }
```
subTopic.practice: Choose resilient font stacks for headings and body text.

subTopic.name: Font Size and Weight
subTopic.notes: font-size sets glyph size and font-weight selects stroke weight (commonly 100–900 for variable or supported families). Use rem-based type scales for user-scalable hierarchy and avoid relying on boldness alone to communicate structure.
subTopic.practice: Build a heading hierarchy with suitable size and weight.

subTopic.name: Font Style and Variants
subTopic.notes: Understand font style and variants as part of practical CSS authoring. Core concepts: font-style, font-variant, variable font axes, and font-feature settings. Know the syntax, what each option changes, when to use it, and its interaction with normal document flow, the cascade, responsive behavior and accessibility. Verify the result in browser DevTools and test keyboard, narrow-screen and long-content cases where relevant.
subTopic.practice: Style emphasis and compare available font variants.

subTopic.name: Line Height and Spacing
subTopic.notes:
line-height controls the line box and is usually best unitless so it scales with font size. letter-spacing adjusts character spacing; word-spacing adjusts spaces between words; text-indent offsets the first line. Use comfortable line height and avoid excessive tracking in body text.

```css
p { line-height: 1.6; letter-spacing: .01em; }
```
subTopic.practice: Improve readability of a long-form article.

subTopic.name: Text Alignment and Decoration
subTopic.notes: Understand text alignment and decoration as part of practical CSS authoring. Core concepts: text-align, text-decoration, text-transform, text-shadow, and text-align-last. Know the syntax, what each option changes, when to use it, and its interaction with normal document flow, the cascade, responsive behavior and accessibility. Verify the result in browser DevTools and test keyboard, narrow-screen and long-content cases where relevant.
subTopic.practice: Style headings, links, and highlighted text consistently.

subTopic.name: Text Wrapping and Overflow
subTopic.notes: Understand text wrapping and overflow as part of practical CSS authoring. Core concepts: white-space, overflow-wrap, word-break, hyphens, text-overflow, and line-clamping concepts. Know the syntax, what each option changes, when to use it, and its interaction with normal document flow, the cascade, responsive behavior and accessibility. Verify the result in browser DevTools and test keyboard, narrow-screen and long-content cases where relevant.
subTopic.practice: Fix overflowing titles and long unbroken strings.

subTopic.name: Web Fonts
subTopic.notes: Understand web fonts as part of practical CSS authoring. Core concepts: @font-face, font formats, font-display, fallback fonts, and font loading. Know the syntax, what each option changes, when to use it, and its interaction with normal document flow, the cascade, responsive behavior and accessibility. Verify the result in browser DevTools and test keyboard, narrow-screen and long-content cases where relevant.

subTopic.name: Responsive Typography
subTopic.notes:
Understand responsive typography as part of practical CSS authoring. Core concepts: Fluid type scales, viewport-relative sizes, clamp(), and readable line lengths. Know the syntax, what each option changes, when to use it, and its interaction with normal document flow, the cascade, responsive behavior and accessibility. Verify the result in browser DevTools and test keyboard, narrow-screen and long-content cases where relevant.

```css
.heading { font-size: clamp(2rem, 5vw, 4rem); }
```
subTopic.practice: Create a typography scale that adapts across viewport sizes.

subTopic.name: Box Model Fundamentals
subTopic.notes: The default content-box width excludes padding and borders: rendered width = content width + horizontal padding + borders. Margins sit outside the border and separate boxes. With border-box, the declared width includes content, padding and border, simplifying layout calculations.
subTopic.practice: Calculate the rendered size of a set of boxes.

subTopic.name: Box Sizing
subTopic.notes:
content-box applies width/height to the content area; border-box includes padding and border in the declared dimensions. A common predictable baseline is * , *::before, *::after { box-sizing: border-box; }.

```css
*, *::before, *::after { box-sizing: border-box; }
```
subTopic.practice: Make card widths predictable using border-box sizing.

subTopic.name: Width and Height
subTopic.notes: Understand width and height as part of practical CSS authoring. Core concepts: width, height, min-width, max-width, min-height, max-height, and auto sizing. Know the syntax, what each option changes, when to use it, and its interaction with normal document flow, the cascade, responsive behavior and accessibility. Verify the result in browser DevTools and test keyboard, narrow-screen and long-content cases where relevant.
subTopic.practice: Create a card with controlled dimensions and responsive constraints.

subTopic.name: Padding and Margin
subTopic.notes: Understand padding and margin as part of practical CSS authoring. Core concepts: Individual sides, shorthand syntax, auto margins, and spacing conventions. Know the syntax, what each option changes, when to use it, and its interaction with normal document flow, the cascade, responsive behavior and accessibility. Verify the result in browser DevTools and test keyboard, narrow-screen and long-content cases where relevant.
subTopic.practice: Align elements and establish consistent spacing.

subTopic.name: Margin Collapsing
subTopic.notes: Adjacent vertical block margins in normal flow can collapse to the larger margin rather than add together. This can occur between siblings and parent/child boundaries. Padding, borders, inline content, a new formatting context, or flex/grid layout can prevent many collapsing cases.
subTopic.practice: Diagnose unexpected vertical gaps between elements.

subTopic.name: Borders and Outlines
subTopic.notes: Understand borders and outlines as part of practical CSS authoring. Core concepts: Border styles, widths, colors, shorthand, outline, and outline-offset. Know the syntax, what each option changes, when to use it, and its interaction with normal document flow, the cascade, responsive behavior and accessibility. Verify the result in browser DevTools and test keyboard, narrow-screen and long-content cases where relevant.
