subTopic.name: Border Radius
subTopic.notes: Understand border radius as part of practical CSS authoring. Core concepts: Individual corners, elliptical radii, and pill-shaped elements. Know the syntax, what each option changes, when to use it, and its interaction with normal document flow, the cascade, responsive behavior and accessibility. Verify the result in browser DevTools and test keyboard, narrow-screen and long-content cases where relevant.
subTopic.practice: Build rounded cards, avatars, and pill buttons.

subTopic.name: Box Shadows
subTopic.notes: Understand box shadows as part of practical CSS authoring. Core concepts: Shadow layers, inset shadows, blur, spread, and elevation systems. Know the syntax, what each option changes, when to use it, and its interaction with normal document flow, the cascade, responsive behavior and accessibility. subTopic.name: Overflow
subTopic.notes:
overflow controls content outside a box: visible allows it, hidden clips and may create a scroll container, clip clips without scrolling, scroll always provides scrolling, and auto scrolls when needed. Set overflow-x and overflow-y deliberately; clipping can affect focus rings and positioned descendants.

```css
.panel { max-height: 20rem; overflow-y: auto; }
```
subTopic.practice: Fix unwanted overflow and create a scrollable panel.

subTopic.name: Intrinsic Sizing
subTopic.notes: Understand intrinsic sizing as part of practical CSS authoring. Core concepts: min-content, max-content, fit-content, and min-width:auto behavior. Know the syntax, what each option changes, when to use it, and its interaction with normal document flow, the cascade, responsive behavior and accessibility. Verify the result in browser DevTools and test keyboard, narrow-screen and long-content cases where relevant.
subTopic.practice: Fix flex and grid children that refuse to shrink.

subTopic.name: Display Values
subTopic.practice: Choose appropriate display values for common layout scenarios.

subTopic.name: Visibility and Opacity
subTopic.notes: display:none removes layout space; visibility:hidden preserves the box but hides it; opacity:0 makes it transparent while it can remain interactive and focusable. Choose the method according to layout and accessibility needs, and disable interaction when visually hidden controls should not be usable.
subTopic.practice: Compare hiding methods and choose the right one for a UI state.

subTopic.name: Formatting Contexts

subTopic.name: Overflow and Clipping

subTopic.name: Containing Blocks

Know the syntax, what each option changes, when to use it, and its interaction with normal document flow, the cascade, responsive behavior and accessibility. Verify the result in browser DevTools and test keyboard, narrow-screen and long-content cases where relevant.
subTopic.practice: Debug an absolutely positioned element using the wrong ancestor.

subTopic.name: Z-Index
subTopic.notes: z-index controls stacking within a stacking context; a larger value does not guarantee appearing above elements in other contexts. It applies to positioned elements and certain layout items. Establish a deliberate layer scale for menus, dialogs and fixed UI.
subTopic.practice: Layer a dropdown, modal, and page header correctly.

subTopic.name: Stacking Contexts
subTopic.notes: Understand stacking contexts as part of practical CSS authoring. Core concepts: How transforms, opacity, isolation, and other properties create stacking contexts. Know the syntax, what each option changes, when to use it, and its interaction with normal document flow, the cascade, responsive behavior and accessibility. subTopic.name: Sticky Positioning

Verify the result in browser DevTools and test keyboard, narrow-screen and long-content cases where relevant.

subTopic.name: Fixed UI Patterns
subTopic.notes: Understand fixed ui patterns as part of practical CSS authoring. Core concepts: Fixed headers, floating action buttons, overlays, and viewport positioning. Know the syntax, what each option changes, when to use it, and its interaction with normal document flow, the cascade, responsive behavior and accessibility. Verify the result in browser DevTools and test keyboard, narrow-screen and long-content cases where relevant.
subTopic.practice: Create a fixed back-to-top control and floating help button.

subTopic.name: Flexbox Fundamentals
subTopic.notes:
Flexbox lays out items along one primary axis. The main axis follows flex-direction and the cross axis is perpendicular. The container controls distribution and alignment; items can grow, shrink and wrap. Use it for one-dimensional component layouts such as nav bars and toolbars.

```css
.row { display: flex; align-items: center; justify-content: space-between; gap: 1rem; }
```

subTopic.name: Flexbox Debugging
subTopic.notes: Understand flexbox debugging as part of practical CSS authoring. Core concepts: Flex overlays, sizing calculations, and alignment diagnosis. Know the syntax, what each option changes, when to use it, and its interaction with normal document flow, the cascade, responsive behavior and accessibility. Verify the result in browser DevTools and test keyboard, narrow-screen and long-content cases where relevant.

subTopic.name: Grid Fundamentals
subTopic.notes:
CSS Grid is a two-dimensional layout system with rows and columns. The grid container defines tracks and gaps; children are grid items placed into cells or spans. Use Grid for page structures, dashboards and galleries where both axes matter.

```css
.cards { display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr); gap: 1rem; }
```
subTopic.practice: Build a basic card grid.

subTopic.name: Grid Tracks and fr Units
subTopic.notes: grid-template-columns and grid-template-rows define explicit tracks. The fr unit distributes available space proportionally after fixed and intrinsic sizing contributions are considered. minmax() sets lower and upper track limits; gaps are separate from track sizes.
subTopic.practice: Create equal and unequal grid tracks.

subTopic.name: Repeat and Minmax
subTopic.notes:
repeat() avoids repeating track definitions. minmax(min,max) bounds a track; auto-fit collapses empty repeated tracks while auto-fill preserves their space. A common responsive pattern is repeat(auto-fit, minmax(min(100%, 16rem), 1fr)).

```css
.cards { display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(16rem, 1fr)); gap: 1rem; }
```

subTopic.name: Grid Placement

subTopic.name: Responsive Design Principles
subTopic.notes: Responsive design adapts content and layout to available space, not to named devices. Start with a usable narrow-screen layout, use flexible sizing and content-driven breakpoints, and test real content. Avoid fixed widths that cause horizontal scrolling.

5.name: JavaScript
5.desc: Master the programming language that makes websites interactive. Begin with variables and basic logic, progress through functions, objects, asynchronous programming, and the DOM, and then explore advanced JavaScript concepts through coding exercises and practical projects.

subTopic.name: What is JavaScript?
History and evolution of JavaScript
subTopic.notes:
JavaScript was created by Brendan Eich at Netscape in 1995 to add behavior to web pages. It was initially developed rapidly and first appeared under names including Mocha and LiveScript before becoming JavaScript. The language was standardized as ECMAScript in 1997 so different implementations could follow a common specification.

Important milestones:
- ES3 (1999) established many familiar language foundations.
- ES5 (2009) added strict mode, JSON support, and array methods such as `map` and `filter`.
- ES2015 (ES6) introduced major features including `let`, `const`, classes, modules, arrow functions, promises, and template literals.
- Annual ECMAScript releases now add features incrementally.

When learning JavaScript, distinguish historical browser-specific behavior from modern standardized language features. Prefer current syntax while understanding older code encountered in projects.

subTopic.name: JavaScript vs Java
subTopic.notes:
JavaScript and Java are distinct programming languages despite their similar names. JavaScript is dynamically typed and commonly uses prototype-based object delegation; Java is statically typed and class-based. JavaScript code is commonly executed by browser or server-side JavaScript engines, while Java commonly compiles to JVM bytecode.

| Aspect | JavaScript | Java |
|---|---|---|
| Typing | Dynamic | Static |
| Typical runtime | Browser, Node.js | Java Virtual Machine |
| Object model | Prototype-based | Class-based |
| Common uses | Web UI, APIs, full-stack apps | Enterprise systems, Android-related and backend systems |

Example JavaScript:
```js
let value = 10;
value = "ten"; // allowed; the variable is dynamically typed
```
A Java variable declared as `int` cannot later hold a `String`. Do not assume that learning one language means the syntax, runtime, or type system of the other is interchangeable.

subTopic.name: ECMAScript and JavaScript versions
subTopic.notes:
ECMAScript (often abbreviated ES) is the language specification; JavaScript is the widely used implementation name. The specification is maintained by Ecma International as ECMA-262. Browsers and runtimes implement the specification, although support for a feature can vary by engine version.

Key points:
- ES5 is common in legacy code.
- ES2015/ES6 introduced a major modernization of the language.
- Since 2016, ECMAScript has generally followed a yearly release cycle (ES2016, ES2017, and so on).
- A feature being standardized does not guarantee that every old browser supports it.

Example of modern syntax:
```js
const greet = (name = "there") => `Hello, ${name}`;
```
Use compatibility data and your project's browser targets to decide whether to use a feature directly, transpile it with a tool such as Babel, or provide a fallback. Transpilation changes syntax; it does not automatically polyfill every missing runtime API.

subTopic.name: Where JavaScript runs: browsers and Node.js
subTopic.notes:
JavaScript runs inside a host environment that provides APIs around the core language. A browser supplies APIs for the DOM, events, storage, networking, and rendering. Node.js supplies APIs for filesystems, processes, networking, streams, and server creation.

The ECMAScript language itself includes values, functions, objects, arrays, promises, and other built-ins. APIs such as `document`, `window`, and `localStorage` are browser-provided; `process` and many filesystem APIs are Node.js-provided.

Browser example:
```js
console.log(document.title);
```
Node.js example:
```js
console.log(process.version);
```
The first example requires a browser document; the second requires Node.js. Code that uses only standard language features is generally easier to share between environments.

subTopic.name: Client-side vs server-side JavaScript
subTopic.notes:
Client-side JavaScript executes in the user's browser. It handles interface behavior, DOM updates, input interactions, and requests to backend services. Server-side JavaScript executes in a server runtime such as Node.js and commonly handles routing, authentication, business rules, database access, and API responses.

Typical request flow:
1. The browser sends an HTTP request.
2. The server validates the request and performs authorized business logic.
3. The server may query a database.
4. The server returns a response, often JSON.
5. The browser updates the interface.

Never place secrets such as database credentials or private API keys in client-side code: users can inspect downloaded JavaScript. Enforce authorization and validate untrusted input on the server even if the client already performs validation.

subTopic.name: JavaScript's role in modern web development
subTopic.notes:
JavaScript is a core technology of interactive web applications. It can control UI state, respond to events, fetch data, validate user input, and coordinate components. Frameworks and libraries such as React, Vue, and Angular build abstractions on top of JavaScript; they do not replace the language.

Common application areas:
- Frontend interfaces and single-page applications.
- Backend APIs and server-rendered applications.
- Real-time features using WebSockets.
- Build tooling, testing, automation, and command-line utilities.
- Desktop and mobile applications through suitable runtimes/frameworks.

A strong developer should understand the underlying language—scope, closures, objects, promises, modules, and the event loop—rather than relying only on framework APIs.

subTopic.name: How JavaScript works with HTML and CSS
JavaScript engines: V8, SpiderMonkey, JavaScriptCore
subTopic.notes:
A JavaScript engine parses, compiles, and executes JavaScript. Different environments use different engines:
- V8 is used by Chromium-based browsers and Node.js.
- SpiderMonkey is used by Firefox.
- JavaScriptCore (also known as JSC) is used by Safari and other WebKit-based environments.

Engines implement ECMAScript and optimize code at runtime. They commonly parse source into an internal representation, execute or compile it, and use runtime feedback to optimize frequently executed code. Garbage collection manages memory used by JavaScript objects.

Engine choice can affect performance characteristics and the timing of feature support, but standards-compliant code should behave consistently. Test applications in the browsers and runtime versions you intend to support.

subTopic.name: Interpreted, compiled, and JIT-compiled execution
subTopic.notes:
JavaScript is often described as interpreted, but modern engines use a combination of techniques. An engine parses source code, checks syntax, creates internal representations, and may execute bytecode or compile code to machine instructions. Just-in-time (JIT) compilation can optimize frequently executed functions using runtime information.

High-level stages:
1. Parsing: source text is checked and converted into syntax structures.
2. Compilation/execution: the engine produces an executable representation.
3. Optimization: frequently used code may be optimized.
4. Deoptimization: assumptions may be revised if runtime behavior changes.

Developers usually do not control these stages directly. Write clear code and measure actual bottlenecks with profiling tools rather than assuming that a particular syntax is always faster.

subTopic.name: Adding JavaScript to HTML: inline, internal, and external
subTopic.notes:
JavaScript can be included in HTML in three common ways.

Inline event-handler attribute (generally avoid for maintainability):
```html
<button onclick="alert('Hello')">Click</button>
```

Internal script:
```html
<script>
  console.log("Page script");
</script>
```

External script:
```html
<script src="./app.js" defer></script>
```
External files are usually preferred because they separate concerns, can be cached, and are easier to test and maintain. Avoid inline handlers in modern applications; attach listeners from a script file instead. When using external scripts, consider loading behavior (`defer`, `async`, or `type="module"`) and ensure the file path is correct.

subTopic.name: The script tag: async, defer, and module
subTopic.notes:
The `<script>` element controls when an external script is fetched and executed.

- Default script: parsing pauses while the script is fetched and executed.
- `defer`: downloads in parallel with HTML parsing and executes after parsing, preserving document order. Deferred scripts run before `DOMContentLoaded`.
- `async`: downloads in parallel and executes as soon as ready; execution order is not guaranteed. Best for independent scripts.
- `type="module"`: loads an ES module, uses module scope and strict mode, and is deferred by default.

Examples:
```html
<script src="app.js" defer></script>
<script src="analytics.js" async></script>
<script type="module" src="main.js"></script>
```
Use `defer` for scripts that depend on the parsed DOM and need predictable order. Use `async` only when scripts do not depend on one another or on a particular execution order.

subTopic.name: Using browser DevTools and the Console
Setting up a code editor
subTopic.notes:
A code editor provides syntax highlighting, navigation, integrated terminals, debugging, and extensions. Visual Studio Code is a common choice for JavaScript development.

Basic setup:
1. Install a current editor release.
2. Open the project folder rather than editing isolated files.
3. Enable JavaScript/TypeScript language support.
4. Add formatting and linting tools when the project needs consistent style.
5. Use the integrated terminal to run project commands.

Recommended habits:
- Keep source files inside a clear project directory.
- Use meaningful filenames and consistent naming conventions.
- Save work in version control (Git).
- Avoid installing extensions without checking their publisher and permissions.
The editor assists development but does not replace understanding JavaScript or the runtime.

subTopic.name: Running JavaScript in the browser console
subTopic.notes:
The browser Console can execute JavaScript directly in the context of the currently open page. It is useful for experimenting with expressions, inspecting DOM elements, testing API calls, and diagnosing errors.

Examples:
```js
2 + 3
document.title
document.querySelector("h1")?.textContent
```
The console retains a history of commands in many browsers. Variables declared with `let` or `const` may behave differently when redeclared across separate console submissions, depending on the browser's console environment.

Use the Console for quick experiments, but move reusable code into source files and test it as part of the application. Be cautious when pasting code from untrusted sources into a console because it runs with the privileges of the current page.

subTopic.name: Creating an HTML page linked to a JavaScript file
subTopic.notes:
An HTML page can load an external JavaScript file using the `src` attribute of a script element. Project structure: ```text my-project/ index.html app.js ``` `index.html`: ```html JavaScript Demo

Welcome

``` `app.js`: ```js const heading = document.querySelector("#heading"); heading.textContent = "JavaScript is connected!"; ``` The relative path must match the file location. `defer` lets the browser parse the document before executing the script. Check the Console and Network panel if the script fails to load.

subTopic.name: Installing and using Node.js and npm
subTopic.notes:
Node.js is a JavaScript runtime that allows JavaScript to execute outside the browser. npm is the package manager commonly distributed with Node.js; it installs dependencies and runs project scripts.

Verify installation:
```bash
node --version
npm --version
```
Create a project manifest:
```bash
npm init -y
```
Install a dependency:
```bash
npm install express
```
Install a development-only tool:
```bash
npm install --save-dev eslint
```
`package.json` records project metadata, scripts, and dependency ranges; `package-lock.json` records a reproducible dependency tree. Use a supported Node.js LTS release for most projects, and review packages before installing them.

subTopic.name: Running JavaScript files with Node.js
subTopic.notes:
Node.js executes JavaScript files from a terminal. Save code in a `.js` file, open a terminal in its directory, and run it with `node`.

Example `app.js`:
```js
const user = "Anshika";
console.log(`Hello, ${user}!`);
```

Run:
```bash
node app.js
```
Node.js provides globals and modules that are not available in a normal browser page. For example, `process` exposes process information, while filesystem access is available through Node's `fs` module.

If Node reports that a module cannot be found, check the import path and whether the dependency is installed. If the command is not recognized, verify that Node.js is installed and that its executable directory is on the system PATH.

subTopic.name: Using the VS Code debugger
subTopic.notes:
The VS Code debugger lets you pause execution, inspect values, and step through JavaScript code. For Node.js, open the project folder, select Run and Debug, and create or choose a suitable launch configuration. For browser code, use the browser debugging integration or the browser's built-in Sources panel.

Typical workflow:
1. Open the file containing the suspected problem.
2. Click beside a line number to set a breakpoint.
3. Start the debugger.
4. Reproduce the behavior.
5. Inspect variables and the call stack.
6. Step over, into, or out of functions.
7. Resume execution after identifying the issue.

A breakpoint pauses execution at a chosen location. Use conditional breakpoints when a problem occurs only for particular inputs. Remove temporary breakpoints when debugging is complete.

subTopic.name: Breakpoints, watch expressions, and call stack
subTopic.notes:
Breakpoints pause a program so you can inspect its state. A watch expression is evaluated while paused, allowing you to monitor a variable or expression. The call stack shows the chain of active function calls that led to the current execution point.

Debugger controls:
- Continue: resume until the next breakpoint.
- Step over: execute the current line without entering called functions.
- Step into: enter the function being called.
- Step out: finish the current function and return to its caller.
- Restart: rerun the debug session.

Example watch expressions might be `items.length`, `user.name`, or `total > limit`. Watch expressions should be side-effect-free; avoid expressions that mutate application state. The call stack is especially useful for tracing unexpected function calls and locating the origin of an exception.

subTopic.name: Reading console output and error messages
subTopic.notes:
Console messages help identify runtime behavior and failures. Read the complete message, note the error type, and inspect the file and line/column location shown in the stack trace.

Common error categories:
- `SyntaxError`: source code cannot be parsed.
- `ReferenceError`: code refers to an unavailable identifier.
- `TypeError`: an operation is invalid for the value's type.
- `RangeError`: a value is outside an allowed range.

Example:
```js
const user = null;
console.log(user.name); // TypeError
```
Debug systematically: reproduce the issue, read the first relevant stack frame in your code, inspect the values involved, and isolate the smallest failing case. Do not simply suppress errors with empty `catch` blocks; handle failures meaningfully and preserve useful diagnostic information.

subTopic.name: Formatting and linting with Prettier and ESLint
subTopic.notes:
Prettier is an opinionated code formatter; ESLint analyzes JavaScript for suspicious patterns, likely bugs, and configurable style rules. They serve different purposes and are commonly used together.

Install locally:
```bash
npm install --save-dev prettier eslint
```
Example formatting command:
```bash
npx prettier --write .
```
Example lint command (after configuring ESLint):
```bash
npx eslint .
```
Prettier handles layout such as indentation, quotes, and line wrapping. ESLint can flag issues such as unused variables, accidental assignments, or problematic patterns. Configure both at project level and run them consistently in development or CI. Avoid relying on formatting rules to detect logic errors; tests and code review are still required.

subTopic.name: Basic project structure and file organization
subTopic.notes:
A clear project structure separates application responsibilities and makes code easier to navigate. The exact layout depends on project size and tooling, but a small browser project might use:

```text
project/
  index.html
  src/
    main.js
    styles.css
    components/
    utils/
  tests/
  package.json
  README.md
```

Good practices:
- Group files by feature or responsibility.
- Keep reusable helpers separate from UI-specific logic.
- Use descriptive names and consistent casing.
- Keep generated output and dependencies (such as `dist/` and `node_modules/`) out of source control when appropriate.
- Document setup and run commands in `README.md`.

Avoid creating excessive folders for a tiny project. Refactor the structure as the application grows and keep module boundaries understandable.

6.name: React Js
6.desc: Learn to build modern web applications using React.js, from your first component to advanced application architecture. Understand how components, state, hooks, routing, and API integration work together to create dynamic, reusable, and maintainable user interfaces.

subTopic.name: What is React.js ?
subTopic.notes: React is a JavaScript library for building component-based user interfaces. It describes UI as a function of data; state or props changes trigger rendering, while React updates the necessary DOM nodes.

subTopic.name: Component Based Architecture
subTopic.notes: Split the interface into small, focused components with explicit inputs and responsibilities. A component owns its presentation and behavior; compose components into larger screens rather than building one monolithic page.

subTopic.name: Class Vs Component Based Architecture
subTopic.notes: Split the interface into small, focused components with explicit inputs and responsibilities. A component owns its presentation and behavior; compose components into larger screens rather than building one monolithic page.

subTopic.name: Reusability and composition
subTopic.notes: Design a component around a clear responsibility and configurable props. Reuse should reduce duplication without creating an overly generic component with many unrelated options.

subTopic.name: Understanding React and React DOM
subTopic.notes: The `react` package provides component and Hook APIs; `react-dom` connects React to the browser DOM. In modern apps, `createRoot` from `react-dom/client` mounts the application.

subTopic.name: React's role in a modern application
subTopic.notes: Understand react's role in a modern application as part of Introduction to React.js. Know its purpose, the React API or browser behavior involved, when it is appropriate, and the trade-offs it introduces. Apply it in a small component, handle edge cases, and verify the result through observable UI behavior.

subTopic.name: Setting Up a React Project
subTopic.notes: Create a project with a tool such as Vite, install dependencies, and run the development server. Understand `src`, `public`, `package.json`, scripts, entry point and production build; keep reusable UI in components.

subTopic.name: JSX — JavaScript XML
Basics of Component
subTopic.notes: A function component is a JavaScript function that returns JSX. Component names start with a capital letter and components should be pure: same props and state should produce the same UI.

subTopic.name: Parent and child components
subTopic.notes: A parent renders a child as JSX and passes data or callbacks through props. Data normally flows downward; a child requests changes by calling a callback supplied by its parent.

subTopic.name: Component nesting
subTopic.notes: Build a component tree by rendering components inside other components. Keep nesting understandable, extract repeated or complex sections, and avoid defining component functions inside another component because that can reset state.

subTopic.name: Reusable UI components
subTopic.notes: Design a component around a clear responsibility and configurable props. Reuse should reduce duplication without creating an overly generic component with many unrelated options.

subTopic.name: Component Composition
subTopic.notes: Build complex interfaces by combining smaller components through props and `children`. Prefer composition and clear boundaries over inheritance or giant components with many conditional branches.

subTopic.name: What are props?
subTopic.notes: Props are read-only inputs passed from a parent to a child. They can contain strings, numbers, objects, arrays, functions or JSX; never mutate props inside the receiving component.

subTopic.name: Passing props from parent to child
subTopic.notes: Pass values as JSX attributes and receive them in the child. Use callbacks as props when a child needs to notify its parent; keep the source of truth in the component that owns the data.

subTopic.name: Accessing props through function parameters
subTopic.notes: A function component receives one props object. Read fields with `props.title` or destructure them in the parameter list; destructuring improves readability but does not change the data-flow model.

subTopic.name: Destructuring props
subTopic.notes: A function component receives one props object. Read fields with `props.title` or destructure them in the parameter list; destructuring improves readability but does not change the data-flow model.

subTopic.name: Conditional props
subTopic.notes: Pass different prop values based on application state, or omit optional props when appropriate. Define sensible defaults and document expected types so a component behaves predictably.

subTopic.name: Passing JSX through the children prop
Props versus state
subTopic.notes: Props are supplied by a parent and are read-only to the child; state is owned by a component and updated with a setter/reducer. Derive values from props/state instead of duplicating them unnecessarily.

subTopic.name: Prop Drilling
subTopic.notes: Prop drilling passes data through intermediate components that do not use it. It is acceptable for short, clear trees; for widely shared state consider composition, Context or a state library.

subTopic.name: Basic about rendering
subTopic.notes: Understand basic about rendering as part of Rendering Lists and Conditional UI. Know its purpose, the React API or browser behavior involved, when it is appropriate, and the trade-offs it introduces. Apply it in a small component, handle edge cases, and verify the result through observable UI behavior.

subTopic.name: Client side rendering vs Server side rendering
subTopic.notes: CSR builds the UI in the browser after JavaScript loads; SSR generates HTML on the server and hydrates it in the browser. SSR can improve initial content and SEO but adds server complexity; choose based on UX, data and deployment needs.

subTopic.name: Conditional rendering with if
subTopic.notes: Use ordinary JavaScript control flow before the return when branches are substantial. Return different JSX for loading, error, empty and success states; ensure every path returns an intentional result.

subTopic.name: Conditional rendering with ternary expressions
subTopic.notes:
Use `condition ? <A /> : <B />` for a concise two-way choice. Keep nested ternaries limited; extract complex conditions into named variables or helper components.

Example (JSX):
```jsx
return isLoggedIn ? <Dashboard /> : <Login />;
```

subTopic.name: Logical AND (&&) rendering
subTopic.notes:
Use `condition && <Component />` when content should appear only for a truthy condition. Beware that `0 && ...` renders `0`; use `count > 0` or an explicit boolean.

Example (JSX):
```jsx
{unreadCount > 0 && <Badge count={unreadCount} />}
```

subTopic.name: React event handlers

subTopic.name: What state means in React

subTopic.name: State versus ordinary variables

subTopic.name: What causes a component to render

subTopic.name: React reconciliation

subTopic.name: Index routes

subTopic.name: Controlled vs uncontrolled components
subTopic.notes:
A controlled input receives its current value from React state and reports edits through `onChange`. React is the source of truth; set the value and update it synchronously in the handler to keep typing responsive.

Example (JSX):
```jsx
const [name, setName] = useState("");
<input value={name} onChange={e => setName(e.target.value)} />
```

subTopic.name: Keys and reconciliation
subTopic.notes: Reconciliation compares the newly returned element tree with the previous one to determine updates. Element type and keys influence identity; stable keys help React preserve the correct item state across list changes.

subTopic.name: useEffect dependencies and cleanup
useMemo vs useCallback vs React.memo
subTopic.notes: Memoization avoids repeating work or changing references when inputs are unchanged; it is an optimization, not a correctness mechanism. Measure first, understand dependency equality, and remove memoization that adds complexity without benefit.

subTopic.name: Context API vs Redux
subTopic.notes: Context makes a value available to descendants without manually passing it through every intermediate component. Create it with `createContext`, provide a value above consumers, and read it with `useContext`.

subTopic.name: Client-side rendering vs server-side rendering
subTopic.notes: CSR builds the UI in the browser after JavaScript loads; SSR generates HTML on the server and hydrates it in the browser. SSR can improve initial content and SEO but adds server complexity; choose based on UX, data and deployment needs.

subTopic.name: Suspense and lazy loading
subTopic.notes:
